textes:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Personalized 3D Asset Generation via Diffusion-based Identity Fusion
PROPOSAL: Train a 3D diffusion model on a large synthetic dataset of objects with diverse appearances, and then fine-tune it using a small number of example images of the specific subject. Introduce an identity fusion mechanism to combine the learned 3D shape and appearance, and adapt the 3D model's diffusion process to preserve the subject's identity across viewpoints.
CONTROLS: Baseline: a vanilla 3D diffusion model; Ablation: identity fusion module removed.
COST: 5000
PREDICTION: The proposed approach successfully preserves the identity of the subject, achieving improved accuracy and personalization in 3D asset generation, but may struggle with cases where the input images have significant pose or viewpoint variations, or when the subject's appearance is highly distinct from the training dataset.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comparative Study of Image-to-3D and Video-to-4D Generation for Personalization
PROPOSAL: Evaluate and compare the performance of state-of-the-art 3D and 4D generative models, trained on synthetic datasets, in achieving personalization for a range of subjects and viewpoints. Assess the robustness of each generation approach to variations in input data, output views, and the realism of generated content.
CONTROLS: Baseline: publicly available 3D and 4D generation models; Ablation: compare performance with/without input data augmentation (image/video noise, blur, etc.).
COST: 12000
PREDICTION: The comparison highlights the strengths and limitations of image-to-3D and video-to-4D generation, showing that video data often leads to more consistent appearance and motion across viewpoints, but can be sensitive to pose and viewpoint changes in the input video, while 3D generation tends to be more robust but suffers from upper-body imagery hallucinations.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: (REVISED) Comparative Study of Image-to-3D and Video-to-4D Generation for Personalization
PROPOSAL: (REVISED to include an analysis of methods for handling subject identity ambiguity) Evaluate and compare the performance of state-of-the-art 3D and 4D generative models, trained on synthetic datasets, in achieving personalization for a range of subjects and viewpoints, including ambiguity cases (e.g., identical subjects under different poses or lighting). Assess the robustness of each generation approach to variations in input data, output views, and the realism of generated content.
CONTROLS: Baseline: publicly available 3D and 4D generation models; Ablations: compare performance with/without input data augmentation (image/video noise, blur, etc.) and with/without identity ambiguity handling methods (e.g., deep clustering, subject hashing).
COST: 12000
PREDICTION: The comparison highlights the strengths and limitations of image-to-3D and video-to-4D generation, showing that video data often leads to more consistent appearance and motion across viewpoints, but can be sensitive to pose and viewpoint changes in the input video, while 3D generation tends to be more robust but suffers from upper-body imagery hallucinations.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Exploring 3D Shape and Appearance Alignment for Improved Personalization
PROPOSAL: (REVISED proposal 2) Develop and evaluate a novel 3D shape and appearance alignment technique that combines the strengths of both image-to-3D and video-to-4D generation approaches. This technique will learn to align the 3D shape and appearance of the generated asset with the input image or video, to improve personalization and reduce hallucinations across viewpoints.
CONTROLS: Baseline: publicly available 3D and 4D generation models; Ablations: compare performance with/without the proposed alignment technique and with/without different alignment methods (e.g., shape-texture alignment, pose-based alignment).
COST: 18000
PREDICTION: The proposed approach significantly improves personalization, reducing hallucinations and improving realism across viewpoints, but may require careful tuning of alignment parameters to avoid overfitting to the specific subject or dataset.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Augmenting 3D Models with Temporally-consistent Identity Features for Improved Personalization
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel technique to augment 3D models with temporally-consistent identity features, learned from sequential input data (e.g., videos). These features will be incorporated into the 3D model's architecture to improve personalization and preserve subject identity across views and time.
CONTROLS: Baseline: publicly available 3D generation models; Ablations: compare performance with/without the proposed temporal identity features and with/without different feature extraction methods (e.g., convolutional LSTM, attention-based features).
COST: 25000
PREDICTION: The proposed approach significantly improves temporal consistency and personalization, reducing drift and hallucinations across views and time, but may require careful design of the feature extraction architecture to avoid overfitting to the specific subject or dataset.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Batch Size and Data Augmentation on Personalized 3D Generation
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effects of batch size and data augmentation on the performance of personalized 3D generation models, using a systematic study of different batch sizes and data augmentation techniques. This will help to identify optimal settings for future experiments and improve the overall quality of generated assets.
CONTROLS: Baseline: publicly available 3D generation models; Ablations: compare performance with different batch sizes and data augmentation techniques.
COST: 35000
PREDICTION: The study reveals that optimal batch sizes and data augmentation techniques significantly improve personalized 3D generation, but may interact with other hyperparameters (e.g., learning rate, number of iterations) in complex ways, requiring careful hyperparameter tuning to achieve best results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Personalized 4D Generation via Video-conditioned 3D Diffusion Models with Temporal Attention
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel video-conditioned 3D diffusion model that incorporates temporal attention to align with the video sequence, allowing for more accurate and personalized 4D generation. This approach will be evaluated on a range of videos with different subjects, poses, and lighting conditions.
CONTROLS: Baseline: publicly available 4D generation models; Ablations: compare performance with/without temporal attention and with/without different attention mechanisms (e.g., attention-based convolution, recurrent attention).
COST: 42000
PREDICTION: The proposed approach significantly improves personalized 4D generation, capturing the nuances of subject appearance and motion across views and time, but may require careful tuning of attention parameters to avoid overemphasis on specific aspects of the video sequence.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Subject-Directed Diffusion for Personalized 3D Generation
PROPOSAL: Train and evaluate the extension of the Diffusion Models for Images to Images (Dm3) framework to the 3D domain, specifically using a subject-directed diffusion approach, where the image-to-3D generator is conditioned on a subject token learned from a text-to-image model. We will test this method using the House3D dataset for indoor scenes and DomainBed dataset for personalized outdoor scenes.
CONTROLS: Compare against state-of-the-art image-to-3D methods such as Pix2Vox++, Pix2Vox refiner, and Laplacian Pyramid Reconstruction; also provide an ablation study for the effectiveness of the subject token and the subject-directed diffusion method.
COST: 120
PREDICTION: Our method should outperform existing state-of-the-art methods in identity preservation and subject-specific fidelity, especially in novel views. However, achieving high-fidelity generation for unseen viewpoints and maintaining appearance consistency without severe hallucination will be challenging.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Conditional Subject Embeddings for Identity-Preserving 4D Generation
PROPOSAL: Develop a 4D generation framework that uses conditional subject embeddings learned from a multimodal fusion of text and video inputs. We will incorporate conditional subject embeddings into a pre-trained multi-view diffusion model, allowing it to generate novel views that are consistent with the observed identity. Evaluate our approach using a pre-recorded video dataset (e.g., EPIC-Kitchens) for 4D scenarios.
CONTROLS: Compare to existing 4D generation methods such as multi-view diffusion models and video2mesh++ with a human editing module, and provide an ablation study to investigate the effectiveness of different modalities (text, video, or both) for subject embedding learning.
COST: 180
PREDICTION: Our conditional subject embeddings method should outperform existing 4D generation methods in preserving identity and achieving consistent appearance across novel views, especially in dynamic scenes. However, capturing complex viewpoints and occlusion patterns may pose difficulties.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unsupervised Personalization through Self-Supervised I2M Training
PROPOSAL: Employ an unsupervised self-supervised learning approach, where we train an image-to-model (I2M) network to generate both 3D and 4D representations of an object from a single image or video. The network will be trained in an unsupervised manner, encouraging adaptation to a given object by minimizing reconstruction losses between noisy input images and the generated model. We will evaluate our approach using synthetic datasets generated for both 3D and 4D scenarios.
CONTROLS: Compare to state-of-the-art image-to-3D and video-to-4D methods with ablation studies on the effects of model input noise levels and image/video distortion.
COST: 240
PREDICTION: Our self-supervised I2M method should improve upon existing personalized 3D/4D generation approaches by learning adaptations directly from input images/videos without requiring explicit supervision or subject tokens. However, ensuring the quality of generated models and adapting to novel objects may be challenging.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Regularization via Diversity-Preservation Constraints
PROPOSAL: Explore the introduction of diversity-preservation constraints to regularize the learning process of subject-directed diffusion and conditional subject embeddings methods to prevent over-specialization to a single object instance. This can be achieved by forcing the network to generate diverse outputs when faced with the same input, thus enforcing the generalizability of learned representations.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the effectiveness of proposed constraints in cases with both over-similar and diverse object populations, and provide performance comparisons with and without diversity constraints.
COST: 360
PREDICTION: Incorporating diversity-preservation constraints should positively impact both subject-directed diffusion and conditional subject embeddings, generalizing learned representations to unseen instances while preserving model's adaptability and robustness. However, tuning constraint strength and handling over-diversification will require delicate balance and potentially decrease performance in specific task settings.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Revised Conditional Subject Embeddings for Identity-Preserving 4D Generation
PROPOSAL: We introduce a novel Gated Oscillator-like Attention (GOA) mechanism that adapts the conditional subject embeddings based on dynamic attention to the input video. The GOA alternates between attending to local, distinctive features and globally coherent information, thus capturing both specific and generalizable information in the video.
CONTROLS: Compare to state-of-the-art 4D generation methods and further investigate the impact of GOA on personalization performance by ablating the mechanism.
COST: 210
PREDICTION: Incorporating GOA should improve the robustness and expressiveness of conditional subject embeddings in 4D generation tasks, especially in capturing nuanced aspects of object behavior. However, over-reliance on specific features might occur and should be mitigated.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Step Personalization through Interleaved Optimization
PROPOSAL: Propose a multi-step personalization approach, where the model iteratively refines the input video using interleaved optimization and cycle-consistency loss, offering a more adaptive and generalizable method for personalization.
CONTROLS: Compare with existing personalized 3D/4D generation methods and evaluate the performance of interleaved optimization in handling various levels of prior knowledge or domain shift.
COST: 540
PREDICTION: This approach should allow for step-wise iterations and gearing improvements in handling the output iteratively allowing better feasibility, but achieving correct convergence and preventing overfitting can be notoriously demanding in terms of computational resources.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Domain Knowledge for Improved Personalization
PROPOSAL: Develop a hierarchical framework that incorporates domain knowledge in the form of low-level visual attributes (e.g., texture, color) and high-level semantic attributes (e.g., scene understanding, object recognition). This framework will enable more accurate and detailed personalization by leveraging domain-specific knowledge to constrain and refine model predictions.
CONTROLS: Compare to state-of-the-art personalized 3D/4D generation methods and investigate the impact of hierarchical domain knowledge on performance in various domain shift scenarios.
COST: 840
PREDICTION: Incorporating hierarchical domain knowledge should significantly improve personalization performance by guiding the model towards producing more accurate and detailed predictions, but handling semantic attribute shifting and incorporating human-in-the-loop feedback may be challenging.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transfer Learning from Pre-Trained 3D Scene Understanding Models
PROPOSAL: Explore the effectiveness of transfer learning from pre-trained 3D scene understanding models (e.g., scene graph prediction, layout estimation) to improve personalized 3D/4D generation. This involves fine-tuning these pre-trained models on small-scale subject datasets to capture subject-specific knowledge and then combining the learned features with personalized generation techniques.
CONTROLS: Compare to state-of-the-art personalized generation methods and evaluate the transfer learning performance in various domain adaptation scenarios.
COST: 1080
PREDICTION: Transfer learning from pre-trained 3D scene understanding models should enable more accurate and efficient personalized generation by leveraging prior knowledge of scene understanding, but addressing the mismatch between pre-trained and subject-specific knowledge and overcoming catastrophic forgetting will be necessary.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analog-Digit Dual-Path Generation for Semi-Supervised Personalization
PROPOSAL: Introduce an analog-digit dual-path generation framework, where the model generates both high-resolution, detailed 3D/4D models and lower-resolution, semantic representations. This framework will enable semi-supervised personalization by allowing the model to learn from a combination of labeled and unlabeled data, leveraging the strengths of both analog and digital representations.
CONTROLS: Compare to state-of-the-art personalized generation methods and investigate the impact of analog-digit dual-path generation on performance in semi-supervised and unsupervised learning settings.
COST: 1440
PREDICTION: The analog-digit dual-path generation framework should significantly improve personalization performance by allowing the model to leverage both high-resolution and semantic information, but addressing the potential trade-offs between detail and semantics, and ensuring efficient learning from both labeled and unlabeled data will be required.

This modification is designed to more accurately extract and utilize relevant features from videos, thereby enhancing the preservation of identity in 4D scenarios.
CONTROLS: Retain ablations for multimodal fusion and incorporate additional comparisons with and without vessel optimization and attention mechanisms.
COST: unchanged at 540

By revising the existing proposal, we can build upon the strengths of the initial idea while introducing novel improvements. This modification aims to effectively adapt conditional subject embeddings to better suit the demands of 4D generation, making it a compelling addition to the current set of proposals.

TITLE: Revised Conditional Subject Embeddings for Identity-Preserving 4D Generation
PROPOSAL: We introduce a novel Gated Oscillator-like Attention (GOA) mechanism that adapts the conditional subject embeddings based on dynamic attention to the input video. The GOA alternates between attending to local, distinctive features and globally coherent information, thus capturing both specific and generalizable information in the video.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Cascade Performance with Existing Training-Free Self-Speculative Decoding Methods
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the performance of Lookahead decoding and SWIFT as single draft models in a cascade with a retrieval-based statistical drafter in three scenarios: LLM inference acceleration, multi-turn conversation, and machine translation. We will measure the walltime improvement and compare it to standard speculative decoding with a retrieval-based drafter alone. Evaluated models will include Llama, Mixtral and Qwen on the XSum dataset.

PREDICTION: Lookahead decoding will achieve better walltime improvement than SWIFT decoding in machine translation tasks, and moderate improvements in LLM inference acceleration. SWIFT decoding might fall short of standard speculative decoding in all scenarios, limiting the appeal of the cascade approach despite the potential of Lookahead decoding.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Cascade Scheduling for Training-Free Self-Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: Develop a scheduler that adaptively adjusts the draft length and the number of cascade rounds for the Lookahead decoding and SWIFT based cascade in scenarios from Turn 1. We will use a reinforcement learning approach to decide when to switch between draft models and how many tokens each should draft, and use the walltime improvement metric to evaluate the performance of the scheduler. Evaluated models will also include Llama, Mixtral and Qwen on the XSum, MS MARCO and Natural Questions datasets. 
CONTROLS: Baseline cascade with fixed hyperparameters, Lookahead decoding, SWIFT decoding, reinforcement learning-based adaptive scheduling
COST: 7200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Adaptive scheduling leads to a median walltime improvement of 15%, with up to 30% reductions observed in machine translation and summarization tasks, validating the potential of adaptively choosing the cascade configuration. However, the reinforcement learning-based scheduler may require in excess of 4 days to converge on optimal parameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Performance of Existing Training-Free Self-Speculative Decoding Methods
PROPOSAL: Experimentally evaluate the performance of training-free self-speculative decoding methods (e.g., Lookahead decoding and SWIFT) in constructing an effective cascade of draft models above retrieval-based drafting methods for lossless, on-the-fly speculative decoding on real-world benchmarks (e.g., Multi30K for machine translation, aristo for question answering, and IROhSum for summarization).
CONTROLS: Compare with standard speculative decoding with a retrieval-based drafter (e.g., prompt lookup decoding) and ablate by removing or modifying different stages of the cascade.
COST: 5000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Training-free self-speculative decoding methods can be effectively used to construct an efficient cascade, especially when combined with a cheap retrieval-based drafter, and can achieve better speedup than using each method individually, while also being more computationally efficient than training separate draft models. However, the results may degrade on more complex tasks or with large input sequences.

PROPOSAL: Conduct experiments on using Lookahead decoding and SWIFT to build an effective cascade of draft models above retrieval-based drafting methods for lossless, on-the-fly speculative decoding. Still much to explore.

PROPOSAL: Experiment with Lookahead decoding as the self-speculative method for a shallow cascade of three draft models, including a full-speed target model, to verify whether a basic self-speculative cascade (SSC) can outperform standard speculative decoding with a single retrieval-based statistical drafter.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Uncertainty-Aware Reward Model with Bayesian Calibration
PROPOSAL: This proposal aims to develop a reward model that estimates the absolute quality of a response while incorporating the uncertainty and annotator disagreement present in preference data. We propose to leverage Bayesian neural networks to learn a calibrated score that quantifies the confidence in each response. During training, we will use a probabilistic variant of the Bradley-Terry objective to maximize the expected score margin between chosen and rejected responses. At inference time, our model will produce a distribution over the possible scores, allowing us to compute the mean and standard deviation of the response quality. We will also investigate the usage of a few pointwise quality annotations to calibrate the model, but only as an auxiliary task during training, and consider evaluating model confidence for a new domain through Bayesian model averaging.
CONTROLS: We will compare our approach to both discriminative and generative baseline models, including the Skywork-Reward and InternLM2-Reward, and evaluate our model on a Best-of-N chatbot response quality evaluation task, the MAVERICK dataset, and also experiment with Θ600-20k (20,000 annotated examples) dataset, which involves assisting users with simple math problems.
COST: 12000 
PREDICTION: Our model is expected to outperform discriminative models in terms of ranking accuracy, but at the cost of additional computational complexity. We anticipate that the Bayesian calibration will help reduce overfitting and improve the robustness of the model to annotator disagreement. However, this approach may also struggle with poorly calibrated models and unstable Bayesian updates.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adversarially Regularized Calibration for Reward Models
PROPOSAL: To address the challenge of calibrating the reward model using only pointwise quality annotations, we propose to develop an adversarial regularization framework that encourages the model to generate calibrated scores. We will add a second model, the "calibrator," that predicts the true quality label from the reward model's output and a corresponding quality annotation. The calibrator will be optimized using a KL divergence loss between the predicted and true label distributions. To protect the reward model from over-fitting to the calibration task, we will use an adversarial loss between the reward model and the calibrator, where the reward model aims to deceive the calibrator and produce non-calibrated outputs.
CONTROLS: This approach will be compared to the Uncertainty-Aware Reward Model with Bayesian Calibration (Proposal 1) and also to a baseline where the quality annotations are used to augment the training data for the Bradley-Terry objective. Evaluation will be performed on the same tasks as Proposal 1, including the MAVERICK dataset and Θ600-20k dataset.
COST: 18000 
PREDICTION: We anticipate that this approach will lead to more accurate and calibrated reward models, as the adversarial regularization will improve the robustness of the model to pointwise quality annotations. However, this method may struggle with the optimization of the calibrator and the reward model simultaneously, and the adversarial loss may compromise the ranking accuracy of the reward model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Self-Supervised Quality Annotation Calibration
PROPOSAL: Given that high-quality annotations are expensive to acquire, we propose a self-supervised calibration method for reward models that relies on weak supervision from the unlabeled responses themselves. We will use a variational autoencoder (VAE) to obtain a latent representation of the responses, and then train a scaler that estimates the true quality label from this representation. The scaler will be optimized using a pseudo-labeling strategy, where the VAE-generated latent representations serve as a proxy for the true quality labels. We will evaluate the effectiveness of this method on models with varying levels of quality annotation data and compare its performance to Proposal 1 and Proposal 2.
CONTROLS: Experiments will involve varying the amount of high-quality annotations from 0% to 10% of the total dataset, training the VAE using a reconstruction loss, and comparing the results to a scenario with full access to high-quality annotations.
COST: 27000 
PREDICTION: This approach may yield impressive results, especially when there are few high-quality annotations, due to the large pool of unlabeled data. However, there is a risk that the VAE-generated labels may not always be accurate, which would negatively impact the performance of the scaler.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Addressing Calibration-Domain Drift Using Invariant Rewards
PROPOSAL: Given that reward models are often trained on a small, fixed domain and may struggle to adapt to new, unseen domains, we propose to develop a reward model that captures domain-invariant patterns and focuses on the absolute quality of responses. We will leverage contrastive learning to learn representations that distinguish between good and bad responses, regardless of the specific domain. By training the model on multiple domains simultaneously and using a margin-based loss, we aim to reduce the calibration-domain drift and improve the robustness of the model across different settings.
CONTROLS: Experiments will be conducted on a diverse set of domains, including chatbots, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and role-play dialogue. We will compare the performance of our model to the previously proposed approaches on these domains, as well as to a baseline that simply fine-tunes a reward model on a new domain.
COST: 36000 
PREDICTION: This approach may lead to improved domain adaptation and robustness, as the invariant representations are learned across multiple domains. However, the contrastive learning mechanism may struggle to capture the nuances of human preferences and may compromise performance on specific tasks.

We will also investigate the use of Bayesian neural networks and meta-learning to improve the robustness and adaptability of the model.

TITLE: Adversarial Sampling for Efficient Exploration in Reward Model Training
PROPOSAL: We propose an adversarial sampling method to improve the efficiency of reward model training. This method generates a subset of LLM outputs that are likely to be most informative for the reward model, while avoiding redundant or uninformative samples. We use a generative adversarial network (GAN) to model the distribution of LLM outputs and generate a set of "adversarial" samples that are most likely to challenge the reward model's current understanding.
CONTROLS: We compare the proposed adversarial sampling method to traditional random sampling and stratified sampling baselines, using our CalibCritique model as the reward model. We also experiment with different GAN architectures and hyperparameters to optimize the performance of the adversarial sampling method.

PREDICTION: Our results will show that adversarial sampling can significantly improve the efficiency of reward model training, leading to faster convergence and improved performance. However, the method may require careful tuning of hyperparameters and may not generalize well to all LLM architectures and reward models.

This will be achieved by incorporating a small neural network that predicts the calibration constant and conditioning this network on the head outputs. Furthermore, we will also study the impact of training the calibration network to predict a quantity of uncertainty for the outputs of the reward estimation network. We will use an AutoML-like approach to do this.
CONTROLS: We will compare our multi-class reward model to a version without calibration and to a simple baseline that ignores uncertainty.
COST: 189000 
PREDICTION: We expect our multi-class reward model equipped with an automatic calibration mechanism to show improved performance in terms of absolute score accuracy, ranking consistency, and reliability. However, we anticipate that it may require additional computational resources due to the extra neural network in the calibration mechanism.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transductive Transfer of Reward Models to New Domains
PROPOSAL: We will explore the use of transductive transfer learning to adapt our reward models to new domains with limited quality annotations by sharing knowledge across data points. We will leverage the idea of meta-learning to train our reward models in a way that allows them to adapt to new domains without fine-tuning the entire model. This will be achieved by using a set of "advisor" tasks to provide supervision signals for the model.
CONTROLS: We will compare our reward model transferred to a new domain with a model trained from scratch, and a state-of-the-art meta-learning method applied to a discriminator.
COST: 360000 
PREDICTION: We expect our transferred reward model to show improved adaptation to the new domain with limited annotations, and better running times compared to the baseline models. However, we anticipate that it may require careful tuning of hyperparameters due to the complex meta-learning process.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reward Models for Evaluating Chatbot Safety
PROPOSAL: We will develop a reward model specifically designed for evaluating chatbot responses in terms of safety, taking into account factors such as offense, politeness, and adherence to social norms. We will leverage the generated critique output from the LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm and incorporate a human evaluation system to generate positive and negative labels for high-quality safety-critical regions of response candidates. This will enable us to train a reward model to recognize and promote chatbot responses that are safe and respectful.
CONTROLS: We will compare our safety-focused reward model to a version of the probabilistic reward model (proposal 1) and a baseline using HEIST (Handling Extraction and Meaning Inference for Scenario Trees).
COST: 405000 
PREDICTION: We expect our safety-focused reward model to outperform both the probabilistic reward model and the HEIST baseline in terms of direct safety promotion and implicit capabilities modeling measures. However, we anticipate that it may require curated datasets for evaluation of its objects of greatest interest.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Uncertainty-Aware Best-of-N Ranking with Ensemble Mechanisms
PROPOSAL: We will develop an ensemble mechanism that combines multiple instances of the probabilistic reward model (proposal 1) to generate multiple rankings for a batch of responses. This will enable us to capture the uncertainty in human preference judgments and estimate the confidence of each ranking. The ensemble will be trained to optimize a ranking-based loss function, taking into account the specific evaluation metrics used in RLHF, such as Top-1 accuracy and consistency.
CONTROLS: We will compare our ensemble-based ranking system to a single-instance probabilistic reward model, a generative reward model, and a state-of-the-art ranking baseline using combination methods (combining different Picking functions together to balance their individual strengths).
COST: 540000 
PREDICTION: We expect our ensemble-based ranking system to outperform all baseline models in terms of ranking accuracy, Top-1 accuracy, and consistency, while effectively handling the uncertainty of human preference judgments. However, we anticipate that it may require careful tuning of the ensemble architecture and training procedure.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Probabilistic Reward Models with Bounded Scores
REVISED PROPOSAL: We will extend the probabilistic reward model (proposal 1) to better handle the inherent ambiguity of human preference judgments by incorporating an additional neural network that estimates the joint probability of the responses, rather than modeling them independently. This will allow us to capture correlations between responses and estimate the confidence in the rankings more accurately. The joint probability neural network will be conditioned on the features of the individual responses.
CONTROLS: We will compare our revised model to the original probabilistic reward model and a state-of-the-art joint probability model.
COST: 720000 
PREDICTION: We expect our revised probabilistic reward model to outperform the original model in terms of ranking accuracy, Top-1 accuracy, and consistency, by better capturing the complex relationships between responses and improving the confidence in the rankings. However, we anticipate that it may require careful tuning of the joint probability neural network and may be computationally expensive to train.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Horizon Transfer for Reward Models
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the use of multi-horizon transfer learning to adapt reward models to new domains or tasks by transferring knowledge from a source domain (or task) with a different horizon (e.g. a short-horizon transfer from a chatbot response domain to a code generation domain). We will use a multiple-task learning approach to train the reward model on multiple horizons, with the goal of adapting it to a new horizon (task or domain) without fine-tuning.
CONTROLS: We will compare our multi-horizon transfer method to a single-horizon transfer method, a baseline without transfer learning, and a state-of-the-art multi-task learning approach.
COST: 810000 
PREDICTION: We expect our multi-horizon transfer method to outperform baseline models and achieve comparable or better performance than a single-horizon transfer method, especially when adapting to new tasks with very different characteristics. However, we anticipate that it may require large amounts of multi-horizon annotated data and may be challenging to tune due to the multiple horizons involved.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Calibrated Uncertainty Estimation for Reward Models
PROPOSAL: We will explore the use of calibrated uncertainty estimation techniques, such as Bayesian neural networks or Monte Carlo dropout, to provide well-calibrated uncertainty estimates for our reward models. This will enable us to better quantify the confidence of our ranking predictions and adapt to changing environments. We will compare our calibrated uncertainty estimation approach to a baselined model without calibrated uncertainty.
CONTROLS: We will compare our model to a baseline using an inverse temperature scaling parameter and quantify improvement by using expected calibration error (ECE) as our metric.
COST: 1080000 
PREDICTION: We expect our calibrated uncertainty estimation approach to outperform the baseline model in terms of ECE and provide more robust and reliable ranking predictions. However, we anticipate that it may require careful tuning of the distribution over neural network models and may be computationally expensive to train.

TITLE: Evaluating Pairwise Ranking Performance with Quantile-based Discriminative Reward Models
PROPOSAL: We'll investigate the robustness of discriminative reward models with Bradley-Terry objectives by comparing their performance with a variant using quantile regression, where scores are decomposed into multiple quantile-specific scores to capture the uncertainty and ambiguity in preference data. We'll adapt InternLM2-Reward as our baseline and test its performance on multiple response ranking tasks (e.g., LLM-generated responses from different datasets).

PREDICTION: This approach may improve the ranking performance and uncertainty modeling, but struggles in scenarios with extremely high agreement or disagreement among annotators, potentially leading to catastrophic performance degradation.

TITLE: Exploration of Self-Supervised Calibration for Discriminative Reward Models
PROPOSAL: We'll extend the baseline InternLM2-Reward by introducing a self-supervised calibration module, trained to predict the confidence of its own scores. This is particularly useful for scenarios with limited quality annotations. We'll experiment with different calibration metrics, such as Brier score, calibrator architecture, and fitting methods.
CONTROLS: InternLM2-Reward with different levels of calibration difficulty (easy: paired, medium: Best-of-N, hard: saw-tooth calibrator), standard InternLM2-Reward without calibration.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adversarial Training for Reward Model Out-of-Distribution Generalization
PROPOSAL: We'll propose an adversarial training paradigm to enhance the robustness of discriminative reward models for handling out-of-distribution (OOD) preference data. We'll train a discriminator to predict whether the input preference data is OOD, and then use an adversarial self-play approach where the reward model and discriminator engage in a series of games, with the reward model trying to produce utility scores that are indistinguishable from those produced on in-distribution data.
CONTROLS: InternLM2-Reward with OOD data distribution (e.g., shifted preferences), baseline InternLM2-Reward without adversarial training.
COST: 210
PREDICTION: This approach may help the reward model generalize better to unseen preference data, but could also lead to decreased performance on standard preference data due to the increased complexity of the training objective, or increase the risk of mode collapse when the discriminator becomes too strong.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reward Model Grounding with Denoising Autoencoders for Absolute Quality Judgments
PROPOSAL: We'll propose a novel grounding strategy that leverages denoising autoencoders to capture the intrinsic quality of language model responses. By training a denoising autoencoder to recover high-quality responses from noisy or degraded ones, we'll show that the autoencoder can be used as a quality-aware feature extractor to ground the reward model in absolute quality judgments, improving its ability to provide calibrated scores and indication of response quality.
CONTROLS: InternLM2-Reward with denoising autoencoder as quality-aware feature extractor, standard InternLM2-Reward without autoencoder.
COST: 300
PREDICTION: This approach may significantly improve the reward model's ability to capture absolute quality judgments, but could also introduce additional computational overhead during training and testing due to the denoising autoencoder, and may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to balance the trade-offs between quality judgment accuracy and reward model performance.

TITLE: Integration of Generative and Discriminative Reward Model Components
PROPOSAL: We'll investigate an ensemble-based approach that combines the strengths of discriminative and generative reward models. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Role of Annotator Disagreement in Reward Model Performance
PROPOSAL: We'll investigate the impact of annotator disagreement on reward model performance by introducing a novel dataset where humans are asked to provide ratings for the same set of responses multiple times, with varying levels of agreement between annotators. We'll then analyze the effect of annotator agreement on the performance of different reward model variants.
CONTROLS: InternLM2-Reward trained on datasets with varying levels of annotator agreement, baseline InternLM2-Reward trained on datasets with complete annotator agreement.
COST: 480
PREDICTION: This study may provide valuable insights into the impact of annotator disagreement on reward model performance, and potentially lead to improvements in the design of annotation protocols and the development of more robust reward models. However, it may also require significant resources and effort to collect and preprocess the dataset with varying levels of annotator agreement.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Quantifying External and Internal Knowledge Utilization in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
PROPOSAL: We will develop and evaluate a new metric, called Contextualized Intrinsic Consistency (CIC), which measures how well the internal knowledge represented by the LLM's output aligns with the external context provided by the retrieved documents. CIC calculates this consistency by analyzing the LLM's output and the retrieved context through a joint word embedding space and applying a novel procedure using inverse covariance embedding. Specifically, we will use the pre-trained RoBERTa and BART language models, and evaluate CIC on several downstream tasks from the dataset used in the ReDeEP paper, as well as on a few others such as the TREC Carbonate and the DocRED datasets.
CONTROLS: The baseline will be the ReDeEP method and a variety of ablations which use simpler auto-regressive and attention-based models.
COST: 1440
PREDICTION: We expect CIC to outperform ReDeEP in terms of accuracy and robustness across the evaluated datasets, due to its more principled and less heuristic nature. The real-world test of limitations is if CIC will fail on scenarios where the external context retrieved is semantically noisy.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Evaluating Transformer Layer Complexity using Graph Signal Processing
PROPOSAL: We will use Graph Signal Processing (GSP) to analyze and quantify the complexity of different transformer layers within RAG models. Specifically, we will construct a graph where vertices represent tokens, edges represent the transformer's self-attention pattern, and node features represent the model's learned embeddings. We will then apply a set of GSP tools, such as spectral clustering and filtered diffusion, to identify the most complex layers that receive the most attention and concentrate learned information. This can help us understand which layers contribute the most to internal knowledge utilization.
CONTROLS: Abolish attention heads and randomly select few attention layers; report performance of GSP on baseline transformer models.
COST: 360
PREDICTION: This approach should shed light on the transformer layers responsible for internal knowledge utilization, but it may struggle to generalize across diverse RAG models and datasets, and might be computationally intensive.

TITLE: Investigating the Role of Weight Decay in Modeling Internal Knowledge Utilization
PROPOSAL: Inspired by recent observations on the relationship between L2 regularization and knowledge distillation, we will conduct a systematic study on the impact of weight decay on internal knowledge utilization in RAG models. We will modify the model's training process to include weight decay at different magnitudes and monitor the changes in internal knowledge utilization, as measured by the complexity scores obtained from proposal 1. This can help us understand whether and how hyperparameter tuning affects internal knowledge utilization.
CONTROLS: Compare results against models with no weight decay, standard RAG pipelines, and explicit knowledge distillation.

PREDICTION: Our findings might reveal an interplay between weight decay, L2 regularization, and knowledge distillation, leading to a more nuanced understanding of internal knowledge utilization. ACTION: REVISE 6
TITLE: Active Learning for Hallucination Detection with Ranking and Retrieval dataset (AL4HDR)
PROPOSAL: We will leverage the newly proposed ranked retrieval dataset with human-labeled ground truth for active learning. Specifically, we will design an active learning framework using uncertainty sampling and its variants (entropy, margin, and internal consistency) to select the most informative samples for labeling. This framework will take into account both the quality of the document ranking and the human-labeled ground truth. We will then analyze the impact of active learning on hallucination detection models and the efficiency of labeling process.
CONTROLS: Compare against traditional passive learning, study human effort required for annotating selected samples.

PREDICTION: By optimizing the labeling process using active learning, our approach can lead to more accurate hallucination detection models, even with limited labeled data. However, it may require careful tuning of hyperparameters for the uncertainty-based sampling strategy and may be limited by the complexity of ranking and retrieval process.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Contextualized Sentence Embeddings for Measuring External Context Utilization (Revised)
PROPOSAL: We will extend the contextualized sentence embeddings approach to directly utilize the knowledge from the external context by incorporating an external knowledge embedding module into the embedding process. The module will be trained to represent the knowledge in the external context using a separate, large-scale external knowledge base. This allows for leveraging the external knowledge more effectively and increasing its utilization in the generated responses.
CONTROLS: Compare against original contextualized sentence embeddings approach, standard retriever-augmented generation models.

PREDICTION: By directly incorporating external knowledge into the context embedding process, our revised approach should be able to more effectively utilize the external context in the generated responses and reduce hallucinations. However, it may require significant additional training data and computational resources to statistically integrate the external knowledge base.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Evaluating Transformer Layer Complexity using Graph Signal Processing
PROPOSAL: We will use Graph Signal Processing (GSP) to analyze and quantify the complexity of different transformer layers within RAG models. Specifically, we will construct a graph where vertices represent tokens, edges represent the transformer's self-attention pattern, and node features represent the model's learned embeddings. We will then apply a set of GSP tools, such as spectral clustering and filtered diffusion, to identify the most complex layers that receive the most attention and concentrate learned information. This can help us understand which layers contribute the most to internal knowledge utilization.
CONTROLS: Abolish attention heads and randomly select few attention layers; report performance of GSP on baseline transformer models.
COST: 1080
PREDICTION: This approach should shed light on the transformer layers responsible for internal knowledge utilization, but it may struggle to generalize across diverse RAG models and datasets, and might be computationally intensive.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Weight Decay in Modeling Internal Knowledge Utilization
PROPOSAL: Inspired by recent observations on the relationship between L2 regularization and knowledge distillation, we will conduct a systematic study on the impact of weight decay on internal knowledge utilization in RAG models. We will modify the model's training process to include weight decay at different magnitudes and monitor the changes in internal knowledge utilization, as measured by the complexity scores obtained from proposal 1. This can help us understand whether and how hyperparameter tuning affects internal knowledge utilization.
CONTROLS: Compare results against models with no weight decay, standard RAG pipelines, and explicit knowledge distillation.
COST: 1380
PREDICTION: Our findings might reveal an interplay between weight decay, L2 regularization, and knowledge distillation, leading to a more nuanced understanding of internal knowledge utilization. However, the results may not generalize to other RAG models or different datasets, and the investigation might not capture all possible effects of weight decay.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Leveraging Retrieval-Gradient Patterns for Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: We will collect a large corpus of responses from a RAG system paired with their source code and internal state snapshots at different generations. Using this unique dataset, we will train a gradient-based model that identifies internal knowledge retrieval patterns that correlate with hallucinations. The model will analyze the gradients of the weights during training with respect to the input and selected retrieved documents, predicting internal knowledge "pull" vs. external context "push". We will validate the results using a set of manually labeled RAG responses.
CONTROLS: We will compare our method to ReDeEP and other baseline methods that rely on attention heads or layer selections.
COST: 5312.3
PREDICTION: Our model is expected to perform well, especially in tasks with detailed internal knowledge retrieval patterns, and may outperform ReDeEP on certain datasets. However, interpreting the gradient patterns and justifying its validity as a reflection of actual internal knowledge pull could be challenging.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of Hallucination Detectors
PROPOSAL: We will systematically evaluate the robustness of state-of-the-art hallucination detectors (including ReDeEP) under various levels of noise in the external context, such as sensorimotor noise, document corruptions, or errors generated by retrieving outdated documents. This will help understand how well the current methods generalize to real-world scenarios and identify the parameter settings, attention mechanisms, and internal knowledge that matter for robust hallucination detection.
CONTROLS: We will first fine-tune ReDeEP on our chosen RAG system and document retrieval, and then apply it to noisified documents, analyzing noise levels, and robustness metrics such as F1-score and corrected accuracy.
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: ReDeEP should hold up well on moderate noise but will likely suffer with extreme corruptions or similar severe perturbations, afflicted by evident perturbations like humanoid auto-generated text going indoors problems.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Transformers as Feature Extractors for Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: To improve the interpretability of hallucination detectors and identify the key factors that contribute to hallucinations, we will leverage Transformers as feature extractors to abstract away the task-specific complexities. This will allow us to capture the underlying patterns in the learned internal knowledge and external context, facilitating the development of more intuitive and directly interpretable hallucination measures. We will investigate various feature extractor architectures, including multi-task learning, cross-modal fusion, or theoretical distillation based features and evaluate their relative effectiveness.
CONTROLS: We will compare our feature extractor-based methods to the existing ReDeEP and other baseline methods, and perform an ablation study to understand how different feature extraction techniques impact performance.
COST: 5500
PREDICTION: Our feature extractor-based approaches should provide more insights into the inner workings of LLMs and help identify potential biases in the hallucination detection process, and potentially lead to more robust detection systems. However, the effectiveness of these approaches may be limited to cases where clear patterns in the internal knowledge and external context can be identified.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Measuring External Context Utilization through Frequent Item Set Mining
PROPOSAL: We will use frequent item set mining to find a set of hitter items/patterns that occur more often in the generated text when the model relies on the external context, and use their absence to identify potential hallucinations. In particular, we will use the Gensim library to extract the top n-grams, then apply Apriori or FP-growth to find the frequent patterns, and select a threshold (e.g., supporting count > 1%) to filter out the rare patterns. We will evaluate this method using the same datasets and baselines used in ReDeEP and its follow-up work.
CONTROLS: Compare with ReDeEP, its follow-up work, and a simple baseline that always predicts the most likely text without using external context. Also, ablate the threshold and n-gram sizes to analyze their effects.
COST: 800
PREDICTION: This method may discover some strong patterns indicating external context utilization, but may struggle to generalize beyond the specific datasets or tasks used during training, and its results might be too coarse-grained to distinguish between reliable and hallucinated responses.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Hash Embeddings for Quantifying Internal Knowledge Utilization
PROPOSAL: We propose to use hash embeddings to quantify the model's internal knowledge utilization. Specifically, we will generate a large number of hash signatures for each hidden state of the transformer layers and calculate the similarity between these signatures to measure the stability and consistency of the model's internal knowledge representation. We will then use a standard clustering algorithm to group the hash signatures and evaluate the cluster stability to indicate the degree of internal knowledge utilization.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the method on news summarization and data-to-text generation tasks, comparing to the Jensen-Shannon divergence used in ReDeEP and its follow-up work. Also, ablate the cluster count and hash signature dimension to analyze their effects.
COST: 1600
PREDICTION: This method has the potential to provide a robust and generalizable measure of internal knowledge utilization, but might be computationally expensive due to the large number of hash signatures generated. It also requires careful tuning of the clustering parameters.

However, its performance may not be significantly better than the scratch-trained model, indicating that the two-stage training strategy may not be necessary or beneficial for multivariate time-series forecasting.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Exploiting Channel-Dependent Encoders with Efficient Capacities
PROPOSAL: Propose a novel channel-dependent encoder architecture that combines a linear embedding layer with a set of adaptive filters to capture cross-variable interactions. The architecture is based on the observation that channel-dependent effects often manifest as orthogonal patterns in the input data. The proposed encoder is trained using a novel "transferable" training objective, designed to filter out redundant features and promote the extraction of essential patterns, thereby reducing the computational cost of the model without sacrificing accuracy.
CONTROLS: Compare proposed architecture to existing channel-dependent encoders (e.g., Res2Net, SE-Net) and channel-independent encoders (e.g., 1D convolutional networks).
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: The proposed architecture outperforms existing channel-dependent encoders in terms of forecasting accuracy and computational efficiency; however, it may perform similarly to channel-independent encoders for some datasets, due to the challenge of identifying orthogonal patterns in more complex inputs.

PROPOSAL: Propose a novel channel-dependent encoder architecture that combines a linear embedding layer with a set of adaptive filters to capture cross-variable interactions. The proposed encoder is trained using a novel "transferable" training objective, designed to filter out redundant features and promote the extraction of essential patterns, thereby reducing the computational cost of the model without sacrificing accuracy.

PROPOSAL: Develop a channel attention mechanism that uses a non-linear kernel to weigh the importance of different channels in the input data. The proposed attention mechanism is integrated with the novel channel-dependent encoder architecture from proposal 1, allowing the model to effectively exploit both cross-channel interactions and non-linear patterns in the data.

TITLE: A new Transformer-based encoder-decoder architecture with explicit channel-dependent and temporal encoding
PROPOSAL: We propose to design a new multivariate time-series forecasting architecture, dubbed MultiViewTransformer, which incorporates both channel-dependent and temporal encoding mechanisms. The proposed architecture will consist of an encoder with self-attention and parallel cross-attention blocks for channel interaction, and a decoder that utilizes a hierarchical attention mechanism to capture long-term temporal dependencies. We will utilize two masking strategies during training: temporal masking and channel masking, and one triple-masking strategy, so the model can understand variability, changes or uncertainty in future predictions.
CONTROLS: We will compare MultiViewTransformer against three existing state-of-the-art models for multivariate time-series forecasting: ProphetNet, Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT), and GRU-ResNet. We will also perform ablation studies to understand the contributions of individual components to the overall performance.

PREDICTION: We expect MultiViewTransformer to significantly outperform the baselines on metrics such as MAE, RMSE, andr-hit on the weather and electricity consumption forecasting datasets. TITLE: Channel-Dependent Encoder with Adaptive Cross-Channel Attention
PROPOSAL: We will design a new channel-dependent encoder that can adaptively allocate attention across different variates based on their similarity and the forecasting task requirements. ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Asymmetric Hierarchical Multivariate Time-Series Forecaster
PROPOSAL: To address the limitations of simple linear projections for decoding, we will develop an asymmetric hierarchical multivariate time-series forecaster. This model will feature a graph-structured encoder that captures complex temporal relationships and channel dependencies through a two-layer graph neural network. The encoded representations will then be upsampled and fed into a set of independent decoder heads, each of which focuses on a specific variate or group of variates. Each decoder head will use an asymmetric architecture that combines a linear projection with a slower-paced recurrent neural network, allowing the model to capture both short-term and long-term dependencies. We will compare this model to existing forecasters and evaluate its performance on a wide range of tasks.
CONTROLS: An ablation study to assess the contribution of each decoder head, and a variant where the encoder and decoder use the same architecture to compare hierarchical modeling with shared and task-specific modeling.
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: We expect our new hierarchical forecaster to significantly outperform existing models in tasks with complex temporal dynamics, such as weather forecasting and electricity transformer temperature forecasting. However, its asymmetric architecture might degrade performance when forecasting tasks require uniform across-channel predictions.

Specifically, we will develop a novel self-supervised task that aims to predict specific features of the time-series data, such as trend, seasonality, and residuals, from the encoded representations. The model will be trained to predict these features in a multi-task fashion, with each task focusing on a particular aspect of the data. This objective is expected to encourage the model to learn more effective temporal dynamics and channel interactions, leading to improved forecasting performance.
CONTROLS: A baseline experiment using the standard masking-reconstruction objective, and an ablation study to evaluate the contribution of each feature-prediction task.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Channel-Interdependent Multi-Head Self-Attention for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose modifying the standard multi-head self-attention mechanism in the Transformer encoder to incorporate interdependencies between different variables in the multivariate time series. In our channel-interdependent multi-head self-attention (CIM-HSA) mechanism, each attention head computes a context vector that considers not only the presence of all variables but also their interactions. This is achieved by introducing a channel-aware feature transform and attention weight calculation. CIM-HSA is applied across multiple heads to capture intricate patterns in the data.
CONTROLS: compared to standard Transformer with self-attention (Transformer-SS) and a recent work using graph attention network for multi-variable forecasting (GAT-forecasting).
COST: 3330
PREDICTION: Our CIM-HSA-Transformers will outperform baseline models on all four downstream tasks, with an average improvement of 2.5% on the weighted mean absolute error, especially on tasks like solar power generation forecasting where variable dependencies play a crucial role, but might have a smaller gain on purely time-series tasks like electricity transformer temperature forecasting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Integrating Cross-Channel Dependency into Decoder with Explicit Channel Interaction Mechanism
PROPOSAL: We propose incorporating an explicit channel interaction mechanism into the decoder to effectively exploit cross-channel dependencies for multivariate time-series forecasting. Our mechanism, called Channel-Interaction Receptive Fields (CIRFs), learns to dynamically identify pairs of channels that interact, and modulates the decoder's prediction based on these interactions. This allows the model to capture complex temporal structures cross-channels.
CONTROLS: compared to linear projection-based decoder (Linear-Desc), and a recent decoder with integrated explainability (Explainable-Dec).
COST: 5000
PREDICTION: Our model with CIRFs will show significant improvement on the solar power generation forecasting task with a 4.2% gain in the weighted mean absolute error, while having comparable performance on other tasks. However, the design of CIRFs might lead to increased computational costs, which could be mitigated by adjusting the size of CIRFs' embedding vector.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multistage Pretraining with Downstream Task Masking for Efficient Alignment of Training and Architectures
PROPOSAL: We propose a multistage pretraining approach that incorporates downstream task masking to more effectively align the model's architecture with the training objective. In our approach, the pretrained model is fine-tuned with a masked task objective that mimics the temporally masked downstream task. We evaluate our approach on four multivariate time-series forecasting tasks and observe improved convergence rates and better adaptation to specific downstream tasks.
CONTROLS: compared to standard pretraining with BERT-style masked language modeling and two-stage fine-tuning approach.
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: Our approach will show faster convergence times and better adaptation to specific downstream tasks (by up to 2% improvement on weighted mean absolute error), particularly on tasks with high variable dependencies like solar power generation forecasting. However, we may observe decreased performance when the downstream task masking is too severe.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Gradual Knowledge Distillation for Large-Scale Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel knowledge distillation approach for large-scale multivariate time-series forecasting, where the teacher model is trained on a high-resolution temporal resolution, and the student model is trained on a lower-resolution data. The knowledge from the teacher model is gradually distilled to the student model through multiple stages of distillation, providing step-wise knowledge transfer.
CONTROLS: compared to standard knowledge distillation techniques and a recent work using online distillation (OD-forecasting).
COST: 12000
PREDICTION: Our approach will significantly reduce the computational burden and memory requirements for large-scale multivariate time-series forecasting, while maintaining an average improvement of 1.3% on weighted mean absolute error, and up to 2.1% for specific tasks like weather forecasting.

TITLE: Measuring View Similarity via Conditional Mutual Information
PROPOSAL: We experimentally compare the mutual information between views under different augmentations, and propose a new metric to quantify view similarity by conditioning mutual information on instance representations.
CONTROLS: We compare our method against a recent variant of SimCLR [Chen et al., 2020] on CIFAR-100 with standard augmentations (rotation, flipping, color jittering) and on ImageNet with a diverse set of augmentations (AutoAugment [Cubuk et al., 2019], RandAugment [Cubuk et al., 2019]).
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: We expect our proposed metric to outperform static measures of view similarity, revealing that certain augmentations significantly increase the information gained from views. However, evaluation may fail if the generator inconsistencies  result in impracticably complex instance representations.

TITLE: Ensemble of Adaptive Augmentation Strategies for Robust Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose an ensemble approach that combines multiple adaptive augmentation strategies, trained using different information-theoretic objectives and designed using our principled framework. The goal is to leverage the collective strengths of each strategy and achieve robustness against mode collapse, overfitting, and dataset shifts.
CONTROLS: We compare our ensemble approach against state-of-the-art fixed-augmentation methods, the MCL framework with adaptive augmentation, and individual adaptive augmentation strategies.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Measuring View Similarity via Conditional Mutual Information
PROPOSAL: We experimentally compare the mutual information between views under different augmentations, and propose a new metric to quantify view similarity by conditioning mutual information on instance representations.
CONTROLS: We compare our method against a recent variant of SimCLR [Chen et al., 2020] on CIFAR-100 with standard augmentations (rotation, flipping, color jittering) and on ImageNet with a diverse set of augmentations (AutoAugment [Cubuk et al., 2019], RandAugment [Cubuk et al., 2019]).
COST: 12000
PREDICTION: We expect our proposed metric to outperform static measures of view similarity, revealing that certain augmentations significantly increase the information gained from views. However, evaluation may fail if the generator inconsistencies  result in impracticably complex instance representations.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Does Instance-Wise Augmentation Impact the Information Landscape?
PROPOSAL: We design and experimentally compare different augmentation Moses sequences tailored to individual instances, with the goal of observing how instance-wise augmentation affects the mutual information between views. We evaluate on a set of 12 complex, real-world datasets (such asImageNet, CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet) and apply a standard contrastive learning framework (SimCLR) with several fixed augmentation settings.
CONTROLS: We compare our results against a strong baseline that uses a pre-defined augmentation Moses sequence on all instances simultaneously, and include ablations to quantify the effect of instance-wise augmentation on mutual information.
COST: 27000
PREDICTION: Instance-wise augmentation can adaptively increase the mututal information between views for complex instances, enabling more effective contrastive learning. However, we expect this approach to fail for noisy or degraded data due to increased sensitivity to instance-specific augmentations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Towards Adaptive Contrastive Learning with Instance-Specific Information Metric
PROPOSAL: Design a novel adaptation of the existing contrastive learning framework (SimCLR) that integrates a dynamic information metric to quantify the informativeness of view pairs for each instance. Specifically, we will use a variational bound of mutual information to integrate a proxy of the information gain through the views of an instance and incorporate this proxy into the existing contrastive loss function. This will enable the model to adaptively select the most informative view pairs for each instance and thus concentrate the learning effort on areas where new information is gained efficiently.
CONTROLS: Ablate the dynamic information metric to evaluate its contribution to the model's performance; compare this adaptive approach to the baseline SimCLR framework without any dynamic adjustments.
COST: 400
PREDICTION: The adaptive approach should yield an average 5-7% improvement over the SimCLR baseline in both design and real-world benchmarks and with a wider margin (10-15% improvement) on the latter, while its performance could degrade with poor estimation of the information gain proxy or overfitting in instances with numerous augmentations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Extension to Spectral Clustering Analysis of Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: Delve into the spectral clustering interpretation of contrastive learning (as it relates to mutual information maximization and noise contrastive estimation) and investigate how the adapted framework integrates with this perspective. We aim to derive a set of hypotheses about spectral clustering performances under the adaptive framework, including how cluster assignment improves or stays when the adaptive strategy is employed.
CONTROLS: Compute spectral clustering for the learned representations of SimCLR and our adaptive method; compare the cluster assignments and the spectral convergence metrics of these two frameworks on the synthetic and real-world benchmarks.
COST: 630.1
PREDICTION: The insight from the spectral clustering analysis may lead to a deeper understanding of the internal workings of the adaptive framework and provide additional evidence for its improved information utilization efficiency.

TITLE: 3. Extension to Spectral Clustering Analysis of Contrastive Learning (revise)
PROPOSAL: Delve into the theoretical properties of mutual information and explore a method for providing more effective sample expandability to avoid redundancy in augmentation, based on the information-theoretic max-margin framework for locally sensitive functions. This has the potential to extend our understanding of contrastive learning beyond the traditional framework of object identity, I-term and noise contrast, incorporating instance variability directly within the modelling.
CONTROLS: Establish the theoretical foundation for accessing better augmentations via locally sensitive functions on top of mutual information; conduct a spectral clustering analysis comparison on a set of simplified benchmark tasks to compare with a standard framework that relies on augmentations following on some arbitrary presentation and common isoaug distribution already enriched; experiment using successful expansion information metrics  & previously predicted success with acceptably malformed comparison task using embedded real labels of noisy data.
COST: 832
PREDICTION: Using this revised perspective, the estimate would be that this adaptation method increases the precision and generalizability of discrepancy between instances augmented from the recently expanded sets up to 20% over baseline in restricted settings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Generalizability of Adaptive Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: To assess the generalizability of our adaptive contrastive learning framework in different scenarios, we will examine its transfer performance on a variety of tasks, including domain adaptation, few-shot learning, and OpenSet classification. This involves training our model on a different dataset and evaluating its performance on a fixed test set.
CONTROLS: Compare our adaptive method to the standard SimCLR framework across various transfer tasks; also examine the baseline method trained with a fixed set of augmentations, and investigate the differences between our model with large-scale pre-training versus adapting it to downstream tasks.
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: By leveraging adaptability through varying augmentations yielding predictive capapcity, we estimate around 10-15% improvement in recognition transfer on standard registry datasets over the baseline compared to a baseline of statically hand engineered preprocess augmentationiors and diminishing specificity To increase scalability, I will be reporting on efficiciency not diminishing estimates to abbreviation.

PROPOSAL: Perform a thorough ablation study to investigate the contributions of the instance-specific information metric to the overall performance of the adaptive contrastive learning framework. We will investigate the impact of removing or modifying the information metric on the learning dynamics and the final representations learned by the model.

TITLE: GPU-Accelerated Parallelization for Large-Scale Adaptive Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: Develop an optimized GPU-accelerated parallelization scheme for the adaptive contrastive learning framework, enabling large-scale experiments with billions of parameters and million-scale augmentations. We will implement synchronous and asynchronous parallelization methods, leveraging parallelization accelerators (CUDA, HIP) and high-performance data structures to reduce training time by several orders of magnitude.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance and memory usage of our parallelization scheme with traditional, non-parallel approaches; also, evaluate the stability and accuracy of our optimized framework with respect to traditional cost functions and distribution Informat Micro Graph(pt(; OCergic Nei analysis evaluating.
COST: 1170
PREDICTION: Using this optimized parallelization scheme, we expect to reduce the training time for large-scale experiments by over 90% with comparable accuracy and robustness as traditional non-parallelized frameworks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Hardware-Aware Sampling Strategy for Adaptive Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: Design and implement an efficient hardware-aware sampling strategy to optimize the batch generation process for adaptive contrastive learning, exploiting the massively parallel architecture of modern GPUs and accelerating sampling operations. We will develop a smart sampler that efficiently leverages contiguous memory alignment, coalesced memory access, and concurrent thread launching to minimize memory access overhead and pipeline stalls.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of our hardware-aware sampler with standard random sampling, also record its comparison to the short-time alternatives whereby GPU specific accelerate technique is clipped from memory whereby one would normally start rewriting. Implement Cuda and PT performance optimization benchmark
COST: 1230
PREDICTION: With our efficient hardware-aware sampler, we estimate a 20-25% increase in training speed for large-scale experiments, resulting in faster convergence, and comparable or even improved performance metrics relative to other competing models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Dynamic Information Landscape of Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: Conduct a set of experiments using SimCLR-S [1] as the target framework, evaluating the mutual information between different views for each instance across the training process. Utilize the contextual variational autoencoder (CVAE) framework [2] to quantify the information shared among views. Barspin [3] will be used as the dataset and InfoNCE V2 as the metric to measure the mutual information. We will randomly select 128,000 data points from the training set, and a view will be considered informative if it contributes non-trivial information (1e-3 bits). We will vary the number of augmentations and batch size to analyze the potential risks of artifact information spreading.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: train SimCLR-S without augmentations and measure mutual information (low expected performance)
- No CVAE masking: include all views in mutual information calculation with CVAE (shifting towards noise contrastive estimation)
COST: 8,320 
PREDICTION: We expect to see performance differences when selecting information-rich views, but we may also identify scenario dependencies where informativeness is heavily inversely correlated with view diversity. Overfitting or excessive preemption of informative views could be problematic with extensively varied scene contexts.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theoretical Analysis of Contrastive Learning through a Mutual Information Lens
PROPOSAL: Derive a theoretical framework for understanding the information-theoretic dynamics of contrastive learning. Specifically, we will analyze the relationship between mutual information and the contrastive loss function. By leveraging techniques from probability theory and information theory, we aim to establish a foundational understanding of how the mutual information between different views of an instance evolves throughout the learning process. This analysis will provide insights into the information gained through different views and how the learning process adapts to changing informative content.
CONTROLS: 
- SimCLR-V2 as the baseline to validate the mutation Information alter series depending React arch contra invol 
COST: 11,700
PREDICTION: The theoretical framework will reveal that the contrastive loss function can be decomposed into components that represent the mutual information between views and the informativeness of individual views. The mutual information will be seen as a crucial component in the optimization process, allowing the model to focus on informative views and adapt to changing informative content. The analysis will also uncover potential limitations and artifacts of current contrastive learning frameworks.

TITLE: Adaptive View Expansion using Information-theoretic Bounds
PROPOSAL: Derive a theoretical framework to characterize the representational capacity captured by each instance in a novel augmentative regime, inspired by rate-distortion theory and the alignment principle of contrastive learning. This involves establishing a lower bound on the mutual information between a source instance and its augmented views using distortion measures (e.g., the Jensen-Shannon divergence). This bound can be used to drive the adaptive modification of existing augmentations and datasets, guiding the selection of relevant augmentations and expanding the diversity of views in a controlled manner.
CONTROLS: 1) Baseline: a standard static augmentation pipeline; 2) Ablation: compare with our bound-driven adaptive augmentation scheme on smaller problem settings.

PREDICTION: We expect that the adaptive augmenter will significantly increase representational diversity while maintaining robust performance, showcasing improved expressiveness and generalization capabilities. If successful, this would lay the groundwork for optimally defying hardware limitations and eliminating the trade-off between invariance and representational capacity.
