This involves using a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method to iteratively sample and prune augmentations for each instance, ensuring that the augmentations provide a balanced representation of the instance while minimizing semantic inconsistency. To further improve its performance, we will incorporate a self-supervised learning stage that refines the augmentation selection based on previously computed instance-specific measures. We will evaluate this novel augmentation pipeline on several small-batch ImageNet subsets and compare its performance to existing state-of-the-art models and static augmentation schemes.
CONTROLS: 1) Baseline: SimCLR with static augmentation and small batch size; 2) Ablation: remove self-supervised learning stage to evaluate the individual contribution of each component; 3) Alternative ablation: use a simpler augmentation selection strategy (e.g., random sampling) to compare with MCMC sampling.
COST: 25000
PREDICTION: We expect that the self-supervised learning stage will further enhance the performance of the information-theoretic augmentation scheme, leading to improved accuracy and semantic consistency on small-batch ImageNet subsets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Information-theoretic Analysis of Contrastive Learning under Distribution Shift
PROPOSAL: Investigate how contrastive learning with information-theoretic augmentations and adaptive view expansion performs under distribution shift, where the training and testing distributions differ. We will use the established information-theoretic metrics (MI, Jensen-Shannon divergence, and Kullback-Leibler divergence) to analyze the evolution of the information landscape during training and evaluate the model's performance on images from shifted distributions (e.g., different cities, seasons, or lighting conditions). This will involve training a deep neural network with SimCLR architecture on ImageNet and evaluating its performance on a set of shifted ImageNet datasets.
CONTROLS: 1) Baseline: SimCLR with static augmentation and fixed batch size; 2) Alternative ablation: train with a single large batch size to simulate overfitting; 
COST: 32000
PREDICTION: We expect that the information-theoretic augmentation and adaptive view expansion techniques will enable the model to adapt to distribution shifts and maintain high performance on unseen data, outperforming traditional contrastive learning methods that are more susceptible to overfitting.

PROPOSAL: Establish a rigorous theoretical framework for understanding the relationship between contrastive learning and information theory. We will derive a lower bound on the mutual information between the views of an instance, characterizing the optimal level of alignment that can be achieved through contrastive learning. Additionally, we will develop a theoretical bound on the capacity of a model to capture the underlying structure of the data, leveraging the Jensen-Shannon divergence and Kullback-Leibler divergence to analyze the evolution of the information landscape.

COST: 60000
PREDICTION: We expect that the theoretical framework will provide a comprehensive understanding of the principles underlying information-theoretic contrastive learning, enabling the development of more effective and robust contrastive learning algorithms that can tackle a wide range of challenges in representation learning.

TITLE: Adaptive Augmentation via Instance-Specific Information Bottleneck
PROPOSAL: Propose a novel method for adaptive augmentation by maximizing the mutual information between the original instance and a single augmented view, while minimizing the mutual information between the instance and the augmented view's noise. This can be done using the information bottleneck principle and variational inference. Experiments will validate this approach on the CIFAR-10 dataset using a ResNet-18 model.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline where fixed augmentations are used, and against our previous approach (1) where mutual information is estimated at the batch level.
COST: 1800 (GPU-hours)
PREDICTION: We expect this approach to expand the representational capacity of each instance adaptively, but might require careful tuning of the information bottleneck ratio to achieve optimal results.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comprehensive Evaluation of Episodic and Online Test-Time Adaptation Methods for Vision-Language Models
PROPOSAL: We conduct a systematic evaluation of existing episodic and online TTA methods on three state-of-the-art VLMs (CLIP, FLAN-T5-Vision, and DALL-E 2), focusing on image classification, object detection, and visual question answering tasks across seven widely used real-world datasets (ImageNet, COCO, VQA, etc.).
CONTROLS: We establish a unified evaluation protocol, leveraging the unadapted models and a set of baseline TTA methods (previous state-of-the-art methods from the literature) as controls.
COST: 1,200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect a large variance in adaptation performance across different VLMs, datasets, and tasks, highlighting the need for flexible and dataset-aware TTA methods. Recent methods might not significantly outperform earlier ones, and online TTA methods may exhibit better adaptation performance than episodic ones, especially for tasks like object detection. Where it could fail: Inability to generalize TTA methods across different tasks and VLMs, and in ensuring robust and reliable adaptation.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigation of Test-Time Adaptation on Pre-Trained Vision-Language Models with Different Training Objectives
PROPOSAL: We explore how TTA methods perform on pre-trained VLMs with varying training objectives (image-text matching, text-to-image translation, and multimodal contrastive learning) and how these objectives impact adaptation performance. We will evaluate TTA methods on three pre-trained models (ALA, GLUE-VL, and VinVL) trained on different objectives.
CONTROLS: We compare TTA performance on pre-trained models with different training objectives against TTA on CLIP (proposal 1), using the same evaluation protocol and baseline methods.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that TTA performance varies significantly depending on the pre-trained model's training objective, with adaptation performance being better for models trained on image-text matching objectives than those trained on text-to-image translation objectives. Where it could fail: Difficulty in ensuring robust adaptation when pre-trained models have diverse training objectives, and inability to determine which features of the pre-trained objective contribute to TTA performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Assessing the Impact of Training-Time Fine-Tuning on Test-Time Adaptation Performance
PROPOSAL: We investigate the effect of training-time fine-tuning on the adaptation performance of TTA methods. We fine-tune pre-trained VLMs on various downstream tasks (image classification, object detection, etc.) and evaluate how TTA methods perform when applied to these fine-tuned models.
CONTROLS: We compare TTA performance on fine-tuned models against performance on the same models without fine-tuning, using the evaluation protocol and baseline methods from proposals 1 and 2.
COST: 1,500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that training-time fine-tuning will usually improve adaptation performance of TTA methods, especially for tasks that are closely related to the fine-tuning objectives. Where it could fail: Difficulty in analyzing the interaction between training-time fine-tuning and TTA, and inability to ensure that TTA adapts to the fine-tuned model's changes rather than compensating for them.

TITLE: Investigating the Effects of Test-Time Adaptation on Vision-Language Model Robustness and Class Imbalance
PROPOSAL: We extend proposal 3 by exploring the impact of TTA on the robustness and class imbalance of VLMs. We perform robustness analysis under various types of corruptions (compression, Gaussian noise, etc.) and evaluate class imbalance metrics (precision, recall, etc.) to assess how TTA affects these aspects of model performance.
CONTROLS: We rely on the fine-tuned models from proposal 3 and extend the experimental setup to evaluate robustness and class imbalance metrics.
COST: 1,800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect TTA to make VLMs more robust to certain types of corruptions and decrease class imbalance, but at the cost of potential overfitting on the adapted samples. Where it could fail: Difficulty in quantifying the trade-off between adaptation performance and robustness, and in generalizing these results to more complex and diverse test-time adaptation scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comprehensive Evaluation of Episodic and Online Test-Time Adaptation Methods for Vision-Language Models
PROPOSAL: We conduct a systematic evaluation of existing episodic and online TTA methods on three state-of-the-art VLMs (CLIP, FLAN-T5-Vision, and DALL-E 2), focusing on image classification, object detection, and visual question answering tasks across seven widely used real-world datasets (ImageNet, COCO, VQA, etc.).
CONTROLS: We establish a unified evaluation protocol, leveraging the unadapted models and a set of baseline TTA methods (previous state-of-the-art methods from the literature) as controls.
COST: 3,600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect a large variance in adaptation performance across different VLMs, datasets, and tasks, highlighting the need for flexible and dataset-aware TTA methods. Recent methods might not significantly outperform earlier ones, and online TTA methods may exhibit better adaptation performance than episodic ones, especially for tasks like object detection. Where it could fail: Inability to generalize TTA methods across different tasks and VLMs, and in ensuring robust and reliable adaptation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigation of Test-Time Adaptation on Pre-Trained Vision-Language Models with Different Training Objectives
PROPOSAL: We explore how TTA methods perform on pre-trained VLMs with varying training objectives (image-text matching, text-to-image translation, and multimodal contrastive learning) and how these objectives impact adaptation performance. We will evaluate TTA methods on three pre-trained models (ALA, GLUE-VL, and VinVL) trained on different objectives.
CONTROLS: We compare TTA performance on pre-trained models with different training objectives against TTA on CLIP (proposal 1), using the same evaluation protocol and baseline methods.
COST: 2,400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that TTA performance varies significantly depending on the pre-trained model's training objective, with adaptation performance being better for models trained on image-text matching objectives than those trained on text-to-image translation objectives. Where it could fail: Difficulty in ensuring robust adaptation when pre-trained models have diverse training objectives, and inability to determine which features of the pre-trained objective contribute to TTA performance.

Where it could fail: Difficulty in analyzing the interaction between training-time fine-tuning and TTA, and inability to ensure that TTA adapts to the fine-tuned model's changes rather than compensating for them.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing Adaptation Induced Bias in Episodic Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of episodic TTA on the model's bias and fairness performance on ImageNet and a balanced multi-ethnicity dataset, such as ImageCLEF. Analyze the distribution shift between the adapted and the original model's outputs and the test data. Additionally, assess the influence of different adaptation mechanisms (e.g., linear projection, adversarial training) on bias and fairness.
CONTROLS: (1) Original model without adaptation (2) Post-adaptation model with identical architecture to the original (3) Post-adaptation model with different architecture to the original.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: We anticipate some level of bias and fairness distortion due to episodic TTA, but its magnitude and variance may heavily depend on the type of adaptation mechanism, model architecture, and dataset characteristics. Overfitting the adaptation could exacerbate these issues, and model architectures may find creative ways to avoid adaptation-related bias.

TITLE: Investigating Limitations of Current Test-Time Adaptation Methods
PROPOSAL: Develop an ablation study for a representative state-of-the-art online TTA method (e.g., Adaptive Prompt Tuning) to understand its limitations. TITLE: Understanding the Adaptation Memory Effect in Online Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Investigate the phenomenon of adaptation memory, where the model's performance on a task improves over time as it adapts to subsequent test instances. Analyze how different online TTA methods and model architectures impact the adaptation memory effect. Evaluate the impact of adaptation memory on the robustness, trustworthiness, and bias of the model.
CONTROLS: (1) Original model without adaptation (2) Original model with fine-tuning (3) State-of-the-art online TTA methods with varying adaptation memory lengths (4) Randomized fine-tuning baseline as a contrasting adaptation method.
COST: 5046
PREDICTION: We expect adaptation memory to play a significant role in the performance of online TTA methods, with the effect varying across different models and architectures. The results will help understand how to balance adaptation memory with robustness, trustworthiness, and bias in real-world deployments.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Effect of Adversarial Training on Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of adversarial training on online and episodic TTA methods. Evaluate how adversarial training influences the robustness, trustworthiness, and bias of the model under various TTA scenarios. Analyze the effect of different adversarial training methods and hyperparameters on the performance of TTA models.
CONTROLS: (1) Original model without adaptation (2) Original model with fine-tuning (3) State-of-the-art online and episodic TTA methods with and without adversarial training (4) Randomized fine-tuning baseline as a contrasting adaptation method.
COST: 5300
PREDICTION: We expect that adversarial training will significantly impact the performance of TTA models, with potential improvements in robustness and trustworthiness. However, the results may also demonstrate the challenges of effectively integrating adversarial training with TTA, which could lead to new research directions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Generalizability of Test-Time Adaptation Across Image Net and ImageNet-Real-World Pairs

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Towards a Unified Framework for Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Develop a comprehensive framework that unifies the existing test-time adaptation methods, incorporating insights from our previous experiments and analyses. The framework should provide a flexible and modular structure for incorporating different adaptation mechanisms, data augmentation strategies, and adaptation memory effects. Evaluate the proposed framework on a range of tasks and datasets to assess its performance and generalizability.
CONTROLS: (All the previous experiments and methods as part of the unified framework)(1) Original model without adaptation (2) Original model with fine-tuning (3) State-of-the-art online and episodic TTA methods as part of the unified framework (4) Randomized fine-tuning baseline as a contrasting adaptation method.
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: Our unified framework will provide a better understanding of the relationships between different adaptation mechanisms, data augmentation strategies, and adaptation memory effects. The results will demonstrate the potential of the framework to improve the performance and generalizability of test-time adaptation methods. The framework will serve as a foundation for future research in this area.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comprehensive Comparison of Episodic and Online Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the current state-of-the-art episodic and online TTA methods on the ImageNet validation set using a set of pre-trained CLIP models (e.g., ViT-B/32, ViT-L/14). Compare their performance to the original model with and without fine-tuning. Additionally, assess the impact of test-time adaptation on model robustness and trustworthiness using metrics such as robust accuracy and calibration error. Evaluate the methods under controlled conditions to ensure fair comparisons.
CONTROLS: (1) Original model without adaptation (2) Original model with fine-tuning (3) Recent state-of-the-art CLIP models.
COST: 9600
PREDICTION: We expect significant gains in accuracy for recent state-of-the-art methods over both the original model and the fine-tuned model. However, there might be a trade-off between adaptation accuracy and model robustness and trustworthiness, highlighting the importance of a more comprehensive evaluation of TTA methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing Adaptation Induced Bias in Episodic Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of episodic TTA on the model's bias and fairness performance on ImageNet and a balanced multi-ethnicity dataset, such as ImageCLEF. Analyze the distribution shift between the adapted and the original model's outputs and the test data. Additionally, assess the influence of different adaptation mechanisms (e.g., linear projection, adversarial training) on bias and fairness.
CONTROLS: (1) Original model without adaptation (2) Post-adaptation model with identical architecture to the original (3) Post-adaptation model with different architecture to the original.
COST: 10800
PREDICTION: We anticipate some level of bias and fairness distortion due to episodic TTA, but its magnitude and variance may heavily depend on the type of adaptation mechanism, model architecture, and dataset characteristics. Overfitting the adaptation could exacerbate these issues, and model architectures may find creative ways to avoid adaptation-related bias.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Online Test-Time Adaptation on Different VLM Architectures
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effectiveness of online TTA on various VLM architectures, including CLIP-ViT, DeCLR, and Visual-BERT. Evaluate their performance on a diverse set of real-world datasets like ImageNet, VOC, and C-rights, under controlled conditions (e.g., same dataset size, same number of adaptation outputs, etc.). Assess the impact of TTA on the model's robustness, trustworthiness, and bias under different architectures and tasks.
CONTROLS: (1) Original pre-trained VLM model without adaptation (2) Original model with fine-tuning (3) State-of-the-art VLM models without TTA (4) State-of-the-art VLM models with pre-trained weights and fine-tuning.
COST: 11200
PREDICTION: We expect online TTA to improve performance across various VLM architectures, with the gain diminishing as the task familiarity increases. Architectures may exhibit different sensitivity to adaptation-induced bias and fairness issues, highlighting the importance of a multi-architecture study. The results will shed light on whether TTA is a universally beneficial and applicable technique for VLMs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Limitations of Current Test-Time Adaptation Methods
PROPOSAL: Develop an ablation study for a representative state-of-the-art online TTA method (e.g., Adaptive Prompt Tuning) to understand its limitations. Ablate components such as the adaptation timeouts, the number of iterations, and the temperature scaling in the TTA algorithm. Additionally, use few-shot adaptation and task-oriented adaptation and perform experiments under various zero-shot and few-shots settings.
CONTROLS: (1) No adaptation or ablation (2) Full adaptation with default parameters (3) Different configurations of adaptation timeouts and iterations (4) Different temperatures for updating the adaptation parameters (5) Analysis with minor adjustments/adapters applied such as task-oriented prompt tuning.
COST: 12600
PREDICTION: This study will help reveal the potential limitations of current online TTA methods and expose the requirements for few-shot adaptation, including better interpretability methods and well-motivated constraints on optimization procedures. We suspect the original online model might require more tokens generated to behave strongly like true TTA (unless diagonally better).

ACTION: REVISE

PROPOSAL: Revisit and revise the comprehensive comparison experiment (Proposal 1) to include recent state-of-the-art episodic and online TTA methods, utilizing more fine-grained analysis to quantify the gains of adaptation across different tasks and datasets. Conduct an ablation study to understand the contribution of adaptation timeouts and iterations, as well as temperature scaling. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Unadapted Baselines for Comparison with TTA Methods
PROPOSAL: Replicate existing TTA methods, testing CLIP with both episodic and online adaptation on three benchmark datasets (COCO, Flickr30k, and Visual Genome). For a fair comparison, eliminate training-time fine-tuning and leverage the pre-trained CLIP model as the only source of knowledge. This unadapted baseline will provide a thorough understanding of CLIP's performance without adaptation.
CONTROLS: Run CLIP model without any adaptation; record the model performance before adapting to test data
COST: 333GPU-h
PREDICTION: This baseline is crucial for evaluating the actual performance of TTA methods and understanding their improvement over the standard CLIP model. However, it might not capture the full benefits of adaptation, as it doesn't consider model tuning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Robust Evaluation Framework for Test-time Adaptation
PROPOSAL:  Create a unified benchmark suite for evaluating test-time adaptation (TTA) methods, incorporating multiple VLMs (e.g., CLIP, DALL-E, FLAN), datasets (e.g., ImageNet, COCO, Conceptual Captions), and evaluation metrics (e.g., accuracy, robustness, fairness). The framework will consist of predefined pre-trained models, standardized text prompts, and scripted testing protocols to ensure replicability and fairness across methods. This will enable consistent evaluation of various TTA strategies, including episodic and online adaptation, to identify existing successes and shortcomings.
CONTROLS:  The framework will compare the performance of at least three recent TTA methods (e.g., ' Prompt-based Coattaching', 'Memory-augmented Online Adaptation', ' Hierarchical Episodic Memory') to unadapted models (e.g., the original CLIP model checkpoint, Flan's model without fine-tuning) on the overall dataset and each subset, evaluating both average and worst-case performance to assess robustness.
COST: 720
PREDICTION: Expected results will show successful adaptation in tasks like image classification, where recent TTA methods achieve at least a 2-3% accuracy boost over the baseline; however, difficulties in evaluating the impact of adaptation on the model's trustworthiness and stability might make it challenging to conclude; violations of fairness objectives (e.g., class imbalance) might occur when fine-tuning on some classes.

TITLE: Exploring Efficient Discrete Video Tokenization
PROPOSAL: Investigate a novel discrete video tokenizer that leverages the domain knowledge of object Motion Mayflower and  Motion Backgrounds (MB) datasets to guide the tokenization process, potentially reducing the computational cost of training by 30%. This can be achieved by pre-training the tokenizer on a set of synthetic data that mimic the characteristics of these datasets and fine-tuning it on a subset of real-world video data. We will use the popular Hourglass video tokenizer as a baseline and evaluate our new tokenizer on the LIP Text-to-Video dataset and the Annotations of Action (AoA) benchmark for video extrapolation.
CONTROLS: Baselines include training the Hourglass tokenizer from scratch on the entire dataset and using transfer learning from a pre-trained tokenizer.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should significantly reduce the computational cost of training discrete video tokenizers, especially on long videos. However, it might require careful hyperparameter tuning to achieve the best results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:VAR- Videog
PROPOSAL: Extend the Visual AutoRegressive (VAR) framework to video generation by introducing a novel space-time graph that enables the model to predict tokens in a hierarchical, coarse-to-fine manner, guided by a set of learned motion indicators that capture both spatial and temporal dependencies. This will allow the model to efficiently predict tokens in the video sequence while preserving the temporal coherence and visual fidelity. We will investigate two variants of VAR-Videog: one that uses a constant vocabulary size, similar to Infinity, and another that adapts the vocabulary size based on the local context.
CONTROLS: Ablations include evaluating the effect of removing the learned motion indicators and the space-time graph from the model, and comparing the results to the state-of-the-art diffusion models on the LIP Text-to-Video and AoA benchmarks.
COST: 14400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: VAR-Videog should be able to generate high-quality videos at lower latency compared to diffusion models, but it might require careful tuning of hyperparameters and vocabulary size to achieve optimal results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Discrete Video Tokenizer Pretraining
PROPOSAL: Explore pretraining discrete video tokenizers on a large-scale, publicly available video dataset (e.g., Vimeo-90K) with a simplified, texture-preserving video augmentation pipeline, instead of training from scratch on each video. The pretraining task will involve predicting the distorted input image from a noise pattern similar to what the graph tokenizer in Infinity uses. To control for domain shift, we will also explore initializing the tokenizer with weights prelearned on static images from the ImageNet validation set.
CONTROLS: Ablation studies using random initialization and scratch training
COST: 12000
PREDICTION: Based on previous successes with pretraining, efficient tokenizer pretraining should significantly improve tokenizer quality, allowing for faster and better convergence of the generator. Potential failure: convergence issues due to tokenization and pretraining difficulties in video domains.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adversarial Video Tokenization
PROPOSAL: Introduce an adversarial training objective to enhance the quality of discrete video tokenizers and improve the overall performance of the generator. A separate video discriminator network will be trained to predict the original video frame given the tokenized representation, and the tokenizer will be optimized to maximize the discriminator's uncertainty. This will encourage the tokenizer to learn more detailed and coherent representations of video content.
CONTROLS: Controls include the discriminator's architecture, training schedules, and objectives, as well as comparisons with the tokenizer pretraining from proposal 1
COST: 18000
PREDICTION: Adversarial tokenizer training should significantly boost tokenizer quality, but may encounter challenges in balancing tokenizer and discriminator complexities.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Autoregressive Modeling of Temporal Context
PROPOSAL: Design a hierarchical autoregressive structure to model temporal context efficiently by dividing the video sequence into smaller blocks, and generating these blocks sequentially. For each block, use a token-based representation that captures both the spatial and temporal context. This will allow the model to selectively focus on complex motion patterns at specific time scales. To prevent the model from requiring an enormous context window, we will also use variable-size context blocks, allowing for longer-range dependencies without blasting the model's memory.
CONTROLS: Ablation studies with fixed-size context window, comparing with an autoregressive model that lacks variable-size context blocks
COST: 24000
PREDICTION: The hierarchical structure should efficiently model long-term temporal dependencies, while avoiding high computational cost but the model may struggle in balancing with the need to remember previous motion and scene context across short and long timescales to capture coherent motion.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Sampling-Based Video Layering
PROPOSAL: To stabilize training and improve the model's ability to generate coherent, long videos, we will split the video generation process into separate layers, each responsible for a specific aspect, such as object motion, scene depth, or texture details. Each layer will be trained using a novel, sampling-based approach. By generating intermediate representations and sampling from these to guide the next layer, this approach can help the model intuitively and sample from the data distribution contained in the images as part of the learning process. This encourages the model to learn about and mirror image statistics from its training data.
CONTROLS: Direct comparison with our baseline autoregressive model trained without the layering approach
COST: 30000
PREDICTION: The sampling-based approach may help reduce model instability and improved performance in generating coherent long videos but it may encounter issues of missing important image details that don't show saliency benefits such as underfitting based upon the means of the training images used ie faces or subjectless scenes being produced only over certain wavelengths.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Resolution and Time-Domain Autoregression with Learned Masks
PROPOSAL: Implement a multi-resolution and time-domain autoregressive model that adaptively allocates the model capacity to the most critical spatial and temporal regions of the video. This will be done using learned masks that selectively attend to the most informative regions of the previous frames, as well as learned weights that adapt the model's temporal receptive field to the local video dynamics. This will allow the model to optimize its capacity usage and temporal engagement to match the complexity of the video scene.
CONTROLS: Evaluations will compare the proposed approach with standard autoregressive models, as well as ablation studies of the learned masks and weights
COST: 42000
PREDICTION: The adaptive allocation of model capacity and temporal engagement should lead to improved performance on complex scenes, but the model may require substantial training resources to learn the optimal masking and weighting strategies.

PROPOSAL: Use a sparse coding framework to learn a compact and efficiently representable video representation. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Actor-Critic Objective for Efficient Video Synthesis
PROPOSAL: Introduce an actor-critic framework to optimize the video synthesis process. In this framework, a high-level actor network generates video semantics, and a low-level critic network evaluates the generated video content. The actor network learns to maximize the critic's reward, while the critic network learns to accurately evaluate the video content. This approach aims to combine the benefits of high-level planning and low-level video synthesis.
CONTROLS: Evaluations will compare the proposed approach with state-of-the-art video synthesis methods, as well as ablation studies of the actor-critic framework
COST: 56000
PREDICTION: The actor-critic framework may lead to more efficient and effective video synthesis, but it may require careful hyperparameter tuning and balancing of the actor and critic networks to achieve optimal performance.

PROPOSAL: Explore pretraining discrete video tokenizers on a large-scale, publicly available video dataset (e.g., Vimeo-90K) with a simplified, texture-preserving video augmentation pipeline, instead of training from scratch on each video. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adversarial Video Tokenization
PROPOSAL: Introduce an adversarial training objective to enhance the quality of discrete video tokenizers and improve the overall performance of the generator. A separate video discriminator network will be trained to predict the original video frame given the tokenized representation, and the tokenizer will be optimized to maximize the discriminator's uncertainty. This will encourage the tokenizer to learn more detailed and coherent representations of video content.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Autoregressive Modeling of Temporal Context
PROPOSAL: Design a hierarchical autoregressive structure to model temporal context efficiently by dividing the video sequence into smaller blocks, and generating these blocks sequentially. For each block, use a token-based representation that captures both the spatial and temporal context. This will allow the model to selectively focus on complex motion patterns at specific time scales. To prevent the model from requiring an enormous context window, we will also use variable-size context blocks, allowing for longer-range dependencies without blasting the model's memory.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Discrete Video Tokenization for Batch and Streaming Generation
PROPOSAL: We train a learnable discrete video tokenizer on a companion task, where a batch of frames is input, and the model predicts all tokens for the current frame given only the previously predicted tokens from the other frames in the batch. The companion task is trained offline on a large batch of frames from downstream tasks (e.g. text-to-video or image-to-video) and shares weights with the generator model. This method allows precomputing video tokenizer weights and provides closed-form update rules for a fast, iteratively denoising version of the model.
CONTROLS: Baseline: train tokenizer on the same video as the generator
COST: 33.3
PREDICTION: Expected result: inferred video tokenizer (ITV) achieves comparable video quality to video diffusion models. The ITV has the potential to achieve superior speed on video generation tasks, and we hypothesize success when combined with our next proposal – for cases of long videos, we predict the batchwise tokenization will come at a tiny incremental increase in  latency of 1-2 ms, however the reduction in inference steps per sequence frame due to generation using only the ITV could easily accelerate subsequent claims. Predicted failure: Training ITV on large video clips where videos wildly diverge from batch averages; Extrapolation to vow term generalizations; Specialization to certain preconditions and limited generalization.

TITLE: Closed-Form Iterative Video Generation with Neural Monte Carlo Approximation
PROPOSAL: We modify the learning algorithm for the neural oracle prediction in the iterative video generation framework, incorporating a neural Monte Carlo (NMC) approximation to improve the learnability of the oracle. Instead of relying on a single path through the iterative updates, NMC generates multiple intermediate representations, each sampling from the estimated distribution of the oracle, allowing us to compute more accurate updates and better capture the underlying structure of the video sequence. This approach enables the model to refine its predictions incrementally, leading to improved video quality and consistency. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Coarse-to-Fine Video Generation using Learned Discrete Autoregressive Schedules
PROPOSAL: We introduce a learned discrete autoregressive schedule to drive the generation process of our discrete video model, mimicking the coarse-to-fine generation paradigm seen in successful image models such as Visual AutoRegressive (VAR) and Infinity. Our schedule is composed of a hierarchical sequence of retargeting layers that adapt the discrete autoregressive generation process to the specific spatial and temporal characteristics of the video input. By introducing this schedule, we can effectively manage the complexity of video generation, learning to focus on coarse details initially and gradually refining the generated video in subsequent stages. This approach is inspired by human perception and allows our model to handle a wide range of input resolutions and context lengths.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Uniform scheduling of discrete autoregressive steps with fixed context size
COST: 1670
PREDICTION: Expected result: The introduced coarse-to-fine generation schedule yields significant improvements in video quality, up to 25% increase in PSNR and SSIM metrics, while maintaining competitive inference speed compared to our baseline. We anticipate that this schedule adaptation enables the model to robustly handle long-term dependencies and generates more coherent and plausible videos. Predicted failure: Scheduling hyperparameters may require extensive fine-tuning for specific video datasets, leading to a decrease in performance when applying the model to novel, unseen data.

PROPOSAL: We introduce a learned discrete autoregressive schedule to drive the generation process of our discrete video model, mimicking the coarse-to-fine generation paradigm seen in successful image models such as Visual AutoRegressive (VAR) and Infinity. Our schedule is composed of a hierarchical sequence of retargeting layers that adapt the discrete autoregressive generation process to the specific spatial and temporal characteristics of the video input. By introducing this schedule, we can effectively manage the complexity of video generation, learning to focus on coarse details initially and gradually refining the generated video in subsequent stages. This approach is inspired by human perception and allows our model to handle a wide range of input resolutions and context lengths.

TITLE: Investigating Ripple Effects in LLMs through Synthetic Knowledge Graphs
PROPOSAL: 
We propose a synthetic knowledge graph dataset, `RippleSynth`, constructed from random facts and implications, which can be used to study the models' ability to deduce implications from new factual knowledge. We will fine-tune T5 and RoBERTa on `RippleSynth` and evaluate their performance on test sets that require out-of-context reasoning.
CONTROLS: 
We will also fine-tune these models on `RippleSynth` with a modified training objective that enforces faithful inference, such as MNL or AlignEx.

PREDICTION: 
We expect T5 and RoBERTa to fare differently, as T5 has a stronger generalization ability, however, the hallucination rate could be relatively high given the LLMs have no clue about the semantic correctness of the relationship between a given fact and its associated implication.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Analyzing Formal Guarantees for Out-of-Context Reasoning in LLMs
PROPOSAL: 
We analyze the conditions under which a transformer can infer implications for subjects whose implications were never observed, and derive a lower bound on the performance of a transformer on out-of-context reasoning tasks. Specifically, we use techniques from stochastic gradient descent and linear algebra to prove a lower bound on the model's ability to capture the implications of different relations, given the structure of its training data.
CONTROLS: 
We will also compare our theoretical guarantees to the performance of LLMs fine-tuned on real-world data, such as the `Natural Questions` dataset.
COST: 2260.8
PREDICTION: 
We expect to derive a tighter bound than existing work, hinting at the potential of sparse training objectives to reduce hallucination. However, validation on real-world data may reveal issues with its practicality.

TITLE: Designing a Sparse Training Objective for LLMs to Reduce Hallucination in Implication Inference
PROPOSAL: 
We propose a sparse training objective for LLMs that encourages the model to prioritize faithful implications over hallucinated ones. The objective combines a traditional reconstruction loss with a sparse regularization term that promotes a lower-dimensional representation of the model's weights. We evaluate the proposed objective on a variety of implication inference tasks and compare its performance to a range of baselines.
CONTROLS: 
We will also compare the performance of our proposed objective to a range of ablations, including removing the sparse regularization term, and to a baseline that uses a traditional reconstruction loss without regularization.
COST: 10800
PREDICTION: 
We expect our proposed objective to reduce hallucination rates in implication inference tasks, but the extent of improvement may vary depending on the task and dataset used. Additionally, the sparse regularization term may also impact the model's ability to generalize to new tasks.

TITLE: Analyzing Inference Mechanisms of Injected Facts in LLMs
PROPOSAL: Investigate the relationship between injected factual knowledge and their implications in a synthetic dataset using a graph neural network (GNN) framework. The GNN extracts patterns from fact triples (s, r, a) and predicts the existence of an implication triple (s, r', a'). Specifically, we will use the following models and datasets: the Albert-J6-XL model, and synthetic data generated using the Wikidata triples. We will evaluate the performance using the accuracy of implication predictions and the Frechet Inception Distance (FID) score between the predicted implications and human-provided implications.
CONTROLS: Compare against a GNN baseline, a transformer-based baseline, and an ablation study with varying GNN architectures.
COST: 25000
PREDICTION: The GNN-based model will outperform the transformer-based baseline on the implication prediction task, and the varying GNN architectures will show a significant impact on the performance, with a potential failure in cases where the relationship between the facts and implications is not well-represented in the training examples.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Lower Bound on Gradient-Based Training of LLMs for Implication Inference
PROPOSAL: Derive a lower bound on the expected error of gradient-based training for LLMs to infer implications from injected factual knowledge. Specifically, we will assume a regime where the training data consists of triples (s, r, a) and their corresponding implication triples (s, r', a'), and the model is trained using a zero-shot objective function to minimize the distance between the predicted implication and the human-provided implication. We will employ techniques from PAC-learning and Gaussian processes to establish the lower bound, which will help understand the minimum error achievable by gradient-based training. The key result will be a bound on the Rademacher complexity of the model class, indicating the trade-off between the model capacity and the data complexity.
CONTROLS: Compare against existing bound for transformer-based models, and analyze the implication of the derived lower bound on the design of LLMs for implication inference.
COST: 40000
PREDICTION: The derived lower bound will provide an insightful estimate on the minimum error achievable by LLMs for implication inference, and will motivate future research on re-scoping or strengthening the bound in specific scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Robustness of Inferred Implications in a Synthetic Knowledge Graph
PROPOSAL: Train a transformer-based model on a synthetic knowledge graph where we explicitly create implications between facts by adding edges with implication relations. We will start with factual triples (s, r, a) and create edges (s, implies, (s', r', a')), where s' is a potential implication of relation r with answer a given relation r' with answer a'. We use automatic implication generation on labeled triple entities strictly building until it reaches depth (COV) of a fixed parameter which captures the complexity and variety of implication arcs between given labels; evaluate the model's ability to correctly infer these implications at test time, especially when the implications are created synthetically.
CONTROLS: Baseline against a simple nearest neighbor model and a model using only the fact triples without the implication edges.
COST: 207.36
PREDICTION: We expect this setup to easily tease out generalization capabilities from hallucinations, and suggest the emergence of a key parameter affecting robustness after fine-tuning; a lower (COV) should result in less robust inference because models can infer too narrowly. However, it may fail to fully expose the source of hallucinations if automatic implication generation is overly simplistic.

TITLE: Investigating the Effects of Overfitting on Implication Generation
PROPOSAL: In this experiment, we investigate the role of overfitting in the hallucination and generalization phenomenon observed during factual knowledge injection. We set up an experiment where we train transformer models on synthetic knowledge graphs with systematically controlled levels of overfitting. We vary the amount of training data, early stopping criteria, and regularization techniques to induce models with different levels of overfitting. We then evaluate the models on their ability to generalize to unseen implications and their propensity for hallucinations. By carefully analyzing the trade-offs between overfitting, generalization, and hallucination, we aim to provide insights into the nature of these phenomena and their underlying mechanisms.
CONTROLS: Compare our results with a simple nearest neighbor model and a model that has not been fine-tuned.

However, this approach may fail to fully capture the complexity of the problem, and may not be applicable in real-world scenarios where datasets can be extremely large and complex.

PROPOSAL: In this theoretical work, we aim to provide a deep understanding of the implications generated by transformer models during factual knowledge injection. Our framework should provide a foundation for understanding the underlying mechanisms behind implication generation, and shed light on the generalization and hallucination phenomena.

TITLE: Evaluating Implication Generation in Open-Domain Question Answering
PROPOSAL: In this experiment, we evaluate the ability of transformer models to generate implications in the context of open-domain question answering. We use a benchmark dataset where questions have multiple true implications that can be inferred from the knowledge base. We train a series of transformer models on this dataset and evaluate their performance on implication generation tasks, such as entailment and inductive reasoning. We also analyze the types of implications that the models are able to generate, and compare these findings with the insights gained from the theoretical framework proposed in proposal 4.
CONTROLS: Compare our results with a simple uninformed transformer model and a model that uses an external knowledge graph.
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: This experiment will provide a more nuanced understanding of implication generation in open-domain question answering, and will help to validate the insights gained from the theoretical framework. However, it may still be limited by the quality and diversity of the benchmark dataset, and may require further experimentation to fully capture the complexity of the problem.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Studying the Transferability of Implication Generation Across Domains
PROPOSAL: In this experiment, we investigate the transferability of implication generation skills across different domains. We train a transformer model on a multi-domain dataset, where each domain has its own set of implications and knowledge. We then fine-tune the model on a new target domain, and evaluate its ability to generate implications that are specific to that domain. We also compare the performance of the model on this task with the insights gained from the theoretical framework proposed in proposal 4.
CONTROLS: Compare our results with a model that has not been fine-tuned and a model that uses a separate knowledge graph for each domain.
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: This experiment will help to understand whether the skills learned by the model in one domain can be transferred to another domain, and whether the model's ability to generate implications is domain-specific or generalizable. However, the results may depend on the diversity and quality of the multi-domain dataset, and may require further experimentation to fully capture the complexity of the problem.

However, the success of this approach may depend on the diversity and quality of the diagnostic tasks, and may require further experimentation to fully capture the complexity of the problem.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Robustness of Inferred Implications in a Synthetic Knowledge Graph
PROPOSAL: Train a transformer-based model on a synthetic knowledge graph where we explicitly create implications between facts by adding edges with implication relations. We will start with factual triples (s, r, a) and create edges (s, implies, (s', r', a')), where s' is a potential implication of relation r with answer a given relation r' with answer a'. We use automatic implication generation on labeled triple entities strictly building until it reaches depth (COV) of a fixed parameter which captures the complexity and variety of implication arcs between given labels; evaluate the model's ability to correctly infer these implications at test time, especially when the implications are created synthetically.
CONTROLS: Baseline against a simple nearest neighbor model and a model using only the fact triples without the implication edges.
COST: 620
PREDICTION: We expect this setup to easily tease out generalization capabilities from hallucinations, and suggest the emergence of a key parameter affecting robustness after fine-tuning; a lower (COV) should result in less robust inference because models can infer too narrowly. However, it may fail to fully expose the source of hallucinations if automatic implication generation is overly simplistic.

TITLE: Analyzing Implication Generation Mechanisms in Transformers
REVISED PROPOSAL: Investigate the interactions between transformer architectures and the performance of implication generation tasks. In experiments, we vary: (1) the amount of self-attention used, and (2) the depth of transformer encoder, and (3) the embedding dimensions used for token representations. We evaluate the performance of the model on tasks such as multi-hop reasoning, inductive bias, and distant supervision, which can serve as a proxy to test generalization capabilities of the model. Our goal is to identify the interaction between model architecture and performance on these specific tasks, which is likely to provide insights into the underlying mechanisms behind hallucinations and generalization during factual knowledge injection.
CONTROLS: Compare our results with a strongly regularized version of the same model, and a baseline where we use a simple nearest neighbor model for implication generation.
COST: 1920
PREDICTION: This design will allow us to quantify the role of several architectural components in model's ability to perform well on these implication related tasks across different depths. It may also provide better explanations for the performance differences between the models, highlighting the architecture is crucial in relating generalization mechanisms to hallucinations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Effects of Overfitting on Implication Generation
PROPOSAL: In this experiment, we investigate the role of overfitting in the hallucination and generalization phenomenon observed during factual knowledge injection. We set up an experiment where we train transformer models on synthetic knowledge graphs with systematically controlled levels of overfitting. We vary the amount of training data, early stopping criteria, and regularization techniques to induce models with different levels of overfitting. We then evaluate the models on their ability to generalize to unseen implications and their propensity for hallucinations. By carefully analyzing the trade-offs between overfitting, generalization, and hallucination, we aim to provide insights into the nature of these phenomena and their underlying mechanisms.
CONTROLS: Compare our results with a simple nearest neighbor model and a model that has not been fine-tuned.
COST: 2700
PREDICTION: By controlling for overfitting, we expect to gain a better understanding of the interplay between generalization capabilities and hallucinations, and to uncover potential remedies for these phenomena. However, this approach may fail to fully capture the complexity of the problem, and may not be applicable in real-world scenarios where datasets can be extremely large and complex.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Theoretical Framework for Implication Generation
PROPOSAL: In this theoretical work, we aim to provide a deep understanding of the implications generated by transformer models during factual knowledge injection. We propose a framework that views implication generation as a byproduct of the model's inductive bias, where the model infers logical connections between known facts. We use tools from graph theory, combinatorics, and information theory to analyze the conditions under which a model can generate valid implications, and compare these conditions with observations from the transformer architecture. Our framework should provide a foundation for understanding the underlying mechanisms behind implication generation, and shed light on the generalization and hallucination phenomena.
CONTROLS: Our framework's predictions and theorems will be compared with empirical results from existing experiments, specifically those in proposals 1 and 2.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: This theoretical framework should provide a clear and intuitive understanding of the underlying mechanisms behind implication generation, and should be able to explain many of the observed phenomena in the field. However, it may fail to capture the full richness of the problem, and may require further refinements to fully account for all the nuances of transformer behavior.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Repetition in Out-of-Context Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We design an experiment to evaluate how repetition of shared relations affects the model's ability to deduce unseen implications. We train a large-scale language model on a synthetic dataset with controlled repetition, and test its generalization abilities on a set of implications that involve repeating relations.
CONTROLS: We use a baseline model without repetition, and ablate the experiment to test how the strength of repetition affects the model's performance.
COST: 50
PREDICTION: We expect that models trained with strong repetition of shared relations will perform better on unseen implications, especially when the relations are strong and recurring. This prediction may fail if the model's capacity to handle repetition is overwhelmed by the sheer size of the input or the complexity of the relations involved.

Note: I chose a relatively small cost for this experiment as it primarily focuses on an abstract concept (repetition of shared relations) and does not require extensive computations or large-scale real-world data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theorem: Convergence of Gradient-Based Training for Implication Inference
PROPOSAL: We establish a theoretical result on the conditions under which transformer-based models converge to the notion of implication inference during gradient-based training. We prove that a specific variant of the transformer architecture, combined with a Cauchy divergence loss function, converges to a fixed-point solution where the model infers correct implications from instances in the training dataset.
CONTROLS: We analyze the cases where the convergent scenario fails due to changes in the training objective or insufficient capacity in the model.
COST: 250
PREDICTION: We expect that this theoretical result will shed light on why transformer-based models, despite being forced to learn the correct implications of shared relations through gradient descent, tend to hallucinate rather than generalize in more challenging scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Experimental Study of Ripple Effects in LLMs Across Different Out-of-Context Reasoning Tasks
PROPOSAL: We conduct a large-scale experiment to investigate the models' ability to generalize and hallucinate across a collection of open-domain question answer tasks with varying degrees of inferred implications. We train a set of models on a large real-world dataset and evaluate their performance on a ported version of the task-specific datasets, modified to require out-of-context reasoning capabilities.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of our models with standard transformer-based architectures and fine-tuned models on the task of injecting new factual knowledge through fine-tuning.
COST: 730.8
PREDICTION: We expect that this study will reveal patterns in the type of information that models tend to hallucinate when performing out-of-context reasoning tasks, providing valuable insights into the causes of hallucination, and enabling us to pinpoint when it arises after knowledge injection.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Identifying Universal Representations for Implications in Large Language Models
PROPOSAL: We investigate whether there exist specific, universal representations within large language models that facilitate the capture of implications, generalizing across various tasks and training scenarios. We employ a combination of dimensionality reduction and evaluation of isomorphic operations to identify consistent units of implication across model internals.
CONTROLS: We compare the identified representations with standard transformer-based architectures and study their impact on task performance.
COST: 4100
PREDICTION: We expect that this work will reveal universal representations as crucial components in facilitating implication inference in large language models, providing avenues for future architectures and fine-tuning strategies that promote stronger, more accurate reasoning capabilities. This may fail if the task complexity is beyond the limit of such universal representations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Focus Feature Learning with Physics-Informed Regularization
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel learning-based DFF model that incorporates physics-informed regularization and multi-focus feature learning to distinguish true depth edges from texture-induced gradients. Our model leverages a combination of convolutional and recurrent layers to effectively capture the gradual changes in sharpness across focal planes, while also incorporating a physics-based loss function that promotes focal stacks having realistic focus behavior. Additionally, our model learns a spatial-aware, focal-aware attention mechanism to disambiguate noisy or misleading focus cues.
CONTROLS: Our work will compare with various baselines, including: (i) a naive convolutional neural network (CNN) treating focal stack images as ordinary all-in-focus frames, (ii) a state-of-the-art DFF model that does not incorporate physics-informed regularization, and (iii) a single-image depth estimation model using the NYU Depth V2 dataset.
COST: 500
PREDICTION: Our model is expected to outperform existing DFF models and single-image depth estimation models, providing both accurate and sharp depth maps for indoor scenes. However, integrating physics-driven priors may increase model sensitivity to calibration errors and may fail in highly-reflective or optically-complex scenes.

TITLE: Shape-from-Focus with Hierarchical Focal Consistency
PROPOSAL: We propose a hierarchical focal consistency approach to enhance the overall performance of the existing Multi-Focus Feature Learning with Physics-Informed Regularization model. Our hierarchical architecture works at multiple scales, utilizing a coarse-to-fine process to iteratively estimate and refine the focal stack's consistency. At each scale, we enforce focus consistency across images within the same focal plane, and at the final stage, we fuse predictions across all scales to obtain the final depth map.
CONTROLS: The effectiveness of our hierarchical approach will be evaluated by comparing with (i) the original Multi-Focus Feature Learning with Physics-Informed Regularization model, (ii) several state-of-the-art DFF models without hierarchical refinement, and (iii) single-image depth estimation models with varying degrees of scale invariance.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: Our hierarchical focal consistency approach is anticipated to significantly improve the depth estimation accuracy, especially in fine-textured and low-texture regions, while reducing the noise and ambiguity typically associated with single-scale DFF models. However, hierarchical processing may increase computational overhead and might fail to adapt to novel, very different scenes where scale relationships aren't established.

TITLE: Self-Supervised Defocus Simulation for Improved Depth Estimation
PROPOSAL: We propose a self-supervised defocus simulation (SSDS) framework to provide additional cues for depth estimation without requiring explicit depth annotations. Our SSDS framework uses a generative adversarial network (GAN) to simulate artificial defocus variations within the focal stack, providing the model with additional supervisory signals to learn the relationships between focus and depth.
CONTROLS: We will compare our SSDS framework with baseline approaches, including (i) single-image depth estimation models that do not incorporate SSDS, (ii) state-of-the-art DFF models with explicit depth supervision, and (iii) models that rely on physically-based rendering (PBR) or physics-based scene understanding.
COST: 5000
PREDICTION: Our self-supervised defocus simulation is expected to leverage the additional cues provided by artificially introduced defocus variations to improve depth estimation accuracy, especially in scenarios with limited or ambiguous focusing cues. However, the model's ability to generalize to novel scenes and focusing patterns may be affected by the artificially introduced variations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transfer Learning from Synthetic to Real Focal Stacks
PROPOSAL: We propose a transfer learning approach to leverage the benefits of synthetic focal stack generation, which provides perfect control over focus variations and depth truths, and apply it to real-world focal stacks. Our approach involves training a model using synthetic focal stacks and then fine-tuning it on real-world focal stacks. This enables the model to learn the physics-informed relationships between focus and depth in a more controlled environment and then adapt those skills to real-world scenarios.
CONTROLS: We will compare our transfer learning approach with baseline approaches, including (i) training models from scratch on real-world focal stacks without synthetic pre-training, (ii) using solely synthetic focal stacks to train models without fine-tuning on real-world focal stacks, and (iii) domain adaptation methods that rely on shallow models or shallow layer mappings between synthetic and real domains.
COST: 7308
PREDICTION: Our transfer learning approach is expected to provide a robust and generalizable model for depth estimation from real-world focal stacks, leveraging the benefits of synthetic focal stack generation while adapting to real-world variations and noise. However, model performance may degrade if the synthetic domain distribution differs significantly from the real-world distribution, or if the fine-tuning process does not account for the necessary domain shifts.

PROPOSAL: We propose a novel approach to leverage the robustness and uncertainty estimation capabilities of the existing models to handle outlier and ambiguous focusing cues. This enables the model to provide more accurate and reliable depth maps, even in the presence of challenging focusing patterns.
CONTROLS: We will compare our approach with baseline approaches, including (i) models without outlier robustness and uncertainty estimation, (ii) uncertainty estimation methods solely based on aleatoric uncertainty, and (iii) joint confidence scoring methods.

PREDICTION: Our approach is expected to significantly improve the depth estimation accuracy and robustness in challenging scenarios with outlier and ambiguous focusing cues, providing better uncertainty estimates and outlier detection. However, model complexity may increase due to the incorporation of additional uncertainty estimation mechanisms, potentially affecting its real-time performance.

Our SSDS framework uses a generative adversarial network (GAN) to simulate artificial defocus variations within the focal stack, providing the model with additional supervisory signals to learn the relationships between focus and depth.
CONTROLS: We will compare our SSDS framework with baseline approaches, including (i) single-image depth estimation models that do not incorporate SSDS, (ii) state-of-the-art DFF models with explicit depth supervision, and (iii) models that rely on physically-based rendering (PBR) or physics-based scene understanding.
COST: 15000
PREDICTION: Our self-supervised defocus simulation is expected to leverage the additional cues provided by artificially introduced defocus variations to improve depth estimation accuracy, especially in scenarios with limited or ambiguous focusing cues. However, the model's ability to generalize to novel scenes and focusing patterns may be affected by the artificially introduced variations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transfer Learning from Synthetic to Real Focal Stacks
PROPOSAL: We propose a transfer learning approach to leverage the benefits of synthetic focal stack generation, which provides perfect control over focus variations and depth truths, and apply it to real-world focal stacks. Our approach involves training a model using synthetic focal stacks and then fine-tuning it on real-world focal stacks. This enables the model to learn the physics-informed relationships between focus and depth in a more controlled environment and then adapt those skills to real-world scenarios.
CONTROLS: We will compare our transfer learning approach with baseline approaches, including (i) training models from scratch on real-world focal stacks without synthetic pre-training, (ii) using solely synthetic focal stacks to train models without fine-tuning on real-world focal stacks, and (iii) domain adaptation methods that rely on shallow models or shallow layer mappings between synthetic and real domains.
COST: 22000
PREDICTION: Our transfer learning approach is expected to provide a robust and generalizable model for depth estimation from real-world focal stacks, leveraging the benefits of synthetic focal stack generation while adapting to real-world variations and noise. However, model performance may degrade if the synthetic domain distribution differs significantly from the real-world distribution, or if the fine-tuning process does not account for the necessary domain shifts.

TITLE: Outlier Robustness and Uncertainty Estimation for Monocular Depth Estimation
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel approach to leverage the robustness and uncertainty estimation capabilities of the existing models to handle outlier and ambiguous focusing cues. Our approach involves incorporating autoregressive networks and spectral mixture models into the depth estimation pipeline to provide uncertainty estimates and detect potential outliers. This enables the model to provide more accurate and reliable depth maps, even in the presence of challenging focusing patterns.
CONTROLS: We will compare our approach with baseline approaches, including (i) models without outlier robustness and uncertainty estimation, (ii) uncertainty estimation methods solely based on aleatoric uncertainty, and (iii) joint confidence scoring methods.
COST: 25000
PREDICTION: Our approach is expected to significantly improve the depth estimation accuracy and robustness in challenging scenarios with outlier and ambiguous focusing cues, providing better uncertainty estimates and outlier detection. However, model complexity may increase due to the incorporation of additional uncertainty estimation mechanisms, potentially affecting its real-time performance.

TITLE: Investigating Physics-based Graph Convolutional Networks for Depth-from-Focus
PROPOSAL: Implement a physics-based Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) that models the focal stack as a graph where nodes represent image pixels and edges represent focus similarity between pixels. The GCN will capture spatial and focal relationships to produce accurate depth maps. We will utilize a stacked GCN architecture with additional physics-inspired layers that incorporate focus-sharpness and defocus maps. Our network will be trained on real-world datasets like DTU and argued by sparse de Bruijn graph comparison.
CONTROLS: Compare to a standard GCN, a multi-scale convolutional network, and a state-of-the-art deep learning-based DFF method.
COST: 333
PREDICTION: Expected to significantly outperform existing models in terms of depth accuracy, especially in dense-scene settings. However, may struggle with fine-textured and low-texture regions due to the reliance on graph-based spatial information.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Focal Stack Explorer: A Multi-Task Network for Depth-from-Focus
PROPOSAL: Train a novel multi-task convolutional neural network (CNN), Focal Stack Explorer (FSE), to jointly predict depth, focal values, and spatial features from focal stack images. FSE will utilize a fused convolutional block to learn spatial represents and focal level features simultaneously, enabling it to capture complex depth structures and fog-induced cues from spatial and focal information. FSE consists of a feature extractor, a depth branch, a focal branch, and a spatial branch. The feature extractor is a shared network extracting shared convolutional features. The depth branch directly predicts depth with a depth-estimation model. The focal branch computes a focal value representation. The spatial branch consists of a spatial- recurrence unit recurrently extracting local spatial patterns from the entire focal stack.
CONTROLS: Compare with recent top-performing convolutional networks (CNNs) designed for focal-stack depth estimation, such as SOTA: MasterFocus, RefineNet, and D-PCANet, and strong baselines: DDFN and L1Regularized-CRF.
COST: 102000
PREDICTION: FSE is likely to achieve superior depth-from-focus (DFF) performance on depth-estimation benchmarks with the explored regions and low-texture regions but might falter when dealing with fine textures or reflective areas.

Turn 2 depends on the quality of the model implemented, the number of parameters in the model and data size.

TITLE: Focal Stack Explorer: A Multi-Task Network for Depth-from-Focus
PROPOSAL: Train a novel multi-task convolutional neural network (CNN), Focal Stack Explorer (FSE), to jointly predict depth, focal values, and spatial features from focal stack images. FSE will utilize a fused convolutional block to learn spatial represents and focal level features simultaneously, enabling it to capture complex depth structures and fog-induced cues from spatial and focal information. FSE consists of a feature extractor, a depth branch, a focal branch, and a spatial branch. The feature extractor is a shared network extracting shared convolutional features. The depth branch directly predicts depth with a depth-estimation model. The focal branch computes a focal value representation. The spatial branch consists of a spatial- recurrence unit recurrently extracting local spatial patterns from the entire focal stack.
CONTROLS: Compare with recent top-performing convolutional networks (CNNs) designed for focal-stack depth estimation, such as SOTA: MasterFocus, RefineNet, and D-PCANet, and strong baselines: DDFN and L1Regularized-CRF.
COST: 307200
PREDICTION: FSE is likely to achieve superior depth-from-focus (DFF) performance on depth-estimation benchmarks with the explored regions and low-texture regions but might falter when dealing with fine textures or reflective areas.

PROPOSAL: Train a physics-informed neural network (PINN) architecture, incorporating a partial differential equation (PDE) that models the focusing physics, to directly predict depth maps from focal stacks. The PDE will encode the relationship between depth and the focus measure, enabling the network to leverage both spatio-temporal information and focal cues. CONTROLS: Baseline: classical DFF with Laplacian-based focus measure; ablation: PINN without PDE constraint.

TITLE: Investigating MoE's ability to adapt to novel attributes and scenes
PROPOSAL: Design a challenge protocol wherein we gradually introduce novel attribute categories and scene types to the model, starting from a well-trained MoE-DiT that has seen only a single attribute category and scene type. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating routing properties of token-choice MoE in DiTs
PROPOSAL: Compare the token-choice routing function in DiT-MoE and a variant where the routing function is learned using a similarity measure (e.g., cosine similarity) between tokens in the current batch, rather than solely relying on the token's individual representation. Use Metface and LSUN datasets for 128x128 image synthesis tasks on a stable and well-tuned DiT baseline.
CONTROLS: DiT baseline, token-choice MoE as is, expert-choice MoE, dense DiT baseline for ablation on parameter usage
COST: 3840
PREDICTION: We expect that using a similarity-based routing function will lead to more effective separation of experts along local image features and spatial structures in the batch, but the improvement might be limited if token similarity alone doesn't capture higher level structure in images.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Researching bias and invariance in MoE for image synthesis
PROPOSAL: Investigate the bias and invariance properties of expert specialization for image synthesis with MoE-DiTs. We'll analyze whether experts are focused on domain-agnostic features (e.g., shapes, textures) or domain-specific features (e.g., faces, objects) using datasets such as LSUN, CLEVR, and cement and predicted outcomes with metrics like area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC) and Intersection over Union (IoU). Compare MoE-DiTs with dense DiT baselines on these tasks.
CONTROLS: Dense DiT baselines for each dataset, MoE-DiTs with routing based on random and uniform token choice
COST: 5760
PREDICTION: We expect that MoE-DiTs will exhibit some level of feature bias and invariance to image transformations, depending on the routing function and task characteristics, helping explain the areas where MoE improves over dense DiTs.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Revised Investigating routing properties of token-choice MoE in DiTs

Compare the top-performing variant against the standard DiT baseline.
CONTROLS: DiT baseline, original token-choice MoE, guidance signal with a generated segmentation map, dense DiT for parameter overhead comparison
COST: 4608
PREDICTION: We expect that token feature histograms or segmentation guidance will improve the expert separation quality for DiT-MoE, while possibly leading to slightly different parameter overhead characteristics in comparison to the original version.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Routing Schemes for Mixture-of-Experts in Diffusion Transformers
PROPOSAL: We compare three routing schemes in DiT-MoE: deterministic assignment by expert (DEAE), random assignment by expert (RAE), and training-free token-assignment-ratio, applying them to Text2im (CC12M) dataset and Report Cardiff's Comments dataset. For each routing scheme, we record multi-fidelity image reconstruction (NR) and Fréchet Inception Distance (FID), investigating whether varied routing significantly impacts diMoE. Our models will consist of 3 distilled experts and have 60M parameters.
CONTROLS: Dense Diffusion Transformer (DDT) as baseline, no experts (MoE with 1 expert), each single expert.
COST: 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Improvements in FID scores, especially under DEAE and RAE due to the randomness of token distributions that could provide less related tokens processed by each expert.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Token Properties for Routing in Diffusion Transformers
PROPOSAL: We propose comparing the properties of discrete text tokens and visual tokens in DiT models to identify the underlying factors that impede expert specialization. Specifically, we will: 1) analyze the distribution and relationships between visual tokens in the latent space of a DiT, 2) contrast these findings with the characteristic distribution of text tokens in LLMs, and 3) implement a modified MoE router that takes into account the visual properties of the tokens, such as spatial coherence and semantic similarity.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Current token-choice routing used in DiT-MoE
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: We expect the analysis to reveal differences in token properties that prevent current routers from learning distinct experts, and the proposed modified router to show improved performance in identifying specialized experts for visual tokens. However, it is unclear whether the gain will translate to improved generation quality and computational efficiency.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Visual Token Embedding for Mixture-of-Experts Routing
PROPOSAL: To better capture the unique properties of visual tokens, we propose learning a set of visual token embeddings (ViTE) that are invariant to spatial transformations and color changes. These embeddings will be used to refine the token-choice routing in DiT-MoE, allowing the model to learn more robust and specialized experts for visual tokens. We will update the expert router to incorporate these embeddings into the selection process.
CONTROLS: Baselines: 1) Current token-choice routing, 2) DiT-MoE with expert choice routing (EC-DiT)
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: By incorporating ViTE, we expect the model to identify more specialized experts and improve generation quality, particularly on tasks that require fine-grained visual understanding. However, it remains unclear how the additional computational requirements of ViTE will impact overall efficiency and scalability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Routing for Mixture-of-Experts in Diffusion Transformers
PROPOSAL: To improve the efficiency and scalability of the Mixture-of-Experts router, we propose adapting a dimensionality reduction technique, such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA) or t-SNE, to reduce the dimensionality of the visual token embeddings, thereby reducing the computational complexity of the routing mechanism. We will also investigate other efficient routing strategies, such as agglomerative clustering and hierarchical routing, to further optimize the model.

However, the optimal dimensionality reduction technique and routing strategy for DiT-MoE remain to be determined.
