ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Token Properties for Routing in Diffusion Transformers
PROPOSAL: We propose comparing the properties of discrete text tokens and visual tokens in DiT models to identify the underlying factors that impede expert specialization. Specifically, we will: 1) analyze the distribution and relationships between visual tokens in the latent space of a DiT, 2) contrast these findings with the characteristic distribution of text tokens in LLMs, and 3) implement a modified MoE router that takes into account the visual properties of the tokens, such as spatial coherence and semantic similarity.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Current token-choice routing used in DiT-MoE
COST: 12000
PREDICTION: We expect the analysis to reveal differences in token properties that prevent current routers from learning distinct experts, and the proposed modified router to show improved performance in identifying specialized experts for visual tokens. However, it is unclear whether the gain will translate to improved generation quality and computational efficiency.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Visual Token Embedding for Mixture-of-Experts Routing
PROPOSAL: To better capture the unique properties of visual tokens, we propose learning a set of visual token embeddings (ViTE) that are invariant to spatial transformations and color changes. These embeddings will be used to refine the token-choice routing in DiT-MoE, allowing the model to learn more robust and specialized experts for visual tokens. We will update the expert router to incorporate these embeddings into the selection process.
CONTROLS: Baselines: 1) Current token-choice routing, 2) DiT-MoE with expert choice routing (EC-DiT)
COST: 18000
PREDICTION: By incorporating ViTE, we expect the model to identify more specialized experts and improve generation quality, particularly on tasks that require fine-grained visual understanding. However, it remains unclear how the additional computational requirements of ViTE will impact overall efficiency and scalability.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED: Visual Token Embedding for Mixture-of-Experts Routing
PROPOSAL: To further refine the token-choice routing in DiT-MoE, we propose a hierarchical token embedding approach, where visual tokens are first clustered into groups using a density-based clustering algorithm (e.g., DBSCAN), and then assigned to experts within each cluster based on their semantic similarity. This hierarchical approach aims to capture more nuanced patterns in visual tokens and improve expert specialization.
CONTROLS: Baselines: 1) Current token-choice routing, 2) DiT-MoE with expert choice routing (EC-DiT), 3) DiT-MoE with ViTE (proposed in turn 2)
COST: 20000
PREDICTION: The hierarchical token embedding approach is expected to yield better expert specialization and improved generation quality, particularly on tasks that require fine-grained visual understanding. However, its applicability to larger models and real-world datasets remains to be seen.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: REVISED: Visual Token Embedding for Mixture-of-Experts Routing
PROPOSAL: We will modify the previous proposal to incorporate an additional clustering step, where the Mixture-of-Experts router is instantiated for each cluster of visual tokens. This will enable the model to learn multiple specialized experts for each cluster of visually similar tokens, further improving expert specialization and generation quality.
CONTROLS: Baselines: 1) Current token-choice routing, 2) DiT-MoE with expert choice routing (EC-DiT), 3) DiT-MoE with ViTE (proposed in turn 2), 4) REVISED: DiT-MoE with hierarchical token embedding
COST: 22000
PREDICTION: With this revised approach, we expect a significant improvement in expert specialization and generation quality, particularly on tasks that require nuanced visual understanding. However, the increased modeling complexity and potential over-specialization of experts may lead to decreased efficiency and scalability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Routing for Mixture-of-Experts in Diffusion Transformers
PROPOSAL: To improve the efficiency and scalability of the Mixture-of-Experts router, we propose adapting a dimensionality reduction technique, such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA) or t-SNE, to reduce the dimensionality of the visual token embeddings, thereby reducing the computational complexity of the routing mechanism. We will also investigate other efficient routing strategies, such as agglomerative clustering and hierarchical routing, to further optimize the model.
CONTROLS: Baselines: 1) Current token-choice routing, 2) DiT-MoE with expert choice routing (EC-DiT), 3) DiT-MoE with ViTE (proposed in turn 2), 4) REVISED: DiT-MoE with hierarchical token embedding
COST: 28000
PREDICTION: By reducing the dimensionality of the visual token embeddings, we expect to improve the efficiency and scalability of the Mixture-of-Experts router, while maintaining or improving the generation quality. However, the optimal dimensionality reduction technique and routing strategy for DiT-MoE remain to be determined.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Quantifying Expert-Input Relationships in Diffusion Transformers
PROPOSAL: Investigate the quality of input tokens for MoE-based DiTs using mutual information and deformable convolution techniques to understand whether current routing schemes can learn non-overlapping patterns in the continuous space of image patches, a key requirement for expert specialization.
CONTROLS: (1) Dense DiT baseline, (2) Token-choice routing with entropy-based routing as used in DiT-MoE, and (3) an ablation where the expert input is directly fed as a static map to reflect complete correlation between input tokens.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: Expected to find that MoE-based DiTs using token-choice routing struggle to learn truly non-overlapping patterns in the continuous space of image patches. Zonewise routing could fail to learn effective expert input representations if the initial segmentation lacks spatial locality, while relying on only static correlation may simply lead to inserting expert weights upon heavily redundant input features.

Paper Classification Info:
 paper type: Experimental only
 data type: Real-world data only
 experimental domains: text-to-image generation

TITLE: Incorporating prior knowledge on offset patterns
PROPOSAL: We incorporate prior knowledge on the distribution of offset patterns using Limited-Memory Gaussian Processes (LMGPs) as the prior distribution of the offset. LMGPs allow us to model the offset as a Gaussian process with a sparse kernel, capturing the complex, abrupt, and non-Markovian patterns of the offset. We will use the LMGP model as a learned prior on the offset and augment our offline RL training with an LMGP-based offset prediction component. This addition enables the agent to leverage prior knowledge and adapt to unknown shifts in the observation function more effectively.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Investigating a Generalized Feature Cancellator for Robust Offline RL
PROPOSAL: Train and test a generalized form of the feature cancellator technique, which modifies the policy update equations to cancel out the effects of stationary features in the observations. This technique has shown promise in extending the applicability of offline RL methods to partially observable environments with additive noise. We will use Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) as the base offline RL algorithm and apply the cancellator to the feature vector while training on the stationary offline dataset from the observation space.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Surrogate-Based Offline Meta-Learning for Adapting to Temporally Ordered Observation Shifts
PROPOSAL: Introduce a meta-learning approach to adapt the pre-trained offline policy to unseen patterns of non-stationarity during evaluation, without interacting with the environment. We leverage a modification of the surrogate loss scheme for meta-reinforcement learning, where the meta-objective is defined as minimizing the expected difference between the pre-trained policy's performance and its performance when robustified against novel offsets appearing during the current episode. The training process involves sampling a subset of the offline dataset, which is then partitioned across episodes with randomly introduced additive offsets. A pre-trained policy is then adapted to each episode subset based on the surrogate loss function.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed meta-learning approach with the generalized feature cancellator in combination with PPO from proposal 1 and evaluate both in conjunction with standard PPO on synthetic benchmarks with temporally ordered observation shifts.
COST: 144
PREDICTION: We expect that on common synthetic benchmarks, the meta-learning adaptation should show robust improvements, around 20-25% better than standard PPO in environments where the pre-trained policy has prior experience with similar offsets, but had limited exposure compared to having the full suite of offsets. Diminishing returns may occur as the number of adaptation episodes increases, given that reducing the pre-trained policy's exposure to offsets could also inflate its variance towards unseen ones.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Contrastive Regularization for Robust Offline RL Policies under Observation Shifts
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel regularization term to the standard offline RL objective, inspired by contrastive learning techniques from computer vision. This term encourages the policy to distinguish between observations from the training data and those from testing data with observation shifts. By regularizing the invariance of the policy to these shifts, the agent learns to generalize more effectively to unseen scenarios. The goal is to improve the robustness of offline RL policies under observation shifts without additional online interaction or hyperparameter tuning.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the contrastive regularization approach alongside the methods from proposals 1-5 on a range of synthetic and real-world benchmarks with observation shifts, such as the robot navigation and manipulation datasets from the Girdhar robot control suite.
COST: 864
PREDICTION: We expect to see consistent improvements in policy robustness and generalization, particularly in scenarios with large or abrupt observation shifts, as the contrastive regularization term encourages the agent to learn more invariant features and behavior. However, there may be some trade-off in terms of training stability and computational efficiency, as the regularization term requires additional computation and potential hyperparameter tuning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Offline Pessimistic Value Estimation with Offset-Aware Exploration
PROPOSAL: 
Train a neural network-based offline RL agent using pessimistic value estimation and a novel exploration bonus that incorporates knowledge of the per-dimension offsets. At each state-action pair, estimate the minimum value it could achieve under any possible offset value. Combine this pessimistic estimate with an exploration bonus that rewards promising actions based on the agent's understanding of the offsets. Train on a MoTiFin dataset which includes fine-grained, simulated control scenes of robot manipulation, with per-dimension offsets introduced following complex real-world time-series patterns.
CONTROLS: Baseline experiments against standard offline RL algorithms using tabular representations, episodic reinforceement learning, and Q-value updates and ablate the exploration strategy to test its contribution to robustness against non-stationarity.
COST: 60000
PREDICTION: The agent trained with this approach should outperform baselines in the majority of manipulation tasks, but might struggle with more complex or rare offset sequences where accurate estimation becomes challenging.

TITLE: Meta-Pose Estimation with Scenario-Diversity Enhancement
PROPOSAL: 
Design a meta-learning framework that trains on a structured set of agent poses (positions, orientations, etc.) and learns to adapt to partially observable observation functions by predicting the underlying state given a corrupted perception of it. To enhance scenario diversity, use data augmentation methods that simulate exposures to unknown, unseen types of offsets, but systematically preserve the transitions and reward structure of the original environment to prevent overfitting. Evaluate the model on the robot navigation simulation where full and corrupted observations are compared, with offsets generated according to temporal patterns specific to robotics applications.
CONTROLS: Perform empty-state pose estimation evaluations as the control to understand how the approach generalizes in different robot configurations and places.
COST: 90000
PREDICTION: The model should effectively adapt to unseen mask configurations and unknown aspects of the environment at test time, then achieve lower error rates in estimating the correct pose in partially observable variants of scenarios that occur in data augmentation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unified Conditional VAEs for Multi-Modal Reasoning and Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose to extend the Conditional Variational Autoencoder (CVAE) framework to handle both visual and text modalities, enabling the model to reason and generate coherent image-text sequences. We introduce a unified probabilistic model that incorporates a stochastic visual encoder and a text decoder, conditioned on the generated visual representation. This will allow the model to capture the complex relationships between visual and text inputs and generate consistent, meaningful image-text pairs.
CONTROLS: We will compare our proposed model with existing CVAE-based approaches that specialize in text or image generation, and ablate the contributions of the stochastic visual encoder and text decoder by conditioning only on one modality or removing the CVAE framework altogether. We will evaluate the performance using a combination of image/text reconstruction likelihood (BCE, BER), text coherence (ROUGE-1, ROUGE- L), and image quality metrics (PSNR, SSIM).
COST: 14000
PREDICTION: We expect our unified CVAE to outperform specialized models in both visual and text modalities, and achieve improved image-text coherence and quality compared to conditional models that don't capture the inter-modal relationships. However, we anticipate potential convergence issues due to the complexity of the probabilistic formulation and increased dimensionality of the model parameters which might slow down the training process.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: REVISED 2. Unified Conditional VAEs for Multi-Modal Reasoning and Learning
PROPOSAL: We revise the proposal for Unified Conditional VAEs for Multi-Modal Reasoning and Learning by placing an emphasis on efficiency and scalability. To address the complexities of traditional CVAE architectures, particularly when dealing with long chains of thought, we shift our focus to a sequence-by-sequence model inspired by the area of state-space transformers. This modification will leverage a richer, learned sequence of states, facilitating more complex reasoning and reducing the number of parameters required. Furthermore, we will utilize graph-based attention to explicitly capture hierarchical relationships in both visual and text inputs, enabling efficient spatial and sequential reasoning.
CONTROLS: We will compare our proposed sequence-by-sequence model with ablated models that exclude the learned states, as well as with other competitive state-of-the-art models for multi-modal reasoning and learning.
COST: 24000
PREDICTION: We expect the proposed sequence-by-sequence model to outperform traditional CVAE-based approaches in efficiency and effectiveness, particularly on visually grounded and reasoning-intensive tasks, such as image-based spatial reasoning and topographic map generation. However, we anticipate reduced interpretability and potential training instability due to the increased complexity of the learned state space, which may undermine desired state-of-the-art performance.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: REVISED 3. Scaling Ranked-Attention Transformers for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Vision-and-Language Models
PROPOSAL: We revise the proposal to refocus on handling the severe memory and computational requirements of Ranked-Attention Transformers for efficient chain-of-thought reasoning in vision-and-language models. We propose to use a dynamic macro-step size, which adjusts the granularity of the attention mechanism based on the input sequence length, to reduce the total number of attention operations and alleviate the memory bottleneck. Additionally, we explore the effects of using knowledge distillation to transfer the knowledge from a larger model to a smaller one, which reduces the computational requirements while still maintaining the performance. These strategies will ensure that efficient chain-of-thought reasoning can be achieved without compromising on model quality and increasing the barrier to entry for these vision-and-language models.
CONTROLS: We will compare our proposed approach with other competitive methods for reducing the computational requirements of vision-and-language models and evaluate the trade-offs between model size, training speed, and performance on visually grounded tasks.
COST: 30000
PREDICTION: We expect the revised approach to offer improved scalability for vision-and-language models, particularly on tasks with complex input sequences, and to achieve comparable performance to larger models while reducing the training time by up to 50%. However, we anticipate reduced performance on tasks requiring fine-grained attention mechanisms due to the coarser macro-step size used in the revised approach.

TITLE: Unified Visual and Logical Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
PROPOSAL: Refine the TT600-DDIM setup by incorporating a switchable attention mechanism and knowledge distillation based on a child model. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Combining Transformers with Iterative Visual Composition for Unified Multi-Modal Reasoning
PROPOSAL: Train a multimodal transformer model, which at each reasoning step generates both textual logic and visual state transitions. For visual generation, instead of relying on autoregressive image synthesis, we use an iterative visual composition method, decomposing the image into smaller components (objects or regions) that are generated and composited together. For each reasoning step, the model conditionally selects an operation from a learned vocabulary (e.g., copy, move, scale, etc.) that transforms the previously generated visual state.
CONTROLS: 
- Textual CoT ablation: disable the visual generation of the model.
- Visual only baseline: use a separate image generator to produce the final image from a set of intermediate textual outputs.
COST: 30000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect this combination to be more stable and efficient than purely autoregressive approaches, especially when the reasoning chain involves transformation of the visual state. However, we also predict that its performance will be strained when the number of visual objects or regions increases, which could limit its scalability in certain scenarios.

PROPOSAL: To address the training instability issue of long multi-modal reasoning chains, we propose a hierarchical CoT (HCotT) framework that breaks down the reasoning process into smaller sub-chains, enabling parallel and distributed computation across sub-chains. Within each sub-chain, we apply a localized attention mechanism to update the visual state, and utilize a set of task-specific sub-goals to re-weight the importance of different sub-chains. This hierarchical approach helps to reduce the length of each sub-chain and disentangle dependencies between sub-chains, stabilizing the training process.
CONTROLS: 
- Standard CoT model for comparison.
- Parallelized CoT ablation: degrade the model to single-chain parallel processing without sub-goals and task-specific re-weighting.
COST: 70000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By effectively dividing long chains into smaller, manageable sub-chains, we anticipate significant improvements in the convergence rate and stability of the HCotT model, allowing for longer reasoning sessions and better generalization performance. However, we also predict that manually specifying sub-goals and task-specific weights may become increasingly challenging with more complex tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Mix-and-Match Initializations for Improved Training in Multi-Modal Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We investigate the effect of initializations on the training process of multi-modal reasoning models. Specifically, we propose a mix-and-match initialization strategy, where we randomly select and use the representations from different pre-trained language and vision models as the initial input to the reasoning model. This strategy encourages the model to explore diverse initialization conditions and learn robust representations, potentially avoiding the overfitting to a specific initialization method.
CONTROLS: 
- Pre-initialized based on a single model (e.g., ViT or DeiT) for comparison.
- Random initialization ablation: use standard random initialization without pre-trained representations.
COST: 120000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate the mix-and-match initialization strategy to exhibit better performance in early training stages, and potentially even achieve more robust and generalizable representations in the long run. However, given the diverse range of pre-trained models used for initialization, it's possible that this approach may also increase the model's propensity to overfit, especially if the dataset is limited or noisy.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Query and Knowledge-Guided Reasoning (QKG) Incorporation for Improved Coherence
PROPOSAL: We propose to incorporate Query and Knowledge Guided Reasoning (QKG) mechanism into our multi-modal reasoning framework. This involves formulating and answering additional questions throughout the reasoning process that probe the model's understanding of the input scene, objects, and their relationships. This additional supervision and feedback further strengthens the model's ability to maintain a coherent and logical flow of reasoning.
CONTROLS: 
- Standard CoT model for comparison without QKG.
- Partial QKG ablation: degrade the model to having only a few selectively chosen questions within the reasoning stream.
COST: 180000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that incorporating the QKG mechanism will significantly enhance the model's ability to divine logically consistent and visually plausible outcomes, leading to more accurate and coherent reasoning. However, it might add extra computational cost due to additional questions formulation and answering, and thereby require optimized inference mechanisms for deployment.

TITLE: Evaluating and Improving Robustness Against Out-Of-Distribution (OOD) Multi-Modal Reasoning 
PROPOSAL: To better understand the behavior of our multi-modal reasoning models and ensure they can adapt to novel situations, we evaluate their robustness against out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios. We propose a set of OOD challenges that assess the model's ability to reason under uncertainty, handle unseen visual features, and cope with changes in the input format or structure.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline OOD challenge without model adaptation.
- Adaptation with data augmentation and domain adaptation for enhanced robustness.
COST: 300000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the OOD challenges will highlight weaknesses in our current models and guide additional improvements in robustness and generalizability. Although we expect some performance degradation in certain OOD scenarios, we predict that the adapted models will demonstrate a substantial improvement in handling uncertainty and unseen data.

TITLE: Combining Transformers with Iterative Visual Composition for Unified Multi-Modal Reasoning
PROPOSAL: Train a multimodal transformer model, which at each reasoning step generates both textual logic and visual state transitions. For visual generation, instead of relying on autoregressive image synthesis, we use an iterative visual composition method, decomposing the image into smaller components (objects or regions) that are generated and composited together. For each reasoning step, the model conditionally selects an operation from a learned vocabulary (e.g., copy, move, scale, etc.) that transforms the previously generated visual state.
CONTROLS: 
- Textual CoT ablation: disable the visual generation of the model.
- Visual only baseline: use a separate image generator to produce the final image from a set of intermediate textual outputs.
COST: 90000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect this combination to be more stable and efficient than purely autoregressive approaches, especially when the reasoning chain involves transformation of the visual state. However, we also predict that its performance will be strained when the number of visual objects or regions increases, which could limit its scalability in certain scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unified Visual Reasoning by Masked Cross-Modal Fusion
PROPOSAL: We will employ the Vision Transformer (ViT) model in conjunction with a large language model like BART to develop a single, unified model that can perform reasoning-driven text-to-image generation. The model will take a text prompt as input and generate intermediate visual representations that capture the evolving visual state transitions, which will then be used to generate images that summarize these transitions. To achieve this, we will introduce a masked cross-modal fusion module where the model is trained to predict the masked parts of the visual representations and the language outputs simultaneously, forcing the model to tightly interleave textual logic with visual state transitions.
CONTROLS: Experiment with text-only and image-only baselines for comparison and check the impact of different masking ratios on the model's performance.
COST: 2675
PREDICTION: This approach will lead to a notable performance boost on text-to-image generation tasks such as generating images from topographic contour maps and solving jigsaw puzzles. However, the model's ability to reason may not generalize equally well to tasks that require more subtle visual or logical reasoning.

CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the revised model with the original masked cross-modal fusion model and experiment with different glimpse schedules (e.g., selective glimpsing, rapid glimpsing) to investigate their impact on the model's performance and training stability.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: The revised model will show a significant improvement in performance on tasks such as jigsaw puzzle solving and visual question answering, and its reliance on glimpses of visual attention will make it more computationally efficient during inference. However, the model's ability to generalize to new tasks and longer reasoning chains may still be limited.

TITLE: Emphasizing Long-Range Dependencies through Stochastic Attention
PROPOSAL: To address the issue of long-range dependency modeling and optimization in the unified visual reasoning model, we will propose a stochastic attention mechanism that samples a set of attention tokens from a scaled mixture distribution. The mechanism will dynamically balance the importance of short-range and long-range dependencies, enabling the model to better capture the structural transformations involved in complex visual reasoning tasks such as navigation and rearrangement.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the model with stochastic attention to the original model and experiment with different scales of the mixture distribution to find the optimal trade-off between short-range and long-range dependencies.
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: The stochastic attention mechanism will enable the model to achieve a notable performance boost on tasks that require complex visual reasoning and long-range dependency modeling, but it may introduce additional noise that affects the model's generalization to shorter reasoning chains or tasks that require more explicit, step-by-step reasoning.

TITLE: Unified Visual Reasoning by Masked Cross-Modal Fusion
PROPOSAL: We will employ the Vision Transformer (ViT) model in conjunction with a large language model like BART to develop a single, unified model that can perform reasoning-driven text-to-image generation. The model will take a text prompt as input and generate intermediate visual representations that capture the evolving visual state transitions, which will then be used to generate images that summarize these transitions. To achieve this, we will introduce a masked cross-modal fusion module where the model is trained to predict the masked parts of the visual representations and the language outputs simultaneously, forcing the model to tightly interleave textual logic with visual state transitions.
CONTROLS: Experiment with text-only and image-only baselines for comparison and check the impact of different masking ratios on the model's performance.
COST: 8000
PREDICTION: This approach will lead to a notable performance boost on text-to-image generation tasks such as generating images from topographic contour maps and solving jigsaw puzzles. However, the model's ability to reason may not generalize equally well to tasks that require more subtle visual or logical reasoning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Assessing the Role of Gaze Information in Egocentric MLLM's Understanding of User Intent
PROPOSAL: We will evaluate the performance of a state-of-the-art egocentric video question answering model (TEDdeo-PT) on a subset of the Egocentric Question Answering in egocentric Egocentric (E QUE C) dataset modified by the addition of eye-tracking gaze data. We compare this model's performance with its performance on the original, non-augmented dataset. To assess the impact of gaze information accuracy on the model's performance, we perform ablation studies using gaze data generated with different accuracy levels (80%, 90% and 95%).
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Evaluate TEDdeo-PT on E QUE C without any gaze information. Baseline 2: Compare the performance of TEDdeo-PT with the recently released GazeGPT system which incorporates gaze information.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: By incorporating gaze information, TEDdeo-PT's performance on the E QUE C dataset should improve significantly, especially in scenarios where gaze information is most relevant. However, if the model fails to fully leverage the provided gaze data, the increase in performance might be limited.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Gaze Signal Presentation on Egocentric MLLM Performance
PROPOSAL: We design and conduct an experiment where we feed gaze information to an egocentric video question answering model in various formats, such as gaze maps, gaze points, and gaze-based attention masks. We use the_Point-Gaze dataset, which provides accurate and precise eye-tracking gaze data. We compare the model's performance with and without gaze information and ablate different components of the gaze feature. To assess the robustness of our findings, we perform a 5-fold cross-validation on the evaluation set.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Evaluate the model on the original, non-augmented Point-Gaze dataset. We also compare our model's performance with the results from proposal 1 (Assessing the Role of Gaze Information in Egocentric MLLM's Understanding of User Intent) for consistency.
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: The model's performance may vary depending on how gaze information is presented to it. However, if the model fails to adapt to the different gaze formats, this may indicate a limit to its ability to learn from gaze data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Efficacy of Gaze-Conditioned Prompting for Egocentric MLLM
PROPOSAL: We develop a gaze-conditioned prompting approach for egocentric video question answering models. We design and test various gaze-conditioned prompt templates that incorporate gaze information from the Point-Gaze dataset. We evaluate the effectiveness of these prompts using an egocentric video question answering model, and compare the results with the baseline case where the model is not provided with gaze information.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Evaluate the model on the original, non-augmented Point-Gaze dataset without any gaze-conditioned prompts. Baseline 2: Compare our results with those from experiments in proposals 1 and 2 for consistency.
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: The gaze-conditioned prompt templates may significantly improve the model's performance on egocentric video question answering tasks, especially when the model is uncertain about the scene context. However, if the model fails to understand the implicit relationships between gaze information and scene context, it may struggle to generalise to unseen data.

PROPOSAL: We train and evaluate an egocentric video question answering model on a dataset containing a mix of seen and unseen tasks, with and without gaze information. However, if the model fails to leverage the gaze information effectively, the transferability may not be significantly improved.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Gaze Information on Model-Specific Attention Mechanisms
PROPOSAL: We analyze the effect of gaze information on the attention mechanisms of various egocentric video question answering models, including self-attention, cross-attention, and multi-head attention. We train and evaluate these models on the Point-Gaze dataset and analyze the gaze-aware attention scores, identifying the specific attention mechanisms that are most influenced by gaze information.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Evaluate the standard attention mechanisms of the model without gaze information. Baseline 2: Compare our results with those from experiments in proposals 1-4 for consistency.
COST: 4800
PREDICTION: The analysis of gaze-aware attention scores should reveal that the model's attention mechanisms are significantly affected by gaze information, particularly when the gaze signal is most relevant to the task. However, if the model's attention mechanisms fail to adapt to the gaze information, the attention scores may not accurately reflect the importance of gaze cues.

TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of Egocentric MLLM to Gaze Signal Distribution Shifts
PROPOSAL: We evaluate the robustness of an egocentric video question answering model to gaze signal distribution shifts, simulating real-world conditions where the gaze signal distribution may vary across different environments, tasks, or individuals. We use a collection of gaze datasets with different characteristics and transfer the model to a novel environment with a different gaze distribution.

However, if the model can adapt to the novel environment, this would suggest that it has learned robust features that are invariant to gaze signal variations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Developing a Framework for Egocentric MLLM with Gaze-Aware Anomaly Detection
PROPOSAL: We propose a framework for detecting anomalies in egocentric video sequences using gaze information. The framework uses a combination of gaze-aware attention mechanisms and deep learning-based anomaly detection techniques to identify irregularities in the user's behavior. We evaluate the framework on the Point-Gaze dataset and compare its performance with state-of-the-art anomaly detection methods.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Evaluate the standard anomaly detection methods without gaze information. Baseline 2: Compare our results with those from experiments in proposals 1-6 for consistency.
COST: 10080
PREDICTION: The proposed framework should improve the accuracy of anomaly detection in egocentric video sequences, particularly when using gaze information. However, if the framework fails to effectively integrate gaze information with the anomaly detection algorithm, the performance may not be significantly improved.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Gaze Exploitation in Egocentric Vision Transformers
PROPOSAL: We will fine-tune the Hugging Face Vision Transformers (ViT) on the recent egocentric video question answering benchmark, Ego4D, to develop a baseline model capable of processing egocentric videos. We will then train a second model on Ego4D, adding gaze data from the same benchmark but including masking to simulate real-world gaze tracking inaccuracies. For comparison, we will train a third baseline on Ego4D without gaze data.
CONTROLS: ViT-B/16 baseline with and without gaze data, ViT-B/16 with real-world gaze-tracking uncertainty.
COST: 4,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the model with gaze data to outperform the baseline by at least 10%, yet possibly fail to reach a higher-than-baseline accuracy if the gaze data is not reliable enough or if the model underutilizes gaze cues.

This proposal should establish our baseline for egocentric vision transformers and begin to investigate the importance of gaze data in MLLMs.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Evaluating Gaze Exploitation in Egocentric Vision Transformers (Extended)
PROPOSAL: Building on our previous proposal, we will extend the baseline model by incorporating a gaze embedder module that generates gaze-based visual tokens. These tokens will be added to the input of the Vision Transformer, allowing it to directly incorporate gaze information into its processing pipeline. We will also introduce a gaze selector module, which will dynamically select relevant gaze information for the model to focus on.
CONTROLS: We will compare our extended baseline to the original baseline model without gaze data, and to the model trained with gaze data from our previous proposal.
COST: 8,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the extended baseline to outperform the original baseline model, and to potentially rival the performance of the model trained with gaze data, depending on how effectively the gaze embedder and selector modules capture relevant visual information.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Robustness of Egocentric Vision Transformers to Gaze Tracking Uncertainty
PROPOSAL: In this experiment, we will test the robustness of our extended baseline model to varying levels of gaze tracking uncertainty. We will create simulated gaze data with different levels of noise, blur, and occlusion, and measure the model's ability to maintain its performance under these conditions. To further investigate the effects of gaze tracking uncertainty, we will also compare the model's performance with different gaze tracking systems (e.g., eye-tracking glasses, head-mounted cameras) and different gaze representation schemes (e.g., gaze maps, gaze tensors).
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the model's robustness across different gaze tracking systems and gaze representation schemes.
COST: 12,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the model to degrade in performance as the gaze tracking uncertainty increases, but to still maintain a reasonable level of accuracy, especially with gaze representation schemes that can effectively handle noise and occlusion.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Transferability of Egocentric Vision Transformers to Different Environments
PROPOSAL: In this experiment, we will train our extended baseline model on Ego4D and evaluate its performance on a different egocentric video dataset (e.g., Egocentric 360-degree video dataset) with varying environments (e.g., indoor, outdoor, night, day). We will also investigate the transferability of our model to different user populations (e.g., children, adults, individuals with disabilities) by collecting and annotating new datasets. By studying the transferability of our model, we can better assess its generalizability and potential real-world adoption.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of our model on the target dataset to a baseline model trained specifically on the target dataset.
COST: 24,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our model to exhibit some degree of transferability to different environments, but its performance may decline due to significant changes in lighting conditions, object appearance, and viewpoint. The model's ability to generalize across user populations remains to be seen.

TITLE: Investigating the Cost-Effectiveness of Using Gaze Information in Egocentric Vision Transformers
PROPOSAL: In this experiment, we will investigate the cost-effectiveness of using gaze information in egocentric vision transformers by estimating the optimal amount of gaze data required to achieve a given performance level. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Gaze Exploitation in Egocentric Vision Transformers
PROPOSAL: We will fine-tune the Hugging Face Vision Transformers (ViT) on the recent egocentric video question answering benchmark, Ego4D, to develop a baseline model capable of processing egocentric videos. We will then train a second model on Ego4D, adding gaze data from the same benchmark but including masking to simulate real-world gaze tracking inaccuracies. For comparison, we will train a third baseline on Ego4D without gaze data.
CONTROLS: ViT-B/16 baseline with and without gaze data, ViT-B/16 with real-world gaze-tracking uncertainty.
COST: 12,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the model with gaze data to outperform the baseline by at least 10%, yet possibly fail to reach a higher-than-baseline accuracy if the gaze data is not reliable enough or if the model underutilizes gaze cues.

This proposal should establish our baseline for egocentric vision transformers and begin to investigate the importance of gaze data in MLLMs.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Evaluating Gaze Exploitation in Egocentric Vision Transformers (Revised)
PROPOSAL: Building on our previous proposal, we will also explore three variations: 
1. a multi-task learning (MTL) approach, where the model is trained to not only answer questions but also predict gaze locations and estimate gaze-tracking uncertainty.
2. a feedback-controlled gaze input (FCGI) variation, where the model receives gaze feedback and adapts its predictions accordingly.
3. a model using gaze-attentive visual encoding (GAVE), where the model incorporates gaze-guided spatial attention for video processing.
We will evaluate these variations on a subset of Ego4D, measuring their ability to capture user intent and object of attention.
CONTROLS: We will compare our variations to the baseline model on the same metric.
COST: 18,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the MTL and FCGI variations to yield significantly improved performance, but the GAVE may perform similarly to the baseline due to the difficulty in encoding gaze information into spatial attention.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Evaluating Gaze Exploitation in Egocentric Vision Transformers (Extended)
PROPOSAL: Building on our previous proposal, we will extend the baseline model by incorporating a gaze embedder module that generates gaze-based visual tokens. These tokens will be added to the input of the Vision Transformer, allowing it to directly incorporate gaze information into its processing pipeline. We will also introduce a gaze selector module, which will dynamically select relevant gaze information for the model to focus on.
CONTROLS: We will compare our extended baseline to the original baseline model without gaze data, and to the model trained with gaze data from our previous proposal.
COST: 24,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the extended baseline to outperform the original baseline model, and to potentially rival the performance of the model trained with gaze data, depending on how effectively the gaze embedder and selector modules capture relevant visual information.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Robustness of Egocentric Vision Transformers to Gaze Tracking Uncertainty
PROPOSAL: In this experiment, we will test the robustness of our extended baseline model to varying levels of gaze tracking uncertainty. We will create simulated gaze data with different levels of noise, blur, and occlusion, and measure the model's ability to maintain its performance under these conditions. To further investigate the effects of gaze tracking uncertainty, we will also compare the model's performance with different gaze tracking systems (e.g., eye-tracking glasses, head-mounted cameras) and different gaze representation schemes (e.g., gaze maps, gaze tensors).
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the model's robustness across different gaze tracking systems and gaze representation schemes.
COST: 36,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the model to degrade in performance as the gaze tracking uncertainty increases, but to still maintain a reasonable level of accuracy, especially with gaze representation schemes that can effectively handle noise and occlusion.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Transferability of Egocentric Vision Transformers to Different Environments
PROPOSAL: In this experiment, we will train our extended baseline model on Ego4D and evaluate its performance on a different egocentric video dataset (e.g., Egocentric 360-degree video dataset) with varying environments (e.g., indoor, outdoor, night, day). We will also investigate the transferability of our model to different user populations (e.g., children, adults, individuals with disabilities) by collecting and annotating new datasets. By studying the transferability of our model, we can better assess its generalizability and potential real-world adoption.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of our model on the target dataset to a baseline model trained specifically on the target dataset.
COST: 72,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our model to exhibit some degree of transferability to different environments, but its performance may decline due to significant changes in lighting conditions, object appearance, and viewpoint. The model's ability to generalize across user populations remains to be seen.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Modality Conflicts in AR UMMs: A Layer-wise Analysis
PROPOSAL: Train and analyze a range of AR UMMs on text-to-image generation, visual question answering, and image editing benchmarks, focusing on a principled layer-wise decomposition of gradient conflicts between text and vision modalities. We will use the CUB-200-2011 dataset for image classification and retrieval, and the COCO dataset for image captioning and visual question answering. To better quantify the conflicts, we will freeze optimizable parameters in the text and vision embedding spaces and analyze how the inter-modal gradients adapt during fine-tuning.
CONTROLS: Compare against a range of baselines that either do not share parameters between modalities ( multimodal UMMs with modality-specific encoder and decoder) or have a completely non-autoregressive (non-AR) architecture
COST: 684
PREDICTION: By analyzing the cosine similarity and KL-divergence between text and vision gradients, we expect to demonstrate that conflict magnitude decreases as the depth of the network increases, which is more pronounced in image editing due to the discrete image-token sequences' high variance. This effect may stem from the gradually locales reclassification in deeper layers, enabling a better convergence of inter-modal gradients. However, accurately analyzing this phenomenon on smaller datasets, like CUB-200-2011, may be trickier and more costly.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Layer-Specific TRPO for Gradient Conflict Mitigation in AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: Apply Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO) on specific layers of the AR UMM to mitigate gradient conflicts between text and vision. This involves training separate TRPO agents for text and vision, and adjusting their learning rates to ensure stable convergence and minimize inter-modal gradient interference. We will also analyze how the specific number and selection of layers for TRPO impacts overall performance and conflict mitigation.
CONTROLS: Compare with a standard TRPO applied across the entire model, and a range of ablations where specific layers are either frozen or removed
COST: 1020
PREDICTION: By selectively applying TRPO to layers where inter-modal conflicts are most pronounced, we expect to observe a significant boost in performance and a reduction in gradient conflicts with respect to more uniform TRPO application. However, a lack of theory on how tractable trust regions are for finitely-sized networks, and in depth characterizing its effects and especially interactions with layer selection may excite budding and publicly famously frequent system instabilities.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: REVISED Investigating Modality Conflicts in AR UMMs: A Layer-wise Analysis
PROPOSAL: Revise the original layer-wise analysis by incorporating additional experiments that utilize different transformer decoder depths, modalities-specific output spaces, and a more robust method for evaluating gradient conflicts across layers, such as the singular value decomposition (SVD) of the layer-wise gradient matrices.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original layer-wise analysis, the ablated versions where specific layers are omitted, and the previous revised layer-wise analysis
COST: 1368
PREDICTION: By using a more comprehensive and mathematically grounded approach to quantify gradient conflicts, we expect to demonstrate a clearer relationship between conflict magnitude and network depth, and further support the hypothesis that AR UMMs struggle with gradient conflicts due to the differences in the statistical properties of text and vision representations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Layer-Agnostic Gradient Projection for Conflict Mitigation
PROPOSAL: Propose a layer-agnostic gradient projection method for conflict mitigation in AR UMMs. This involves learning a shared projection layer that maps both text and vision gradients to a lower-dimensional space, where they can be combined more effectively. We will evaluate this approach on both synthetic and real-world datasets.
CONTROLS: Compare with the Layer-Specific TRPO and the standard AR UMM without conflict mitigation
COST: 6144
PREDICTION: By decoupling conflict mitigation from layer-specific optimization, we expect to improve the stability and performance of training AR UMMs, as well as reduce the computational overhead of training and inference.

TITLE: Gradient Alignment via Adversarial Training
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of adversarial training to align the gradients of text and vision in AR UMMs. We will train a generator to produce gradients that are indistinguishable from the actual gradients, while a discriminator tries to differentiate between the two.
CONTROLS: Compare with the baseline AR UMM and Layer-Specific TRPO method
COST: 6840
PREDICTION: By aligning the gradients through adversarial training, we expect to reduce the gradient conflicts and improve the performance of the AR UMM on various tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Modality Conflicts in AR UMMs: A Layer-wise Analysis
PROPOSAL: Train and analyze a range of AR UMMs on text-to-image generation, visual question answering, and image editing benchmarks, focusing on a principled layer-wise decomposition of gradient conflicts between text and vision modalities. We will use the CUB-200-2011 dataset for image classification and retrieval, and the COCO dataset for image captioning and visual question answering. To better quantify the conflicts, we will freeze optimizable parameters in the text and vision embedding spaces and analyze how the inter-modal gradients adapt during fine-tuning.
CONTROLS: Compare against a range of baselines that either do not share parameters between modalities ( multimodal UMMs with modality-specific encoder and decoder) or have a completely non-autoregressive (non-AR) architecture
COST: 2048
PREDICTION: By analyzing the cosine similarity and KL-divergence between text and vision gradients, we expect to demonstrate that conflict magnitude decreases as the depth of the network increases, which is more pronounced in image editing due to the discrete image-token sequences' high variance. This effect may stem from the gradually locales reclassification in deeper layers, enabling a better convergence of inter-modal gradients. However, accurately analyzing this phenomenon on smaller datasets, like CUB-200-2011, may be trickier and more costly.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Layer-Specific TRPO for Gradient Conflict Mitigation in AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: Apply Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO) on specific layers of the AR UMM to mitigate gradient conflicts between text and vision. This involves training separate TRPO agents for text and vision, and adjusting their learning rates to ensure stable convergence and minimize inter-modal gradient interference. We will also analyze how the specific number and selection of layers for TRPO impacts overall performance and conflict mitigation.
CONTROLS: Compare with a standard TRPO applied across the entire model, and a range of ablations where specific layers are either frozen or removed
COST: 3072
PREDICTION: By selectively applying TRPO to layers where inter-modal conflicts are most pronounced, we expect to observe a significant boost in performance and a reduction in gradient conflicts with respect to more uniform TRPO application. However, a lack of theory on how tractable trust regions are for finitely-sized networks, and in depth characterizing its effects and especially interactions with layer selection may excite budding and publicly famously frequent system instabilities.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED Investigating Modality Conflicts in AR UMMs: A Layer-wise Analysis
PROPOSAL: Revise the original layer-wise analysis by incorporating additional experiments that utilize different transformer decoder depths and modalities-specific output spaces. We will analyze how the conflicting magnitudes change with the number of layers, varying any and when the AR text-to-image translation interactions are represented. Additionally, to gain insight into the cause of the conflicts, we will also examine the marginal distributions of text and vision representations at different layers.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original layer-wise analysis and the ablated versions where specific layers are omitted
COST: 3072
PREDICTION: This added analytical depth should provide further support for the hypothesis that gradient conflict magnitude decreases with the depth of the network, and demonstrate how the need to infer this information assings numeral relation mask.

 ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Assessing the Statistical Gap between Image-Tokens and Natural Language Sequences
PROPOSAL: Investigate the statistical properties of discretized image-token sequences and natural language sequences, to better understand why AR UMMs struggle with gradient conflicts. We will perform a range of statistical tests (KL-divergence, mutual information, etc.) to characterize and compare the two domains.
CONTROLS: Use the image-token and text sequences generated by the UMMs as input
COST: 4096
PREDICTION: By revealing the nature of the statistical gap between these two modalities, we expect to gain valuable insights into why UMMs struggle with gradient conflicts, and potentially inform the design of more effective conflict mitigation strategies.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: REVISED Investigating Modality Conflicts in AR UMMs: A Layer-wise Analysis
PROPOSAL: Revise the original layer-wise analysis by incorporating additional experiments that utilize different transformer decoder depths, modalities-specific output spaces, and a more robust method for evaluating gradient conflicts across layers, such as the singular value decomposition (SVD) of the layer-wise gradient matrices.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original layer-wise analysis, the ablated versions where specific layers are omitted, and the previous revised layer-wise analysis
COST: 4096
PREDICTION: By using a more comprehensive and mathematically grounded approach to quantify gradient conflicts, we expect to demonstrate a clearer relationship between conflict magnitude and network depth, and further support the hypothesis that AR UMMs struggle with gradient conflicts due to the differences in the statistical properties of text and vision representations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Layer-Agnostic Gradient Projection for Conflict Mitigation
PROPOSAL: Propose a layer-agnostic gradient projection method for conflict mitigation in AR UMMs. This involves learning a shared projection layer that maps both text and vision gradients to a lower-dimensional space, where they can be combined more effectively. We will evaluate this approach on both synthetic and real-world datasets.
CONTROLS: Compare with the Layer-Specific TRPO and the standard AR UMM without conflict mitigation
COST: 6144
PREDICTION: By decoupling conflict mitigation from layer-specific optimization, we expect to improve the stability and performance of training AR UMMs, as well as reduce the computational overhead of training and inference.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Improving Gradient Alignment using Modality-Specific Covariance Matrices
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of modality-specific covariance matrices to improve the alignment of text and vision gradients in AR UMMs. We will learn separate covariance matrices for text and vision and use them to normalize the gradients before combining them.
CONTROLS: Compare with the Layer-Specific TRPO and Layer-Agnostic Gradient Projection methods
COST: 8192
PREDICTION: By accounting for the differences in the distribution of text and vision gradients, we expect to enhance the alignment of the gradients and improve the performance of the AR UMM on various tasks.

ACTION: ADD

PROPOSAL: Perform a hyperparameter search to identify the optimal settings for the Layer-Specific TRPO, Modality-Specific Covariance Matrices, and Layer-Agnostic Gradient Projection methods. PREDICTION: By identifying the optimal hyperparameters and adaptively adjusting them, we expect to achieve state-of-the-art performance on various tasks and reduce the gradient conflicts in AR UMMs.

PROPOSAL: Revise the Layer-Specific TRPO method by incorporating a feedback loop that adjusts the learning rates of individual layers based on the performance on a validation set. PREDICTION: By incorporating the feedback loop, we expect to improve the stability and performance of the Layer-Specific TRPO method and reduce the gradient conflicts in AR UMMs.

TITLE: Transfer Learning for Conflict Mitigation in AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of transfer learning to adapt the knowledge learned from one task to conflict mitigation in another task. We will train a multi-task model on a range of AR UMM tasks and then fine-tune it on a specific task with conflict mitigation methods.
CONTROLS: Compare with the training from scratch and baseline AR UMM
COST: 16384
PREDICTION: By leveraging the transferred knowledge, we expect to improve the performance of the AR UMM on the target task and reduce the gradient conflicts.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Uncovering the85xE discrepancies: A Layer-wise Gradient Analysis for AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: Investigate the gradient disagreements between text and image modalities in autoregressive Unified Multimodal Models (AR UMMs) using a proposed layer-wise gradient analysis. This will involve modifying an AR-UMM to compute and visualize gradients separately for text and image inputs at each transformer layer, and then analyzing the results across selected benchmark datasets (e.g. COCO, Flicker30k, Conceptual Captions). The goal is to elucidate the spatial and temporal distribution of inter-modal conflicts.
CONTROLS: Compare with a UMM without modality-sharing and a vanilla transformer baseline, also assess the effect of removing vector quantization regularization.
COST: 700
PREDICTION: This layer-wise gradient analysis will reveal a complex interplay between text and image gradients, with discrepancies emerging in the mid-to-upper layers, where abstract and semantic representations begin to dominate. AR UMMs will outperform non-modality sharing UMMs, but be outperformed by vanilla transformers at early layers, highlighting the need for modality-specific tuning or augmentations. 

Assuming you're implementing this layer-wise gradient analysis in the mid-to-upper transformer layers, total training time may be quite high, this might very well drop to 2100 GPU hours given the Architecture plus many (those many) back-and-forth passes in the training loop.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Modality-Specific Perturbations for Gradient Regularization
PROPOSAL: Design and evaluate modality-specific perturbation strategies to regularize the learning process of AR-UMMs and reduce inter-modal conflicts. This will involve adding a small perturbation term to the loss function for either text or image inputs during training, and tuning its strength to observe improvements in modality sharing while minimizing performance drops for individual tasks. Investigate perturbation schedules, including fixed-strength, dynamic-strength, and inverse-frequency-based perturbations.
CONTROLS: Compare with standard L2 regularization and explore how perturbation strength affects performance on selected benchmarks.
COST: 5200
PREDICTION: By regularizing text and image inputs separately, we will observe significant improvements in modality sharing and inter-modal conflicts, especially on tasks like text-to-image generation. A modality-specific perturbation strength, possibly decreasing at early layers, will emerge as a key hyperparameter choice, even outperforming standard L2 regularization methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Meta-Optimization for Modality-Specific Hyperparameter Tuning
PROPOSAL: Design a meta-optimization approach to automatically tune modality-specific hyperparameters, such as perturbation strengths, learning rates, and optimizer schedules, for the AR-UMM. This will involve training a meta-model to adapt the hyperparameters of the AR-UMM across tasks and datasets, using a subset of the available data for meta-training and validating its performance on a hold-out set. Investigate two different meta-learning algorithms: Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) and Reptile.
CONTROLS: Compare with manual hyperparameter tuning and explore how the meta-optimization approach affects performance on a range of tasks and benchmarks.
COST: 8640
PREDICTION: By meta-optimizing modality-specific hyperparameters, we expect significant performance improvements across a range of tasks, including text-to-image generation, visual question answering, and image editing. The meta-model will learn to adapt to the specific characteristics of each task and dataset, resulting in better generalization and efficiency.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Asymmetric Architecture Search for AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: Introduce an asymmetric architecture search approach to modify the AR-UMM architecture, allowing for the exploration of different module arrangements and complexities for text and image modalities. This will be achieved by using a combination of reinforcement learning and gradient-based optimization to dynamically adjust the architecture during training. Investigate two different search objectives: one focused on modality-specific accuracy and the other addressing inter-modal conflict.
CONTROLS: Compare with a fixed architecture and analyze the effect of the searched architecture on modality-specific performance and inter-modal conflict.
COST: 10800
PREDICTION: By applying asymmetric architecture search, we will observe significant improvements in inter-modal conflict and modality-specific accuracy. The searched architecture will reveal an interesting asymmetry, with more complex text modules and simpler image modules emerging as the best configuration. This approach will offer a new paradigm for designing and adapting AR-UMM architectures to specific tasks and datasets.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Graph-Based Modality Fusion for AR-UMMs
PROPOSAL: Design a graph-based modality fusion approach to explicitly model and mitigate inter-modal conflicts in AR-UMMs. This will involve representing each modality as a separate graph, and then defining a fusion operation that combines the two graphs in a way that preserves their structural properties. Investigate using graph attention networks (GATs) or graph diffusion operators (GDOs) for fusion.
CONTROLS: Compare with a joint embedding space approach and assess its impact on modality-specific performance and inter-modal conflict.
COST: 13200
PREDICTION: By using graph-based modality fusion, we will see significant reduction in inter-modal conflict and improvement in modality-specific accuracy. The graph-based approach will allow for more nuanced control over the fusion process, enabling better preservation of modality-specific information and leading to more coherent joint representations. This approach will provide a flexible framework for exploring different modality fusion strategies and architectures.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Mixed-Scale Training for Efficient Inter-Modal Learning
PROPOSAL: Introduce a mixed-scale training approach to mitigate inter-modal conflicts and improve the efficiency of AR-UMMs. This will involve training the model on multiple scales (e.g., small, medium, large) and manipulating the model architecture accordingly (e.g., increasing/decreasing the number of transformer layers) during training. Investigate using a coarse-to-fine training schedule or a fixed-scale approach with adjustable hyperparameters.
CONTROLS: Compare with fixed-scale training and standard hyperparameter tuning, and assess the effect on modality-specific performance and training efficiency.
COST: 15600
PREDICTION: By applying mixed-scale training, we will observe improvements in both modality-specific accuracy and training efficiency. The mixed-scale approach will allow the model to adapt to different scales and complexities, enabling more effective learning of inter-modal relationships and facilitating the transfer of knowledge across tasks and datasets. This approach will provide a scalable and efficient way to train AR-UMMs on large-scale datasets.

TITLE: Uncovering the85xE discrepancies: A Layer-wise Gradient Analysis for AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: Investigate the gradient disagreements between text and image modalities in autoregressive Unified Multimodal Models (AR UMMs) using a proposed layer-wise gradient analysis. This will involve modifying an AR-UMM to compute and visualize gradients separately for text and image inputs at each transformer layer, and then analyzing the results across selected benchmark datasets (e.g. COCO, Flicker30k, Conceptual Captions). The goal is to elucidate the spatial and temporal distribution of inter-modal conflicts.

AR UMMs will outperform non-modality sharing UMMs, but be outperformed by vanilla transformers at early layers, highlighting the need for modality-specific tuning or augmentations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Quantifying Inter-Modal Conflicts in AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: Train a unimodal AR transformer for text-to-image generation on a real-world benchmark (e.g. Meshed-MC or COCO) and a unimodal AR transformer for language modeling on the standard language dataset (e.g. Text8 or BooksCorpus). Then, train a multimodal AR UMM that combines the two tasks on the same transformer architecture. Compute the difference in gradients and representational similarity across each layer between the multimodal and two unimodal models, and analyze them to identify modality-specific differences and conflicts.
CONTROLS: The unimodal language model serves as a control for the vision-language similarities in the multimodal model, while the unimodal vision model controls for the potential differences between different datasets.
COST: 1331.84
PREDICTION: This experiment will help identify the source of modality conflicts and where they arise in the network, and we expect to see statistically significant differences in gradients and representational similarity between multimodal and unimodal models. However, the identified conflicts may not directly suggest a clear solution to reduce them.

TITLE: Modality-Aware Transformer Architectures
PROPOSAL: Introduce a new lineup of modality-aware transformer architectures, each designed to respect modality-specific differences and reduce conflicts while preserving the architectural simplicity of pure autoregressive models. These architectures will include: (1) a copy mechanism that learns to copy visual or textual information selectively, (2) a two-stream architecture that separates text and vision processing entirely, (3) a hybrid architecture that combines autoregressive and diffusion-based processing, and (4) a modular architecture that allows for component-wise swapping between text and vision modules. Evaluate each architecture on real-world benchmarks (text-to-image generation, visual question answering, image editing) and compare their performance to baselines.
CONTROLS: Compare each new architecture to a set of established baselines, including the original autoregressive UMM, diffusion-based models, and task-specific architectures.

PREDICTION: These architectures will show efficiency improvements and, in some cases, performance gains over existing baselines, particularly in tasks where modality conflicts are severe. However, implementing and training these models may require significant computational resources, and optimizing their performance may require extensive hyperparameter tuning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Quantifying Inter-Modal Conflicts in AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: Train a unimodal AR transformer for text-to-image generation on a real-world benchmark (e.g. Meshed-MC or COCO) and a unimodal AR transformer for language modeling on the standard language dataset (e.g. Text8 or BooksCorpus). Then, train a multimodal AR UMM that combines the two tasks on the same transformer architecture. Compute the difference in gradients and representational similarity across each layer between the multimodal and two unimodal models, and analyze them to identify modality-specific differences and conflicts.
CONTROLS: The unimodal language model serves as a control for the vision-language similarities in the multimodal model, while the unimodal vision model controls for the potential differences between different datasets.
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: This experiment will help identify the source of modality conflicts and where they arise in the network, and we expect to see statistically significant differences in gradients and representational similarity between multimodal and unimodal models. However, the identified conflicts may not directly suggest a clear solution to reduce them.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Gradients' Intersection, Union, and Difference
PROPOSAL: Build on the previous experiment and divide each transformer layer into a set of sub-networks, each operating on the total token sequence but focusing only on text tokens, only on vision tokens, or on interactions between text and vision. Calculate the gradients of the loss function for each sub-network and compare their intersection, union, and difference to pinpoint the sources of modality conflicts and synergies. This will help us understand whether conflicts arise from competing objectives, modality-specific representations, or interactions between text and vision.
CONTROLS: Compare the gradients' intersection, union, and difference across layers to understand when and where modality conflicts and synergies emerge.
COST: 8000
PREDICTION: This analysis will reveal interesting patterns on when and where modality conflicts emerge, but identifying clear rules or strategies to mitigate them may require additional experimentation or theoretical analysis. This approach might overfit to specific layer types or input/output formats if not properly regularized.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Investigating Gradients' Intersection, Union, and Difference (Revised)
PROPOSAL: Update the previous experiment by incorporating an attention-weighted version of the input tokens. Instead of dividing the transformer layer into sub-networks, apply a modality-specific attention mask to each token in the input sequence, allowing the model to selectively focus on either text or vision tokens (or their interactions). Compute the gradients of the loss function for each attention-masked input sequence and compare their intersection, union, and difference to pinpoint the sources of modality conflicts and synergies.
CONTROLS: The revised experiment controls for the previous sub-network division by testing the effect of modality-specific attention on gradients' intersection, union, and difference.
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: This revised experiment will provide a more fine-grained understanding of how modality-specific attention affects gradients and representational similarity, potentially revealing insights into the mechanisms driving modality conflicts and synergies. However, choosing optimal attention masks and evaluating their impact on training efficiency may require extensive tuning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Modality-Aware Transformer Architectures
PROPOSAL: Introduce a new lineup of modality-aware transformer architectures, each designed to respect modality-specific differences and reduce conflicts while preserving the architectural simplicity of pure autoregressive models. These architectures will include: (1) a copy mechanism that learns to copy visual or textual information selectively, (2) a two-stream architecture that separates text and vision processing entirely, (3) a hybrid architecture that combines autoregressive and diffusion-based processing, and (4) a modular architecture that allows for component-wise swapping between text and vision modules. Evaluate each architecture on real-world benchmarks (text-to-image generation, visual question answering, image editing) and compare their performance to baselines.
CONTROLS: Compare each new architecture to a set of established baselines, including the original autoregressive UMM, diffusion-based models, and task-specific architectures.
COST: 12000
PREDICTION: These architectures will show efficiency improvements and, in some cases, performance gains over existing baselines, particularly in tasks where modality conflicts are severe. However, implementing and training these models may require significant computational resources, and optimizing their performance may require extensive hyperparameter tuning.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Modality-Aware Transformer Architectures (Revised)
PROPOSAL: Update the modality-aware architectures to incorporate a novel global-local attention mechanism, which balances the global context information from both text and vision modalities while selectively focusing on local, modality-specific information. This mechanism, coupled with a weight-tied, shared-transformer-weights strategy, will share statistical patterns and relationships between text and vision while respecting their distinct characteristics. Combine this with the modality-specific copy mechanism from the previous design. Evaluate this revised architecture on a range of tasks and compare its performance to the previous designs and established baselines.
CONTROLS: The weight-tied, shared-transformer-weights strategy will serve as a good control for understanding the impact of shared transformer weights across text and vision, while the global-local attention mechanism will help identify its effect on modality-specific information.
COST: 18000
PREDICTION: This revised architecture will show significant efficiency improvements and potential performance gains over existing baselines, particularly in tasks where modality conflicts are subtle, due to its ability to balance global and local information. However, optimizing the global-local attention mechanism and weight-tied strategy may require extensive hyperparameter tuning. Additionally, the validation on a range of tasks may introduce variability in performance metrics.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Understanding Modality Conflicts through Information Bottlenecks
PROPOSAL: Introduce a series of experiments to investigate how modality conflicts arise and propagate through the model's information bottleneck. By computing the mutual information between text and vision embeddings at different stages of the transformer, we can identify where and when the model loses the ability to capture multimodal relationships. We will also analyze the effect of modality-specific regularization (e.g., feature dropout or modality masking) on the model's ability to capture modality distinctions while preserving the information bottleneck.
CONTROLS: The modal-specific regularizations will serve as a good control for understanding the impact of enforcing modality distinctions on the information bottleneck.
COST: 9000
PREDICTION: This analysis will reveal interesting insights into how modality conflicts arise and propagate through the model, and we expect to see a clear relationship between modality-specific regularization and the preservation of the information bottleneck. However, evaluating the full impact of these techniques on performance and efficiency may require extensive experimentation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Model Robustness to Modality Corruptions
PROPOSAL: Design a suite of corruption-based evaluations to assess the robustness of the modality-aware transformer architectures and the standard UMM to modality-specific corruptions (e.g., noise, distortions, variations in image size or resolution, text misspellings). We will apply these corruptions to the input data and evaluate the model's performance under these conditions, comparing the results to the standard UMM and the modality-aware architectures.
CONTROLS: The corrupteds datasets will control for the robustness of the models under different types of corruptions.
COST: 14000
PREDICTION: We expect to see marked robustness improvements in the modality-aware architectures over the standard UMM, as these architectures are designed to respect modality distinctions and capture modality-specific relationships. However, identifying the most effective corruption-based metrics for evaluating robustness may require significant experimentation and discussion with domain experts.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Investigating Gradients' Intersection, Union, and Difference (Revised Again)
PROPOSAL: Update the gradient intersection, union, and difference analysis to incorporate a phase-change-based analysis. By computing these metrics at different stages of the training process, we can understand how the modality conflicts evolve and change as the model learns and adapts. We will also examine the relationship between modality conflicts and the convergence of the model, hypothesizing that reduced modality conflicts will lead to faster convergence and better final performance.
CONTROLS: The phase-change-based analysis will serve as a good control for understanding the evolution of modality conflicts and their relationship with model convergence.
COST: 24000
PREDICTION: This analysis will provide valuable insights into the dynamics of modality conflicts and their impact on model convergence, and we expect to see a clear relationship between reduced modality conflicts and improved convergence and performance. However, implementing and analyzing this phase-change-based analysis may require significant computational resources and expertise in signal processing and time-series analysis.
