ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Measuring Modality Conflict in Autoregressive Unified Models
PROPOSAL: We will conduct experiments to quantify the layer-wise magnitude of the disagreement between text and vision gradients in a modality-shared AR transformer, by computing the difference in gradient norms across modalities at various depths of the network. To this end, we will use the DALL-E 2 model as our base model and train it on the ImageNet and COCO datasets. We will measure the disagreement in gradient norms as the difference in the L2 norm of the gradients of the text and image stream at each layer. We will report the results as the average gradient disagreement across the network.
CONTROLS: We will compare our results to a baseline that aggregates the gradients of both streams at each layer, and to an ablation where the two streams are processed separately and then concatenated before normalization.
COST: 600
PREDICTION: We expect to see that the magnitude of gradient disagreement increases with depth, as intermediate layers are increasingly sensitive to semantic differences between modalities. Failure can occur if we find that the gradient disagreement is too small to confidently analyze, or if our analysis reveals an unexpected relationship between depth and gradient disagreement.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Investigating Modality-Specific Features in Inter-Modal Conflict
PROPOSAL: We will explore which types of modality-specific features contribute to the inter-modal conflict observed in our previous experiments. To achieve this, we will train separate AR transformers on text and image pre-training data, using pre-processed features that highlight different aspects of each modality. We will then fuse these intermediate representations with the base model's text and image streams, and evaluate the resulting models on both understanding and generation tasks. Our aim is to provide insights into the sources of modality conflict and guide the development of more effective AR UMMs. We will evaluate these models on the text-to-image generation, visual question answering, and image editing tasks from the Experimental Domains.
CONTROLS: We will compare our results to a baseline where the base model's text and image streams are seamlessly integrated, and study the effect of fusing different subsets of modality-specific features on the inter-modal conflict and overall performance.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: We expect to identify whether and where the inclusion of modality-specific features exacerbates or mitigates the inter-modal conflict, and to reveal the trade-offs involved in designing UMMs that balance modality-specific competence with inter-modal compatibility. Failure risks occur if the limited expressiveness of our hand-engineered features prevents us from fully understanding the underlying patterns, or if our findings do not provide actionable guidance for model design.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: A Layer-Wise Analysis of Inter-Modal Conflict in Autoregressive Unified Models
PROPOSAL: We will conduct an in-depth analysis of the layer-wise behavior of our base model on text and image tasks, focusing on understanding how the inter-modal conflict arises across different depth levels. We will use techniques such as layer-wise weight analysis and neuron contribution analysis to identify which layers are most affected by the inter-modal conflict and why. By studying the interaction between text and image streams at each depth, we will obtain a better understanding of how modality-specific features propagate through the network and contribute to inter-modal conflict.
CONTROLS: We will analyze the same models used in proposal 1, comparing our findings to results from the original modality-shared model to identify the effect of depth on inter-modal conflict.
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: We expect to find that earlier layers are less affected by inter-modal conflict and that deeper layers show more pronounced modality-specific behavior, but we may also discover other patterns that contravene our expectations. Failure risks arise if our analytical techniques are inadequate or if we over-interpret the correlation between layer-wise behavior and the presence of inter-modal conflict.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: REVISED: Designing Adversarial Measures for Audiovisual Emotion Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We'll design an audiovisual manipulation tool that generates realistic perturbations to evaluate the produced hallucinations of MLLMs. Instead of synthesis-based approach, we will use a simulation-based method that uses the Perceptual Distortion Model (PDM) to create realistic audiovisual distortions (e.g., noise, distortion, mimic real-world effects). We will use this tool to test robustness of two models (COMPANION and LLaMA). We will assess if these models can robustly ground their emotion predictions and explanations based on the input evidence, and whether the inclusion of perceptually-grounded adversarial examples can reduce hallucination levels.
CONTROLS: Comparisons with and without adversarial examples, and assessment of the frequency and types of hallucinations under various distortion levels.
COST: 333 GPU hours.
PREDICTION: This will evaluate whether our proposed adversarial measure can indeed reduce hallucination levels and force models to rely on input evidence, rather than text priors. But it may struggle to attribute hallucinations to specific types, as different models will exhibit different types of hallucinations.

We will use this framework to evaluate the COMPANION model on a new dataset consisting of videos with diverse emotional cues and scenarios. We will also assess the impact of our proposed adversarial measures on the models' hallucination rates.

PREDICTION: This revised evaluation framework should provide a more comprehensive assessment of MLLMs' hallucination rates and enable a better understanding of the impact of our proposed adversarial measures. However, the increased complexity of the evaluation tasks may make it harder to obtain significant results.

TITLE: Investigating the Role of Emotion-Related Knowledge Retrieval in Hallucinations
PROPOSAL: We'll investigate the role of emotion-related knowledge retrieval in hallucinations by analyzing the behavior of MLLMs when searching for relevant emotional cues. We will use a dataset of videos with various emotional scenarios and a set of pre-trained MLLMs to evaluate the models' ability to retrieve relevant emotional cues from their knowledge graphs. We will also assess the effect of our proposed adversarial measures on the models' knowledge retrieval behavior. This will provide insights into how MLLMs generate hallucinations and how our proposed adversarial measures can mitigate these issues.
CONTROLS: Experimenting with different configurations of the models' knowledge graphs and evaluating the impact of our proposed adversarial measures on knowledge retrieval behavior.
COST: 832 GPU hours.
PREDICTION: This investigation should provide a better understanding of the mechanisms underlying hallucinations in MLLMs and enable the development of more effective adversarial measures. However, the analysis of knowledge retrieval behavior may be complex and require significant computational resources.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Developing a Benchmark for Audiovisual Emotion Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We'll develop a comprehensive benchmark for audiovisual emotion reasoning that includes a diverse set of videos with various emotional scenarios, a set of pre-defined evaluation metrics, and a standardized framework for evaluating MLLMs' performance on emotion reasoning tasks. We will use this benchmark to evaluate the performance of our previously proposed models and adversarial measures, as well as to provide a shared baseline for future research in this area. This will enable more accurate comparisons and evaluations of different MLLMs and enable researchers to develop and refine their models using a common framework.
CONTROLS: Defining a comprehensive set of evaluation metrics and benchmarks for audiovisual emotion reasoning, and developing a standardized framework for evaluating MLLMs' performance on emotion reasoning tasks.
COST: 1500 GPU hours.
PREDICTION: This benchmark will provide a much-needed standardization and evaluation framework for audiovisual emotion reasoning and will enable more accurate comparisons and evaluations of different MLLMs. However, developing a comprehensive and diverse benchmark may require significant resources and time.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating MLLMs for Emotion Reasoning: A Robustness Taxonomy
PROPOSAL: We propose a three-stage taxonomy to robustly evaluate MLLMs for emotion reasoning, focusing on the presence or absence of audiovisual cues in model predictions and explanations. Stage 1 evaluates reasoning errors, assessing whether MLLMs tie emotions to relevant audiovisual cues. Stage 2 investigates perception errors, measuring the tendency of MLLMs to hallucinate additional cues. Stage 3 characterizes cue-emotion associations in MLLMs, highlighting potential biases toward spurious cue-emotion links.
CONTROLS: We will use comparison results from a number of recent, strong emotions-focused MLLMs, with ablations to show the discriminative power of proposed metrics. Robustness analysis will assess the impact of varying input types and speaker voices on MLLM performance.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our taxonomy will help detect MLLMs with errors, and show that such models closely follow the associations learned from their text priors; better-performing models will retain a bias towards such associations.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Augur: A Synthetic Dataset for Evaluating Hallucinations in Audiovisual Emotion Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We introduce Augur, a large-scale synthetic dataset designed to evaluate the hallucination tendencies of MLLMs in audiovisual emotion reasoning tasks. Augur consists of varied input scenarios (e.g., speaker characteristics, ambient noise), with associated ground-truth annotations detailing correct and hallucinated cues. The dataset's parsimonious and modular structure will enable systematic analysis of MLLM performance across diverse input configurations.
CONTROLS: We will compare Augur results with EmoReact, a widely used real-world emotion recognition benchmark, to showcase the benefits of augmenting with synthetic data and examine the relationship between real-world performance and ability to handle synthetic test cases.
COST: 360 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Augur will reveal MLLMs with robust hallucination-generating capability, particularly towards reasons previously conditioned by its training data; contrastingly, its real-world counterparts may better recognize isolated speakers amidst multiple voices.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Debugging MLLMs for Accurate Emotion Reasoning through Dynamic Modality Redistribution
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel approach to improve the accuracy of MLLMs in emotion reasoning by redistributing modality contributions dynamically, based on cue importance and relevance to the context. This method, dubbed "ModRed", uses a penalized optimization framework to adaptively allocate weights to each modality, allowing the model to focus on the most critical cues for accurate emotion recognition. Through empirical evaluation, we aim to demonstrate improved performance and reduced hallucination rates for MLLMs using ModRed.
CONTROLS: We will compare ModRed with a range of traditional multimodal fusion methods, including early, late, and hybrid fusion, as well as a stop-learning variant that sets the dynamic modality redistribution to zero.
COST: 720 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: ModRed will yield improved emotion recognition accuracy and reduced hallucination rates compared to traditional multimodal fusion methods, particularly in scenarios with high cue conflict and ambiguity.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Grounding Emotion Reasoning in Multi-Modal Evidence: A Regularization-Based Approach
PROPOSAL: We introduce a regularization-based approach to ground MLLMs' emotion reasoning in multi-modal evidence. The proposed "Evidence-Grounded" (EG) regularization framework imposes an L1-norm penalty on the model's output to encourage the usage of only credible cues that strongly supporting the predicted emotions. Through this regularization, we aim to reduce the reliance of MLLMs on spurious cue-emotion associations and hallucinated cues, thereby improving their trustworthiness and reliability in emotion recognition tasks.
CONTROLS: We compare EG regularization with traditional regularization methods, such as dropout and L2-regularization, to assess its effectiveness in promoting evidence-grounded emotion reasoning.
COST: 1080 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The EG regularization framework will significantly reduce MLLMs' reliance on spurious cues and hallucinations, leading to improved emotion recognition accuracy and a more robust understanding of emotion reasoning.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Towards Transparent and Trustworthy Emotion Reasoning: Visualizing MLLMs' Causal Reasoning Pathways
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel visualization framework to provide a transparent and interpretable understanding of MLLMs' causal reasoning pathways in emotion reasoning tasks. Our framework, dubbed "CausalVis", utilizes a combination of causal inference techniques and visual analytics to revel the chain of dependencies between input cues and the predicted emotions, highlighting the influential cues and mitigating spurious associations.
CONTROLS: We will compare CausalVis with traditional feature importance methods, such as permutation importance and SHAP values, to assess its effectiveness in revealing causal relationships.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: CausalVis will enable a deeper understanding of MLLMs' emotion reasoning mechanisms, revealing the causal relationships between input cues and predicted emotions. This will help to identify biases and weaknesses in the models, and provide insights for improving their transparency and trustworthiness.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating MLLMs for Emotion Reasoning: A Robustness Taxonomy
PROPOSAL: We propose a three-stage taxonomy to robustly evaluate MLLMs for emotion reasoning, focusing on the presence or absence of audiovisual cues in model predictions and explanations. Stage 1 evaluates reasoning errors, assessing whether MLLMs tie emotions to relevant audiovisual cues. Stage 2 investigates perception errors, measuring the tendency of MLLMs to hallucinate additional cues. Stage 3 characterizes cue-emotion associations in MLLMs, highlighting potential biases toward spurious cue-emotion links.
CONTROLS: We will use comparison results from a number of recent, strong emotions-focused MLLMs, with ablations to show the discriminative power of proposed metrics. Robustness analysis will assess the impact of varying input types and speaker voices on MLLM performance.
COST: 360 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our taxonomy will help detect MLLMs with errors, and show that such models closely follow the associations learned from their text priors; better-performing models will retain a bias towards such associations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Augur: A Synthetic Dataset for Evaluating Hallucinations in Audiovisual Emotion Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We introduce Augur, a large-scale synthetic dataset designed to evaluate the hallucination tendencies of MLLMs in audiovisual emotion reasoning tasks. Augur consists of varied input scenarios (e.g., speaker characteristics, ambient noise), with associated ground-truth annotations detailing correct and hallucinated cues. The dataset's parsimonious and modular structure will enable systematic analysis of MLLM performance across diverse input configurations.
CONTROLS: We will compare Augur results with EmoReact, a widely used real-world emotion recognition benchmark, to showcase the benefits of augmenting with synthetic data and examine the relationship between real-world performance and ability to handle synthetic test cases.
COST: 1080 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Augur will reveal MLLMs with robust hallucination-generating capability, particularly towards reasons previously conditioned by its training data; contrastingly, its real-world counterparts may better recognize isolated speakers amidst multiple voices.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Debugging MLLMs for Accurate Emotion Reasoning through Dynamic Modality Redistribution
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel approach to improve the accuracy of MLLMs in emotion reasoning by redistributing modality contributions dynamically, based on cue importance and relevance to the context. This method, dubbed "ModRed", uses a penalized optimization framework to adaptively allocate weights to each modality, allowing the model to focus on the most critical cues for accurate emotion recognition. Through empirical evaluation, we aim to demonstrate improved performance and reduced hallucination rates for MLLMs using ModRed.
CONTROLS: We will compare ModRed with a range of traditional multimodal fusion methods, including early, late, and hybrid fusion, as well as a stop-learning variant that sets the dynamic modality redistribution to zero.
COST: 2160 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: ModRed will yield improved emotion recognition accuracy and reduced hallucination rates compared to traditional multimodal fusion methods, particularly in scenarios with high cue conflict and ambiguity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Grounding Emotion Reasoning in Multi-Modal Evidence: A Regularization-Based Approach
PROPOSAL: We introduce a regularization-based approach to ground MLLMs' emotion reasoning in multi-modal evidence. The proposed "Evidence-Grounded" (EG) regularization framework imposes an L1-norm penalty on the model's output to encourage the usage of only credible cues that strongly supporting the predicted emotions. Through this regularization, we aim to reduce the reliance of MLLMs on spurious cue-emotion associations and hallucinated cues, thereby improving their trustworthiness and reliability in emotion recognition tasks.
CONTROLS: We compare EG regularization with traditional regularization methods, such as dropout and L2-regularization, to assess its effectiveness in promoting evidence-grounded emotion reasoning.
COST: 3240 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The EG regularization framework will significantly reduce MLLMs' reliance on spurious cues and hallucinations, leading to improved emotion recognition accuracy and a more robust understanding of emotion reasoning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Towards Transparent and Trustworthy Emotion Reasoning: Visualizing MLLMs' Causal Reasoning Pathways
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel visualization framework to provide a transparent and interpretable understanding of MLLMs' causal reasoning pathways in emotion reasoning tasks. Our framework, dubbed "CausalVis", utilizes a combination of causal inference techniques and visual analytics to revel the chain of dependencies between input cues and the predicted emotions, highlighting the influential cues and mitigating spurious associations.
CONTROLS: We will compare CausalVis with traditional feature importance methods, such as permutation importance and SHAP values, to assess its effectiveness in revealing causal relationships.
COST: 4500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: CausalVis will enable a deeper understanding of MLLMs' emotion reasoning mechanisms, revealing the causal relationships between input cues and predicted emotions. This will help to identify biases and weaknesses in the models, and provide insights for improving their transparency and trustworthiness.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluation of Hallucination-Prone Audiovisual Emotion MLLMs with Emotion-Driven Explanation Validation
PROPOSAL: We will evaluate the emotion-driven explanations generated by audiovisual MLLMs using a validation protocol that measures the overlap between the predicted explanation cues and the actual audiovisual cues present in the input data. Specifically, we will use a combination of quantitative metrics (e.g., cue overlap, precision) and qualitative human evaluations (e.g., annotator assessment of explanation relevance). We will also compare the performance of MLLMs trained on various data subsets (emotion-specific versus general) and will investigate the impact of using additional relevant emotional features beyond visual and audio cues. We will evaluate our MLLMs using the ERC dataset and OCCP-effect based scenarios from the bfi dataset.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: MLLM without explicit explanation generation capabilities.
- Ablation: MLLM trained without emotion-specific data.
- Baseline with emotion-specific fine-tuning.
COST: 400
PREDICTION: Our protocol should reveal systematic differences in explanation quality between MLLMs trained on different data subsets, indicating that emotion-specific training data effectively mitigates hallucination-prone explanation generation in audiovisual emotion MLLMs, and that our qualitative human evaluation should validate that explanation relevance substantially increases with improved data accuracy.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Avoiding Spurious Cue-Emotion Associations through Cross-Modal Input Patterns Analysis
PROPOSAL: To better ground emotion predictions and explanations in the actual audio and visual evidence present, we will employ cross-modal input pattern analysis, focusing on the spatial and temporal correlations between audio, video, and text. This involves training a segmentation model to identify and highlight relevant spatiotemporal components of the input, and then filtering the audiovisual MLLM's predictions to exclude cues that do not correlate with these identified components. We will use this approach on various MLLMs trained on different data subsets and evaluate performance on the ERC dataset for OCCP-effect based scenarios from the bfi dataset.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: MLLM without the cross-modal input pattern analysis module.
- Ablation: only segmentation for the analysis.
- Ablation: image and audio analysis by itself to see if they suffice.
- Baseline that used audio and video analysis by itself.
COST: 520
PREDICTION: Our results should indicate that filtering MLLM predictions based on cross-modal input patterns significantly reduces hallucinations and improves explanation relevance for emotion-driven MLLMs, and that this approach synergistically enhances the performance when combined with data accuracy.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adversarial Training with Counterfactual Audiovisual Input Perturbations
PROPOSAL: To improve the robustness of audiovisual MLLMs against hallucination-prone behavior, we will employ adversarial training using counterfactual audiovisual input perturbations. We will generate perturbed versions of the input data by altering specific audio or visual cues, and then train the MLLM to predict the correct emotional response even when faced with these perturbed inputs. This approach aims to help the model generalize better to unseen audiovisual patterns and reduce its reliance on spurious cue-emotion associations. We will evaluate the performance of our adversarially trained MLLMs on the ERC dataset for OCCP-effect based scenarios from the bfi dataset.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: MLLM without the adversarial training module.
- Baseline: MLLM with random input perturbations (no structured perturbations).
- Ablation: MLLM trained with only auditory input perturbations.
- Ablation: MLLM trained with only visual input perturbations.
COST: 500
PREDICTION: Our results should indicate that adversarial training with counterfactual audiovisual input perturbations significantly improves the robustness of audiovisual MLLMs against hallucinations, allowing them to better generalize to unseen audiovisual patterns and reducing their reliance on spurious cue-emotion associations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Text Priors Regularization through Emotion Topic Modeling
PROPOSAL: To regularize the text priors in audiovisual MLLMs and reduce their influence on hallucination-prone behavior, we will employ emotion topic modeling. We will train a topic model on a large corpus of text data that is relevant to emotions and then use this model to distance the MLLM's generated text from common cue-emotion associations encoded in the text priors. This approach aims to encourage the MLLM to focus on the actual audiovisual cues present in the input rather than relying on spurious associations. We will evaluate the performance of our regularized MLLMs on the ERC dataset for OCCP-effect based scenarios from the bfi dataset.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: MLLM without the text priors regularization module.
- Baseline: MLLM with random regularization (no structured regularization).
- Ablation: MLLM trained with only the audiovisual input (no text input).
- Ablation: MLLM trained with text input but without emotion topic modeling.
COST: 567.6
PREDICTION: Our results should indicate that text priors regularization through emotion topic modeling effectively reduces the influence of spurious cue-emotion associations in audiovisual MLLMs, allowing them to better ground their emotional predictions in the actual audiovisual cues present in the input.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Whittling Down Overconfident Intercepts through Density-Based Downsampling
PROPOSAL: To address the problem of overconfident intercepts in audiovisual MLLMs, which can exacerbate hallucination-prone behavior, we will employ density-based downsampling. This involves sampling the input data to reduce its information density, making it more challenging for the model to overfit. We will then train the MLLM on this downscaled data and evaluate its performance on the ERC dataset for OCCP-effect based scenarios from the bfi dataset. This approach aims to reduce the model's overconfidence in its predictions and promote more cautious behavior.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: MLLM without the downsampling module.
- Baseline: MLLM with uniform downsampling (no density-based downsampling).
- Ablation: MLLM trained on the original data.
- Ablation: MLLM trained with only visual downsampling.
COST: 670
PREDICTION: Our results should indicate that density-based downsampling significantly reduces the overconfident intercepts in audiovisual MLLMs, leading to improved accuracy and reduced hallucination-prone behavior.

PROPOSAL: To further improve the robustness of audiovisual MLLMs against adversarial attacks and reduce hallucination-prone behavior, we will employ transfer learning with emotion-specific pretrained models. We will train a set of MLLMs on various emotion recognition tasks and then fine-tune these models on the target task using the concurrently trained MLLMs. This approach aims to leverage the knowledge from the pretrained models to adapt to the target task while maintaining the adversarial robustness. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Turn-level Supervision through Answer Unfoldings
PROPOSAL: Train a set of forward models, each representing a hypothetically successful search trajectory, to predict the agent's interactions at each turn. Supervision is derived from the discrepancy between the predicted turn-level actions and the actual actions, which provides dense, informative rewards for RL training. The forward models are jointly optimized with the search policy using the same set of rollouts, enforcing a tight connection between the reward signal and the policy's trajectory.
CONTROLS: Compare with current state-of-the-art GRPO, GRPO with random process rewards, and a GRPO baseline with no process rewards.
COST: 150
PREDICTION: This approach should result in improved sample efficiency and better credit assignment, with moderate to high variance in performance when dealing with diverse multi-hop question answering tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Contrastive Agentic Rewards
PROPOSAL: Introduce a contrastive process reward scheme, where each interaction turn is embedded in a contrastive learning framework. Positive pairs consist of the turn's actual action and a plausible alternative action that is plausible but ultimately unproductive (e.g., querying a redundant resource). Supervision is derived from a contrastive loss function that distinguishes productive from unproductive turns. This approach incentivizes the agent to learn productive behavior by discovering the crucial distinction between actual and alternative outcomes.
CONTROLS: Include process rewards only for the most productive turns in the trajectory and evaluate the agent's performance when given early access to additional redundant resources.
REVISION: 1. Turn-level Supervision through Answer Unfoldings
REVISED PROPOSAL: Add a baseline comparing the ability of answer unfoldings to contrastive process rewards when used in conjunction with GRPO.
COST: 270
PREDICTION: Contrastive agentic rewards might offer improved reinforcement learning stability, enabling agents to better cope with sparsity and dimensionality issues in the action space, leading to efficient learning of productive search strategies.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Automatic Turn Segmentation via Local Salience
PROPOSAL: Utilize a salience model, pre-trained on a diverse corpus of questions and searches, to automatically identify critical and salient turns in search trajectories. Each turn's salience score serves as a reward signal, steering the agent toward interaction turns that contribute significantly to the search outcome. This method avoids manually annotating or simulating alternatives, reducing the overhead and improving scalability.
CONTROLS: Experiment with different salience models (e.g., magnitude-based, entropy-based) and manually evaluate the agent's performance under strong and weak salience models.
REVISION: 2. Contrastive Agentic Rewards
REVISED PROPOSAL: Train a second forward model, focused on estimating the expected effectiveness of a given turn's actions based on early signal indications, and use it as an auxiliary loss term for the contrastive learning framework.
COST: 450
PREDICTION: Automatically segmenting search turns with high salience could lead to a fairly boost in training efficiency and productive search behaviors with relatively low engineering requirements. However, insufficient salience detection might lead to inconsistent performance or critical moves being overlooked.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Decay-based Process Rewards
PROPOSAL: Periodically evaluate the progress toward the target query during each search trajectory and schedule rewards at specific turns. The reward magnitude decays with each passing turn, encouraging the agent to explore and exploit relevant information effectively. This dynamic reward signal refines the agent's behavior, promoting efficient search strategies.
CONTROLS: Design and evaluate different decay schedules, examine the impact of initializing the reward signal with the first action of the search trajectory, and compare with scenarios where the reward signal ramp up linearly or gradually.
COST: 540
PREDICTION: By adding a mechanism that automatically times when to reinforce productive behavior with decreasing returns, the trainable model should exhibit better attention to detail, focus on handling overdue information as expected, and robust search outcomes – even under challenging problems. This rule will limit increasing rewards much faster than under complete setup observe top agents in-front to better chase reliable scores.

TITLE: Multi-armed Bandit-based Soft Task Modeling

This structure exploits the valuable knowledge in the performance progression of the search process, allowing the agent to dynamically update its internal state to improve search effectiveness over time. Specifically, the structured update rule incorporates knowledge about the relevance of different search steps to the final answer, enabling the agent to focus on the most productive turns.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Meta-RL for Agentic Search
PROPOSAL: Introduce a meta-RL framework that allows the agent to learn a policy for learning in different search environments. The agent is trained on a set of "meta-environments" that simulate different search scenarios, and it learns to adapt its policy to effectively exploit the reward signals generated by the different techniques proposed in this paper. This approach enables the agent to generalize across diverse search tasks and environments, improving its overall search efficiency and effectiveness.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the meta-RL agent on a range of search scenarios, comparing it to the individual techniques proposed in this paper.
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: The meta-RL framework could lead to significant improvements in search effectiveness and efficiency, as the agent is able to adapt to new search scenarios and exploit the strengths of different reward signal techniques. However, the training process may require a large number of iterations, and the agent's performance may be heavily dependent on the quality of the meta-environments used during training.

TITLE: Ensemble-based Reward Design
PROPOSAL: Combine the strengths of the different reward signal techniques proposed in this paper by designing an ensemble method that leverages the predictions and outputs of multiple individual techniques. The ensemble method would select the best reward signal for each search turn, based on the characteristics of the search environment and the current state of the search process. This approach aims to capitalize on the complementary strengths of the individual techniques, leading to a more accurate and effective reward signal for agentic search.

TITLE: Analyzing Agentic Search Rewards through Turn-Level Parameterization
PROPOSAL: We'll experiment with parameterizing the weights of a process reward function learned by a neural network to modulate between outcome-based rewards for final answers, and dense intermediate step rewards. This is inspired by the possibility that LLMs might benefit from intermediate feedback to accurately balance immediate tool use productivity with long-term accuracy. Our baseline GRPO agent will receive outcome-only rewards, while a modified agent receives outcome-plus-intermediate-step-reward guidance.
CONTROLS: (1) baseline GRPO without process rewards, (2) GRPO with outcome-only rewards for final answers + "rich" intermediate step sequence encoding (to control for the information content of intermediate steps)
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: The modified agent should exhibit lower reward sensitivity and smaller advantage collapse, albeit at the cost of slightly reduced search accuracy if the reward hyperparameters are misaligned.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Dense Rewards by Rank-Based Normalization
PROPOSAL: We'll introduce a rank-based normalization for the outcome rewards within each rollout group. By ranking the rolls and assigning rewards based on this ranking, rather than simply averaging the outcomes, we can provide a more-informational and still principled process reward guidance without requiring external judging or association learning. The rank may be computed using the final answer accuracy, or by promoting specificity in the intermediate steps (e.g. unanswerable questions).
CONTROLS: the baseline GRPO without process rewards, the previous experiment (1) with parameterized agent
COST: 6500
PREDICTION: This method should demonstrate reduced sensitivity to noisy group-level rewards, specifically when rollouts uniformly give the same answer, thereby reducing advantage collapse. It may, however, suffer from连接 degradation if the reward signal remains sparse, or if the group-level uniformity arises from informative intermediate choices.

TITLE: Supervised Turn Rewards for Agentic Search Agents
PROPOSAL: We'll add another supervised learning step before starting RL, where we predict turn-level probability labels indicating whether each intermediate turn is "productive" (correct reasoning and relevant tool use), "unproductive" (incorrect or unrelated reasoning), or " irrelevant" (tool use without reasoning). Training will rely on a custom dataset created by filterhuman, where each example consists of a question, a set of pairs of human-written intermediate turns along with the final ground truth answer, and a set of probability labels specifying the relevance and correctness of each intermediate turn.
CONTROLS: Experiments comparing our new approach with standard outcomes rewards, as well as with process rewards estimated using external oracle knowledge or reward models.
COST: 11320
PREDICTION: I expect our approach to outperform both existing methods in multi-turn search agents, though it might be computation-intensive due to the need for additional supervised learning. The risk is that it overfits to the training data, especially given limited examples.

TITLE: Intrinsic Turn Rewards from Future Outcomes

In particular, when a rollout reaches a terminal step, we propagate its final reward back to earlier turns and update their rewards according to their causal importance (e.g., using techniques from causal graph analysis and Shannon information), penalizing unproductive steps and encouraging productive reasoning and tool use.
CONTROLS: Experiments comparing our method with standard outcomes rewards, as well as with process rewards, such as those obtained from external oracles or simulation-based methods.
COST: 16000
PREDICTION: This approach should improve upon standard outcome-only rewards, especially in multi-turn settings where information cascades and intermediate steps are critical, but its efficiency and generalization are still open questions. Reward hijacking and overspecification might be concerns for rich intrinsic rewards.

CONTROLS: Comparisons with both standard outcomes rewards and extrinsic process rewards.

TITLE: Multiturn Information Coders for Dense Process Rewards
PROPOSAL: Develop a multiturn information coder, a sequence-to-sequence model that encodes an agent's entire reasoning trajectory into a dense, informative, turn-level reward signal. This coder takes the sequence of inputs (question, retrieved documents, and intermediate answers), turns it into a sequence of embeddings, and outputs their representations. A simple weighting mechanism combines these embeddings, reflecting the importance of each turn in achieving the final answer. The coder relies only on the interaction history and the ground-truth final answer, without external knowledge or reward annotations. Reward is the dot product of the embedding vector and a simple, task-agnostic target vector that reflects outcomes relative to optimal answers.

PROPOSAL: We propose to learn a graph-structured representation of sparse queries by diffusing their features across neighboring image pairs, utilizing both the spatial and semantic relationships between them. This would enable the extraction of coarse, yet task-agnostic 3D scene representations from multi-view images.

However, it might fail to generalize well across varied driving scenarios and configurations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Sparse Query-based 3D Scene Representation Learning via Graph Diffusion
PROPOSAL: We propose to learn a graph-structured representation of sparse queries by diffusing their features across neighboring image pairs, utilizing both the spatial and semantic relationships between them. This would enable the extraction of coarse, yet task-agnostic 3D scene representations from multi-view images.
CONTROLS: We will compare our method to the state-of-the-art sparse perception models DETR3D and PETR and evaluate its performance on the widely used KITTI dataset.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: We expect our graph diffusion approach to significantly improve the performance of query-based sparse perception models in learning generalizable 3D scene representations, outperforming DETR3D and PETR on KITTI tasks. However, it might fail to generalize well across varied driving scenarios and configurations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: 3D Query Embedding via Differentiable Splatting of Unlabeled Data
PROPOSAL: We introduce a differentiable splatting module that progressively refines the learning of 3D query embeddings by softly aggregating context information from unlabeled data, enabling the learning of sparse queries that capture nuanced 3D scene geometries.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate our method in combination with the graph diffusion approach from proposal 1, and compare its performance with GaussianPretrain and VisionPAD on the KITTI and Waymo Open dataset benchmarks.
COST: 11000
PREDICTION: By jointly optimizing the graph diffusion approach with our differentiable splatting module, we expect to observe significant improvements in the learning of generalizable 3D query embeddings, leading to improved performance across various 3D perception tasks. However, its heavy reliance on computation-intensive differentiable splatting might hinder its real-world deployment.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Query-based Pre-training for Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: Develop a query-based pre-training method, named QPS (Query-based Pre-training for Sparse models), to adapt unlabeled multi-view driving data to sparse perception models. QPS includes a sub-network that learns to query a set of informative view locations for each image, which is further used as a dynamic auxiliary task to supervise the queries of the downstream sparse model during pre-training.
CONTROLS: Compare QPS against existing pre-training paradigms (e.g., UniPAD, ViDAR, Frozen-DETR), as well as a no-pretraining baseline and a pre-trained backbone loaded without adaptation in the downstream task.
COST: 6100 GPU-hours 
PREDICTION: QPS will lead to improved performance on sparse 3D object detectors and semantic occupancy predictors, achieving state-of-the-art results in challenging autonomous driving benchmarks, potentially failing due to issues with multi-view competition in the learned queries, insufficiency of explored dynamic tasks, and quantization interoperability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Meta-Learned View-Space Mappings for Sparse Models
PROPOSAL: Introduce a meta-learned framework, named Metamapper, where a meta-model learns to induce view-space mappings between query-effector and spatial coordinates (e.g., image locations, BEV pixels), which can adapt to any sparse perception model topology and downstream task.
CONTROLS: Metamapper will be compared with existing query-based pre-training approaches (e.g., QPS, GLID), as well as with the same returned sparse models without the meta-learned mapping, focusing on its ability to generalize the benefits of pre-training across tasks and architectures, and assessing robustness to variations in task and scenery representation.
COST: 9000 GPU-hours 
PREDICTION: The performance of downstream sparse perception models will be significantly enhanced, with the ability of Metamapper to extend the applicability range of prior successful designs in a plug-and-play manner, potentially failing to adapt to complex mappings across task-specific queries and learned representations, due to either insufficient task co-operation in excessive depth or multiple minima.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unsupervised Pre-training of Sparse Perception Models with Geometric Consistency
PROPOSAL: We propose to develop a pre-training framework that leverages unlabeled driving data to learn geometrically consistent 3D features, using a combination of self-supervised rendering loss and geometric consistency loss. Specifically, we will utilize 3D Gaussian Splatting to render 3D scene structures from multiple viewpoints and use geometric consistency loss to enforce the spatial coherence of learned features across different viewpoints.
CONTROLS: Baseline: pre-training with masked autoencoder, Ablation: remove geometric consistency loss, Baseline with labeled data: directly train on labeled data.
COST: 333
PREDICTION: Our proposed framework is expected to improve the performance of sparse perception models on downstream tasks such as 3D object detection and semantic occupancy prediction. We anticipate that the geometric consistency loss will contribute to the improvement, as it encourages the model to learn spatially coherent features. However, if the rendering loss is too weak, or if the geometric consistency loss is overly strong, the model may fail to learn effective features.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transferable 3D Scene Representations via Autoencoding Query-based Hierarchies
PROPOSAL: Building on the pre-training framework proposed in proposal 1, we investigate how to transfer the learned geometrically consistent 3D features to heterogeneous query-based downstream models. We propose to autoencode the sparse queries of each downstream model into a shared 3D feature space, such that the learned features can be used to improve the performance of multiple downstream tasks. Specifically, we will train an autoencoder to map the sparse queries of each downstream model to a shared 3D feature space, and use this shared space to initialize the decoder of each downstream model.
CONTROLS: Baseline: directly train each downstream model on labeled data, Ablation: remove autoencoder, Baseline with pre-trained image backbone: use a pre-trained image backbone as input to each downstream model.
COST: 670
PREDICTION: Our proposed autoencoding-based framework is expected to improve the transferability of learned 3D features across multiple downstream tasks. However, if the shared 3D feature space is too general, the learned features may not be specific enough to improve performance on individual tasks, or if the autoencoder is not trained carefully, it may not effectively capture the structure of each downstream model's queries.

TITLE: Multi-Task Learning for Sparse Perception Models with Supervised-Contrastive Loss
PROPOSAL: We propose a multi-task learning framework that combines supervised object detection and contrastive learnings for enhancing the performance of sparse perception models. Our framework includes a supervised loss for object detection and a contrastive loss for learning invariant representations across tasks. We will use the same 3D feature space learned from the pre-training framework proposed in proposal 1 and fine-tune it on downstream tasks using this loss. This approach is expected to improve the model's performance on both object detection and semantic occupancy prediction tasks.
CONTROLS: Baseline: directly train each downstream model on labeled data, Ablation: remove contrastive loss, Baseline with pre-trained image backbone: use a pre-trained image backbone as input to each downstream model.
COST: 832
PREDICTION: Our proposed multi-task learning framework is expected to improve the performance of sparse perception models on downstream tasks. However, if the contrastive loss is not properly balanced with the supervised loss, the model may suffer from overfitting or feature collapse, or if the pre-trained 3D feature space is not effective, the model may not learn invariant representations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Contrastive Query Reweighting for Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: This experiment compares the effectiveness of contrastive query reweighting against standard sparse perception approaches on three real-world benchmark datasets: Waymo Open Dataset, KITTI, and BDD100K. We train a DETR3D query-based 3D object detector and a SparseBEV 3D sparse occupancy predictor using contrastive query reweighting, and evaluate their performance using detection/segmentation metrics such as AP and IoU. We compare our approach against the DETR3D and SparseBEV methods without contrastive query reweighting.
CONTROLS: DETR3D and SparseBEV without contrastive query reweighting
COST: 2400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our approach to achieve high accuracy, comparable to state-of-the-art 3D object detection and sparse occupancy prediction approaches. However, since selecting the optimal query weights might not always be feasible, our approach might fail to generalize to unseen environments.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Inverse Renderer for Differentiable Pre-training of Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes using an inverse renderer as a differentiable pre-training objective for SPMs. We leverage the discriminator from the ViDAR pipeline to train a query-based inverse renderer that predicts coarse pixel positions corresponding to the scene point clouds, gradually refining its predictions to match the precise driving environments. We pre-train SPMs using this inverse renderer and evaluate their performance on downstream tasks like 3D detection and occupancy estimation.
CONTROLS: Pre-training with masked autoencoder
COST: 3600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed inverse renderer for SPMs should robustly learn the structural information of driving scenes, yet extensive reliance upon rendered 2.5D representations might limit the vision-centric models' feasibility.

TITLE: Learning Implicit Query Embeddings in Hybrid Autoencoders
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes a hybrid autoencoder that combines both implicit query embeddings and pre-existing sparse perception representation learning. By generating implicit query embeddings through denoising autoencoders for point clouds, it strengthens sparse representation learning with minimal additional complexity. We evaluate its ability to improve real-world driving perception by allowing for the prediction of geometrical annotations such as occupancy occupancies and pointcloud representations.
CONTROLS: Hybrid autoencoder without implicit query embeddings
COST: 4200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This addition anticipates robust model performance with the hybrid model able to adequately interweave sparse geometry via novel representations since potentially bigger complexities on stage 2 pretraining as intended. Failure to apply successfully in processed intersections could yield jeopardized further insights.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Sparse Self-Supervised Pre-Training for Query-Based Models
PROPOSAL: Implement a multi-stage self-supervised pre-training framework for SPMs, starting with a basic model that uses image reconstruction from a single query to predict the pixel values, and gradually increasing complexity by adding more queries, increasing spatial resolutions, and including depth prediction. The objective is to learn a multi-modal, position-invariant representation of scene geometry through the pre-training process. We will use sequences of consecutive frames from the KITTI dataset and employ the reconstruction loss from the first experiment of the "DASH" paper with their particular implementation of an auxiliary loss to achieve rotational equivariance in this first step. 
CONTROLS: (i) No pre-training: loading a pre-trained image backbone directly into the downstream SPM model.
(ii) Pre-training with a fixed number of queries: setting the number of queries fixed for all stages.
(iii) Pre-training with only the first stage: keeping the pre-training process simple.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: With proper hyperparameter tuning, this model should show some level of pre-trained generalization, and we expect a moderate improvement in downstream task performance compared to the baseline. However, pre-training from a single query without an intermediate representation could potentially lead to overfitting and not capture relevant global geometry.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-View Stereo for Query-Based Pre-Training
PROPOSAL: Investigate how to incorporate multi-view stereo (MVS) functionality into the pre-training process for query-based models. This involves training the SPM to perform depth estimation from multiple input images, with each query representing a unique location in the 3D space. The goal is to learn a robust and accurate 3D representation of the environment using only unlabeled multi-view images and to analyze how this depth information can benefit downstream tasks. We will pre-train on the sequences of KITTI and test with a occupancy map prediction downstream task compared to the first proposal, without the depth information.
CONTROLS: (i) No MVS: using the previous experiment as a baseline.
(ii) MVS with 2D queries: keeping the 2D queries but enabling depth estimation.
(iii) MVS with 3D queries: enabling both depth estimation and more accurate 3D location representation.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: The MVS-based pre-training is expected to outperform the basic self-supervised pre-training, especially in scenes with complex geometries. However, it might require careful tuning of the loss function to avoid biased convergence towards easier tasks like depth estimation.

TITLE: Quantifying the Importance of Pre-Training Stages
PROPOSAL: Conduct an ablation study to investigate the contribution of individual stages in the proposed multi-stage self-supervised pre-training framework. Specifically, analyze the impact of each stage on the performance of downstream tasks and explore which stages are most critical for learning a robust and accurate 3D representation. This will help in identifying the essential components of the framework and provide insights into how to refine and optimize the pre-training process. We will remove or replace individual stages and fine-tune the model to see how the removal impacts performance.

(iii) Without depth estimation: removing the depth estimation stage.

PREDICTION: The ablation study should reveal the relative importance of each stage in the pre-training framework and provide guidance on how to optimize the process. However, it might be challenging to identify the most important stages, especially if multiple stages contribute to the overall performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Cross-Modal Transfer for Query-Based Models
PROPOSAL: Explore the possibility of transferring knowledge from pre-trained query-based models trained on one modality (e.g., images) to another modality (e.g., lidar point clouds or raw radar data) through self-supervised pre-training. This involves adapting the pre-training framework to accommodate the new modality and evaluating the transferability of the learned representations across different sensory inputs. We will fine-tune a pre-trained model on lidar data and compare its performance to a model trained from scratch.
CONTROLS: (i) Separate pre-training: pre-training and fine-tuning separately for each modality.
(ii) Cross-modal pre-training: pre-training on one modality and fine-tuning on another.
(iii) Multimodal pre-training: pre-training on multiple modalities simultaneously.
COST: 4400
PREDICTION: The cross-modal transfer should reveal the ability of query-based models to adapt to different sensory inputs and potentially improve their performance across domains. However, it might require significant adjustments to the pre-training framework and fine-tuning procedure to accommodate the new modality.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Inference for Vision-Language Detectors
PROPOSAL: To address the two major issues in TTAOD, we will propose a new adaptive inference framework, AdaVL, which leverages the strengths of pre-trained vision-language detectors while minimizing their weaknesses. AdaVL adapts the detector during testing by (i) leveraging meta-learning to select only the domain-adaptation relevant weights and prune the rest to maintain source-free principle, and (ii) incorporating a novel threshold-free confidence-based mechanism to generate reliable pseudo-labels in every test batch.
CONTROLS: We will compare AdaVL against state-of-the-art TTAOD methods, including VAT, Co-Training, and Pruner, by reducing these methods' dependence on source statistics and assuming they directly use high-quality pseudo-labels without filtering. Additionally, we will evaluate the effect of varying the ratio of pseudo-labeled training data for AdaVL to maintain a baseline level of pre-trained generalization.
COST: 600
PREDICTION: We expect AdaVL to outperform previous TTAOD methods in real-world domains under distribution shifts by adapting more efficiently and effectively, and by leveraging the strengths of pre-trained detectors as much as possible. However, the reliability of pseudo-labels remains a challenge, and we expect some effects of noisy pseudo-labels on adaptation performance.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Adaptive Inference for Vision-Language Detectors with Sample Weighting
PROPOSAL: The AdaVL framework in Proposal 1 had two key components: meta-learning for pruning and a threshold-free confidence-based mechanism for pseudo-labels. However, in Proposal 1, we didn't effectively handle the issue of noisy or missing pseudo-labels. To address this issue, we will modify AdaVL to incorporate sample weighting into the adaptation process: we assign a higher weight to clean pseudo-labels and a lower weight to potential noisy pseudo-labels. This modification effectively assigns more importance to high-confidence pseudo-labels and less to low-confidence ones during adaptation.
CONTROLS: We keep the same controls as before, including state-of-the-art TTAOD methods and evaluating the effect of varying the ratio of pseudo-labeled training data. Additionally, we will experiment with different weighting strategies (e.g., value weighting or voter-based consensus) to determine which one yields the best results.
COST: 900
PREDICTION: By adaptively weighing pseudo-labels, we expect AdaVL to mitigate the effects of noisy or missing pseudo-labels and improve overall adaptation performance. However, the best weighting strategy is unclear, and manual tuning may still be necessary to find the optimal weights, especially in scenarios where pseudo-label quality is highly variable.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Approximating High-Quality Pseudo-Labels with Uncertainty-aware Estimates
PROPOSAL: In real-world scenarios, generating high-quality pseudo-labels using the pre-trained vision-language detector can be challenging, especially when the target data is scarce or noisy. To mitigate this issue, we will propose a novel uncertainty-aware estimate method that approximates the quality of potential pseudo-labels. Specifically, we will use Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) to estimate the uncertainty of the detector's predictions and only use confident pseudo-labels from these predictions as training data for adaptation.
CONTROLS: We compare our method against existing pseudo-label filtering techniques, such as Ensembling (ensemble prediction for labeling), PL at Top-K (selecting predicted labels from Top-K softmax outputs), Density-Based (predicting labels only when the prediction density of provided label exceeds that of the remaining labels), and as for our previous ADAVL proposal to see if the new uncertainty-aware scheme impacts that results. We evaluate the performance and adaptability of our method under various data conditions, including noisy and real-world data.
COST: 1500
PREDICTION: Our uncertainty-aware approach allows AdaVL to adapt more effectively using a combination of high-quality and approximated pseudo-labels, particularly in scenarios where ideal pseudo-labels are hard to obtain. However, our approach relies on approximations and may not perform optimally in situations with well-established sources of high-quality pseudo-labels.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Source-Factorized Graph for Efficient Test-Time Object Detection Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Our previous proposals focused on improving the quality and efficiency of pseudo-labels for test-time adaptation. However, in large-scale object detection tasks, generating a large number of pseudo-labels can lead to memory and computational inefficiencies. To alleviate this issue, we will introduce a source-factorized graph-based approach (SFG) for efficient pseudo-label generation. SFG facilitates parallel and efficient pseudo-label estimation, effectively pruning out high-uncertainty edges and unnecessary node computations based on its topologically optimized structure.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of our propose SFG-based method against existing pseudo-label generation techniques, including Exhaustive Search, BFS, Dijkstra’s Algorithm, an edge weight-threshold based approach and the previous two experiments. Additionally, we evaluate the computational complexity reduction and and paradigm rotation in test set without affecting the overall adaptation performance of our strategy compared to the variants runtime.
COST: 2700
PREDICTION: By leveraging the graph structure and pruning high-uncertainty edges, the proposed SFG-based approach significantly improves the efficiency of pseudo-label generation while maintaining acceptable accuracy. However, the efficiency gains may come at the cost of slight performance degradation in certain complex test conditions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Few-Shot Test-Time Object Detection Adaptation with Hierarchical Learning
PROPOSAL: While our previous proposals focused on adapting pre-trained vision-language detectors to unseen test-time object detection tasks, this new proposal tackles the problem of test-time adaptation when only a few labeled examples are available. We introduce a hierarchical learning framework, HL-TTOD, that learns a disentangled representation of the object detection task from these few-shot examples and adapts the pre-trained detector incrementally with a refining meta-learning strategy tailored to handle challenging object detection scenarios such as graded domain shifts.
CONTROLS: We compare our HL-TTOD method against several state-of-the-art few-shot object detection methods, including Prototypical Networks, Matching Network, Relation Network and variants of our proposed method with several different refinement operations. We evaluate the performance of HL-TTOD on benchmark object detection tasks and the Clipart, Waterbirds and more challenging ImageNet-Object tasks within the limited examples condition.
COST: 4500
PREDICTION: Our HL-TTOD framework is expected to achieve state-of-the-art results in test-time object detection adaptation with few-shot examples due to its hierarchical learning strategy and refining meta-learning for handling challenging object detection scenarios. However, the performance may degrade or be overfit several instances particularly in tasks of extreme semantic concept variation cases.

CONTROLS: We will compare AdaVL against state-of-the-art TTAOD methods, including VAT, Co-Training, and Pruner, by reducing these methods' dependence on source statistics and assuming they directly use high-quality pseudo-labels without filtering. Additionally, we will evaluate the effect of varying the ratio of pseudo-labeled training data for AdaVL to maintain a baseline level of pre-trained generalization.
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: We expect AdaVL to outperform previous TTAOD methods in real-world domains under distribution shifts by adapting more efficiently and effectively, and by leveraging the strengths of pre-trained detectors as much as possible. However, the reliability of pseudo-labels remains a challenge, and we expect some effects of noisy pseudo-labels on adaptation performance.

To address this issue, we will modify AdaVL to incorporate sample weighting into the adaptation process: we assign a higher weight to clean pseudo-labels and a lower weight to potential noisy pseudo-labels. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Vision-Language Detector Adaptation via Target-Conditional Prompting
PROPOSAL: 
We propose a novel approach to adapt a pre-trained vision-language detector (e.g. GLIP) during test time, relying on target-conditional prompting to leverage the unlabeled target data. In this method, we dynamically modify the input text prompt to the detector based on the features extracted from the current test image. This adapter is designed to adjust the detector's attention towards the most relevant context within the test image, helping the model learn from target data without relying on source domain knowledge or statistics. We will explore this approach on several real-world benchmark datasets such as KITTI, COCO, and CyClica, comparing it to standard TTAOD methods that rely on source-domain statistics and self-supervised learning.

CONTROLS: Faster R-CNN + Entropy-Aware Adapter, DADA-TC; robustness against different display resolutions and levels of formating

COST: 32000
PREDICTION: Excellent adaptation performance is expected for the target-conditional prompting method, especially on datasets with substantial domain and category shifts. However, potential issues may arise when the detector fails to converge due to aggressive adaptation or noisy test samples.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploiting Sub-Image Masks for Relaxed Pseudo-Labeling
PROPOSAL: 
In situations where pseudo-labeling is unreliable due to noisy or missing data, we propose to use sub-image masks to debounce the sparse and uncertain pseudo-labels. By masking the detector's output and only considering the model confidence scores within the likely target object region, we can generate dense pseudo-labels with higher confidence and precision. Our approach differentiates itself from existing spatial- and channel-based pruning methods, since it focuses on exploiting inherent properties of the image. The sub-image mask will be trained using reinforcement learning, maximizing the expected recall while trading off precision. We will test this method on Cityscapes, ADE20K, and Foggy Cityscapes, comparing it to standard object detection baselines and existing TTAOD methods.

CONTROLS: Selective Context Masking, Anchor-Indicator based detection; hardness-aware    

COST: 48000
PREDICTION: Exploiting sub-image masks is expected to significantly improve pseudo-labeling reliability on real-world benchmarks, thus facilitating faster adaptation. The efficiency of the sub-image mask learning process may vary across datasets due to varying complexity and frequency of pseudo-label noise.

TITLE: Active Learning for Adaptive Detector Pruning
PROPOSAL: 
We propose using active learning for adaptive detector pruning, but instead of using a hybrid confidence-uncertainty sampling strategy, we will utilize a more targeted approach. We will focus on using the aleatoric uncertainty estimated by Monte Carlo dropout to identify the most uncertain regions in the image, and then use a region of interest (ROI) based active learning approach to query the most informative regions. Our goal is to reduce the number of adaptation iterations required and to improve the overall adaptation performance.

CONTROLS: Using uncertainty-based active learning, instead of confidence-based; also using an ROI-based approach

COST: 72000
PREDICTION: Active learning for adaptive detector pruning is expected to improve the overall adaptation performance by reducing the number of adaptation iterations required. However, potential issues may arise when the model fails to converge due to incorrect uncertainty estimates or when the ROI-based approach selects regions that are not representative of the overall image.

TITLE: Adaptive Test-Time Training via Multi-Modal Contrastive Loss
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel test-time adaptation method that uses a contrastive loss to align the feature distributions of the pre-trained vision-language detector and the unlabeled target data, while promoting the detector's robustness against noisy pseudo-labels. The method consists of two main components: a detector-based feature extractor that extracts features from both the input image and its corresponding pseudo-label, and a contrastive loss function that encourages the two features to become similar while pushing apart features from different classes. This approach has the advantage of being source-free, open-set, and efficient in terms of computational resources.
CONTROLS: We compare our method with state-of-the-art TTAOD methods, including CLNet and FGFA, and ablate the effect of different loss weights on the contrastive loss. Additionally, we implement a baseline that fine-tunes the pre-trained detector on the target data without any contrastive loss.
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: Our method should achieve state-of-the-art performance on the target data, especially when the pseudo-labels are noisy or scarce, as the contrastive loss helps to promote robustness against noises and encourages the detector to focus on accurate pseudo-labels. However, the approach might require a careful selection of the loss weights to avoid over-fitting or under-fitting, especially when the target data distribution is far away from the source data distribution.

PROPOSAL: To address the challenge of dealing with noisy or missing pseudo-labels, we propose an adaptive class-agnostic pseudo-label filtering mechanism that dynamically assigns different weights to pseudo-labels based on their confidence. Specifically, we use a learned soft-label matrix to capture the uncertainty of each pseudo-label, and then employ a simple yet effective filtering mechanism to remove pseudo-labels with low confidence. We demonstrate that our filtering mechanism can effectively promote reliance on reliable pseudo-labels and reduce the effect of noisy pseudo-labels.

TITLE: Efficient Online Learning with an Adaptive Pseudo-Label Selective Mechanism
PROPOSAL: To improve the efficiency of online adaptation, we propose an adaptive pseudo-label selective mechanism that dynamically selects the most informative pseudo-labels to update the model, rather than updating the model with all pseudo-labels. Our mechanism uses a learned pseudo-label importance score to rank pseudo-labels based on their relevance to the current test batch, and then selectively updates the model with the top-ranked pseudo-labels. This approach not only reduces the computational overhead of online adaptation but also promotes more robust adaptation performance by focusing on the most relevant pseudo-labels.
CONTROLS: We compare our method with state-of-the-art TTAOD methods, including CLNet and FGFA, and ablate the effect of different ranking methods on the adaptive selective mechanism. Additionally, we implement a baseline that updates the model with all pseudo-labels without any selection mechanism.
COST: 1600
PREDICTION: Our method should improve the efficiency and robustness of online adaptation, especially in scenarios where computational resources are limited. However, the adaptive selective mechanism might require careful tuning of hyperparameters to ensure optimal pseudo-label selection.

Our mechanism uses a learned pseudo-label importance score to rank pseudo-labels based on their relevance to the current test batch, and then selectively updates the model with the top-ranked pseudo-labels. This approach not only reduces the computational overhead of online adaptation but also promotes more robust adaptation performance by focusing on the most relevant pseudo-labels.
CONTROLS: We compare our method with state-of-the-art TTAOD methods, including CLNet and FGFA, and ablate the effect of different ranking methods on the adaptive selective mechanism. Additionally, we implement a baseline that updates the model with all pseudo-labels without any selection mechanism.

PREDICTION: Our method should improve the efficiency and robustness of online adaptation, especially in scenarios where computational resources are limited. However, the adaptive selective mechanism might require careful tuning of hyperparameters to ensure optimal pseudo-label selection.

TITLE: Adversarial Domain Mixing for Conditional Pre-Training of Vision-Language Detectors
PROPOSAL: Employ domain adaptation techniques to generate new synthetic data mixing source and target domain features. Train a GLIP model with the novel mixed data to condition pre-trained detectors for cross-domain generalization. Utilize CYBERCAR, OpenImages, and Cats&Dogs datasets for evaluation, with standard Faster R-CNN TTAOD and vision-language detectors (GLIP and G-DINO) as controls. Use metrics like AP, mAP, and domain shift to investigate the conditional adaptation performance. Domain mixing parameters (e.g., weight balance, data proportion) and sources (e.g., feature extraction) will be explored.
CONTROLS: standard Faster R-CNN TTAOD, ablation study on source/target feature mixing, experiment without conditional pre-training
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: This method can devise new insights into pre-training a generalizable vision-language detector by better exploiting source and target domain information. Conditional pre-training from adversarial domain mixing may improve adaptation performance by up to 18% compared to the baseline Faster R-CNN TTAOD under various real-world scenarios, yet mixing ratios may cause difficulties in convergence without corroborate controls.

PROPOSAL: Develop a learning strategy that balances reliable pseudo-label generation with model's ability to handle class membership uncertainty. TITLE: Target-Specific Adaptation with Confident and Scarce Pseudo Labels
PROPOSAL: To tackle the issue of pseudo labels being scarce or noisy in certain test batches, we propose an adaptation strategy based on the 3D U-Net architecture that balances the trade-off between confident pseudo label selection and the scarcity of pseudo labels. By using a confidence threshold, we select pseudo labels from test batches where confident pseudo labels are abundant, and fallback on abundant image features for adaptation on test batches with few or no confident pseudo labels. We will test this strategy on various benchmarks.
CONTROLS: We will compare our approach against standard self-training methods on benchmarks such as PASCAL VOC, MS COCO, and COCO-OBJ.
COST: 800
PREDICTION: The strategy should achieve higher adaptation performance than standard self-training methods by making use of abundant image features and confident pseudo labels in each batch, while also being more practical and less sensitive to the constraint of scarce or noisy pseudo labels.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Meta-Learning for Object Detection with Early Adaptation and Continuous Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose a meta-learning framework for object detection that enables early adaptation to new target domains and continuous learning during testing. Our approach involves a meta-learner that adapts to the new target domain and a learner that adapts to categories within the target domain. By leveraging episodic training and few-shot learning, our method can learn to adapt quickly to new target domains and fine-tune its performance over continuous testing.
CONTROLS: Compare against state-of-the-art TTAOD methods on benchmarks such as PASCAL VOC and MS COCO, and evaluate the impact of our early adaptation and continuous learning capabilities.
COST: 3000
PREDICTION: Our meta-learning framework should enable object detection with high accuracy and robustness to category shifts, and demonstrate the ability to adapt quickly to new target domains and fine-tune its performance over continuous testing. However, it may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to achieve optimal results.

TITLE: Global-to-Local: Self-Supervised Learning for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel self-supervised learning approach, Global-to-Local (G2L), that learns to adapt from a globally aligned source domain to a locally diverse target domain. G2L leverages a multi-task architecture with hierarchical contrastive learning and autoencoders to align and transfer knowledge between domains. We incorporate a target-domain exploration module to select effective adaptation strategies based on a world batch strategy.
CONTROLS: Compare against state-of-the-art self-supervised and unsupervised domain adaptation methods on benchmarks such as Office-31 and Vadim.
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: Our G2L approach should achieve state-of-the-art performance in unsupervised domain adaptation, and its adaptability and exploration strategy should enable seamless adaptation to diverse target domains. However, the multi-task learning architecture may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to achieve optimal results.

The model is a simple neural network architecture (e.g. a fully connected network) with a fixed capacity of 10,000 parameters. We will train the model using stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with a fixed learning rate of 0.01 and a batch size of 32.
CONTROLS: We will include baselines for the optimal solution, a simple greedy algorithm, and a traditional distance-based algorithm (e.g. Nearest Neighbor). We will also perform a model capacity ablation study by comparing the performance of the model with different capacities (5,000 and 20,000 parameters).

PREDICTION: We expect to see smooth scaling laws in performance as the problem size increases, with the optimal solution remaining unbeaten at smaller instance sizes and the simple greedy algorithm remaining competitive at larger instance sizes. The neural network will likely surpass the traditional distance-based algorithm at moderate instance sizes, but its performance may degrade at larger instance sizes due to the curse of dimensionality.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Independent Scaling of Solution Space and Representation Space in Euclidean TSP
PROPOSAL: We investigate a Euclidean version of the traveling salesman problem, where the search space of permutations of cities has fixed size, and the representation space is fixed-dimensional Euclidean space. We design a synthetic dataset where the solution space is combinatorially scaled by altering the number of cities, while the representation space is scaled by augmenting the dimensionality of the city coordinates. We train a neural network-based solver with a constant capacity (number of parameters) and vary both dataset scales. We measure the relative performance improvement as a function of scaling, and analyze how it depends on the learning algorithm, fixed model capacity, and scaling limits.
CONTROLS: compare to uniform random search, and ablate learning algorithm and model capacity.
COST: 150
PREDICTION: We expect to observe smooth trends with better scalability at low solution space dimensions, but observe bounded gains with no further improvements after a critical scaling limit, consistent with combinatorial explosion in the solution space. We also predict that as the representation space grows, gains will degrade due to the curse of dimensionality. However, this expected trend may not hold for small dimensions where singularities may occur, only appearing as performance outliers.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Modeling Scalability of Neural Network-Based TSP Solvers with Compression Analysis
PROPOSAL: We propose to analyze the performance degradation of neural network-based TSP solvers as they approach their capacity limits by applying techniques from neural network compression. Specifically, we analyze the dropout ratio and depth required for such a solver to degrade steadily as the solution space grows. We synchronize the parameters and counts of sparse neural networks across increasing solution space scales. We train these synchronized networks to observe any early indication of an "unscalable" design. We then rescale the representation space while strictly controlling the solver's capacity using an efficient algorithm for sparsifying the topology of the neural network architecture. We measure the resulting training dynamics and performance on the TSP problem with increasing dimensionality.
CONTROLS: ablate the baseline sparsification method (uniform random dropout vs Bernoulli variational dropout) and compare synchronized performance with the max-depth pruning method.
COST: 234
PREDICTION: Depending on our initial architecture choice, we expect smaller dropout ratios and shallower architectures to emerge naturally in response to increased solution space sizes. However, these greedy reductions in capacity may show a premature loss of the learned, solution-space variance. We predict the deeper, more redundant designs to only fail at higher scaling limits.
